Remember how the widow's two small coins <note>original Latin: "minuta duo viduæ". This is a reference to the "Widow's Mite" from the Gospels (Luke 21:1–4), where a small gift from a poor person is honored above the large donations of the wealthy.</note> were often praised.
Neither do I seek praise for myself by writing, nor rewards;

The time will come when your most celebrated and praiseworthy deeds

<meta>This page follows the dedication to Joachim von Ahlefeld. Having addressed his patron, the author Troels Arnkiel now turns to his general readership to explain the origins, research process, and methodology of his study on North Germanic paganism, specifically following his earlier work on the Golden Horns of Gallehus.</meta>

# To the Christian Reader:

When in the year 1683 I published the *Golden Horn*—found near <term>Tønder</term> <note>original: "Tundern". A town in Southern Jutland where the first of the two famous Golden Horns of Gallehus was discovered in 1639.</note> in our times—and explained it as a memorable antiquity and a monument valued more highly than gold for the pagan idolatry of our ancestors hidden within it, I also promised a separate work on the Cimbrian Pagan Religion to further illuminate the aforementioned Golden Horn. This work would have come to light shortly thereafter, had a dark cloud not risen over us in the following year, when for the sake of my conscience I had to resign my post and temporal welfare. During that time, while visiting the churches of Holstein, I had the opportunity to search through the famous libraries in Lübeck and Hamburg, and otherwise to obtain various books useful for this work from both spiritual and secular sources. In particular, I made frequent use of the Princely Library at Gottorf.

Thus, I have once again taken up my <term>manuscript</term> <note>original: "M. S. C.", an abbreviation for *manuscriptum*.</note> regarding the pagan faith of our ancestors, revised it, and worked it out more thoroughly. I had enough time and leisure for this work following the resignation of my <term>ministry</term> <note>original: "Ministerii". Arnkiel was a pastor who lost his position due to political and religious disputes in the 1680s.</note>, although it was often interrupted by all sorts of adversities and bodily weaknesses. I have endeavored (1) to recount the matter itself in a historical manner, and occasionally, where necessary, to mention in passing what might be argued <term>for and against</term> <note>original Latin: "pro & contra".</note> it. (2) To illustrate everything mainly contained in this work with testimonies, and to append a register at the back of those authors whom I have cited in this work and had in my hands, so that the kind reader may better seek out the <term>sources</term> <note>original Latin: "fontes", meaning the original primary texts or "fountains" of information.</note> themselves and inquire more closely into the matters. (3) To strive for brevity, and to that end, to condense as much as possible what I had initially drafted at great length. Although I had originally intended to always cite the words of the authors themselves, I had to change my mind for fear that the work might become too large and thus make its <term>publication</term> <note>original: "Verlegung", referring to the financial and logistical burden of printing.</note> difficult. Nevertheless, I could not help but present the words of the authors when they were either unusual, or the matter was noteworthy, or controversial, or doubtful, or required further explanation in the text. (4) In controversial matters, to maintain the most probable opinion and modestly decline the opposing view, examining it where necessary; but in doing so, to disparage no one, and for that reason I often omit the names of the authors of opposing opinions. (5) In doubtful things, to conclude nothing, but to proceed <term>problematically</term> <note>In a scholarly context, this means to present the issue as an open question or a problem to be solved rather than a settled fact.</note> and leave the conclusion and judgment to the Christian reader. Should I not have reached the goal in one thing or another, as can easily happen, I will gladly be instructed. If the kind reader would be so good as to first give notice of this privately, I offer to accept such feedback with thanks and to willingly change my opinion if the opponent's reasons are significant. However, if one intends to do this in <term>public writings</term> <note>original Latin: "publicis scriptis".</note>, I ask that Christian moderation be used, and the matter

->itself be modestly examined as a contribution<-
->to the truth.<-

# Preface
## Of the Compelling Reasons to Consider the Pagan Beliefs.

The Apostle reminds his Ephesians that they should remember that they were once Pagans: Remember, he says, that you were formerly Pagans according to the flesh, that at that same time you were without Christ, strangers, and outside the citizenship of Israel, and strangers from the testaments of promise, so that you had no hope and were without GOD in the world: Ephesians 2:11–12. First, the Apostle admonishes his Ephesians to remember their former Paganism; likewise, he also reminds his Corinthians of their Paganism: You know, he says, that you were Pagans, and went along to the dumb idols: 1 Corinthians 12:2. He calls the Pagan gods "dumb idols" because they have mouths and do not speak: Psalm 115:5, 135:16. Secondly, he describes the wretched state of Paganism—that they were at that time without Christ, that is, deprived of the knowledge and merit of Christ and all His benefits; excluded from the community of the Israelite Church; alienated from the testament and <term>covenant of grace</term> <note>The "Gnadenbund" or Covenant of Grace is a central concept in Lutheran theology, referring to God's promise of salvation through faith in Christ.</note> which GOD established with His people through His Holy Word and Sacrament; and lived without God, that is, without knowledge and fear of the true GOD, whereby they had no hope of salvation. We cannot comply with this admonition of the Apostle in any other way than by considering the Pagan <term>idolatries</term> <note>Arnkiel uses "Abgöttereyen" to describe the worship of false gods, a term common in 17th-century polemical history.</note> of our ancestors: <note>original: "Jucunda est memoria pristinæ miseriæ, si ea jam est superata. Ideo Paulus Ephesios suos meminisse vult, quod quondam gentes fuerint. Facit hæc memoria nos DEO, pro exoptata liberatione gratos, & præsenti forte contentos. Quemadmodum autem hæc memoria in omnibus est necessaria, & utilis: ita inprimis in rebus spiritualibus, sæpe inculcanda est."</note> The memory of former misery is pleasant if it has already been overcome. Therefore, Paul wants his Ephesians to remember that they were once Gentiles. This memory makes us grateful to GOD for our longed-for liberation, and perhaps content with the present. Just as this memory is necessary and useful in all things, so it must be frequently impressed upon us, especially in spiritual matters: Balduin <note>Friedrich Balduin (1575–1627) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and professor at Wittenberg known for his biblical commentaries.</note> in his *Commentary on this passage*, page 889.

<summary>In this preface, the author justifies the study of northern paganism as a spiritual exercise, quoting St. Paul to argue that Christians should remember their ancestors' "wretched" idolatrous past to better appreciate their current salvation.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Paganism, Theology, St. Paul, Idolatry, Friedrich Balduin, Church History, Covenant of Grace</keywords>

# Preface

Accordingly, in the preparation of this work, I have endeavored—following this Apostolic admonition—to remember that our ancestors were once Pagans and lived in abominable <term>idolatries</term> <note>German: *Abgöttereyen*. In this context, it refers to the worship of false gods, a central concern for 17th-century theologians studying pre-Christian history.</note>. This should primarily serve us so that, by contemplating the Pagan religion, we may learn to recognize:

I. **Their wretched condition:** They walk in abominable idolatries (1 Peter 4:3) and sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Isaiah 42:7, Luke 1:79). They know nothing of GOD, but instead hold fire, or water, or the stars to be gods; they call the works of men "God," such as gold and silver artfully prepared, and images of animals and men made of wood, which they worship (Wisdom 13:1, 2, 10). Thus they have transformed the glory of GOD into an image resembling men and irrational animals, living moreover in Sodomitic and other abominable sins (Romans 1:23, 26). They are wretched people (Wisdom 13:10) under the power of Satan (Acts 26:18). They sacrifice to devils, are in the fellowship of devils, and drink the cup of devils (1 Corinthians 10:20). They worship devils and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which can neither see nor hear, nor walk (Revelation 9:20). They are unmerciful murderers of their sons, who eat human flesh and drink abominable blood to show their devotion, and parents strangle their own children (Wisdom 12:5, 6) and burn their sons and daughters with fire for their gods (as a <term>burnt offering</term> <note>German: *Brandopffer*</note>) (Deuteronomy 12:31). 

Just as our ancestors once lived in such terrifying darkness, many Pagans in the Old and New Worlds still live this way today. Thus, it has happened—doubtless by the special permission of Almighty GOD—that in these latter times such writings (concerning Pagan idolatry) have come to light, from which posterity can learn in how great and dark a night the Pagans lived. The noble Casparus Barthius writes: *Doubtless by the singular permission and indulgence of Almighty God, such writings have been brought to light in this final age—not having been extinguished through the calamities of so many centuries—so that posterity might learn in what great night mortality once lived, while despising the fear of God.* <note>Original Latin: "Haud dubie Dei omnipotentis singulari permissione, atque indultu, extremô ævô in lucem redacta sunt talia scripta, per tot seculorum calamitates non extincta, ut discere posteritas possit, quanta in nocte Dei timorem contemnens mortalitas quondam vixerit." Caspar von Barth (1587–1658) was a renowned German scholar and philologist.</note> Christian love now requires us to have heartfelt compassion and mercy for such poor, blinded people, and to call upon dear GOD on their behalf, that He might grant His grace to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to GOD, to receive forgiveness of sins and the inheritance among those who are sanctified through faith (Acts 26:18).

II. **The blind zeal in serving their idols:** It is a wonder how zealous and devout they were in their sacrifices and idolatry, and how much effort and expense they applied to it. Consider how they held their feast days and their temples and altars so holy, how they fell down there before their idols to worship them in the deepest humility, and to appease them through so many kinds of sacrifice. Finally, consider how they [supported] their priests and idol-servants so rich-

<meta>Catchword: rich- [richly]</meta>

# Preface

They believed that the soul is immortal, and that our hour of death is determined by GOD. They believed that the world would perish, the dead would rise again, and that in the next world the pious would be rewarded, but the ungodly would be punished. These are the honorable heathens <note>German: *erbahre Heyden*; refers to ancient Greeks and Romans who lived morally according to natural law.</note>, so named to distinguish them from the barbaric heathens, as they applied themselves to virtue much more than most among the Christians. *Some of the Gentiles were more observant of many virtues than the Christians* <note>original Latin: "Gentilium aliqui multarum Virtutum observantiores fuerunt, quam Christiani"</note>: Balduinus on **1 Corinthians 5, p. 345**. It is a wonder how virtuously they taught and lived: one may read what the pagan Valerius Maximus <note>A 1st-century Roman author known for his collection of historical anecdotes.</note>, as well as Langius, among others, have written about this, and what has been collected regarding their heartfelt sayings on virtue by Erasmus, Neander, Mirandula, Langerius, Gruterus, and Kirchmannus. For this reason, the ancient Church Father Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea, a 4th-century bishop.</note> wrote a small book: *On the Reading of Pagan Books* <note>original Latin: "De legendis libris Ethnicorum"</note>. In it, he exhorts us to read pagan writings and reminds us how they should incite us to virtue. In this booklet, he also gathered all sorts of beautiful moral and life-sayings from the majority of the Greek writings of the pagan philosophers. In this, St. Basil served as a guiding light to the aforementioned collectors. These honorable heathens will rise on the Last Day and condemn the atheists and children of Belial <note>A biblical term for wicked or worthless people; here referring to those who reject all religious and social order.</note> among us, who cling to the "doctrines of demons": **1 Timothy 4:1**, and who—either inwardly in their hearts or outwardly in words or deeds—deny GOD’S essence or providence, and regard religion as nothing more than a political tool to keep the common people in check. They reject spiritual and secular government, as well as the holy estate of marriage, and conversely permit all manner of unchastity, imagining that humans die by chance like cattle, perishing body and soul together, never to rise again or be rewarded according to their works. Ask among the heathens: "Who has ever heard the like, that the virgin Israel (the people of GOD) does such horrible things?" **Jeremiah 18:13**.

# Objections:

Although the benefits that arise from the study of pagan religion are clearly evident from what has been said, and the holy Church Fathers have preceded us in this, and our church teachers and other learned men have followed in their footsteps, there are nevertheless those among them **who think nothing is right except what they do themselves** <note>original Latin: *Qui, nisi quod ipsi faciunt, nihil rectum putant*; a quote from the Roman playwright Terence</note>, as the comic poet says. These people slander and reject this and similar work based on the following reasons:

**I.** Because God commanded in Exodus 23:13: "Make no mention of the names of other gods, neither let it be heard out of your mouth." Martin Luther answers: "You shall not preach of any saints as gods who help you, nor give thanks to them, but to God alone. For 'mentioning' is the same as preaching, praising, thanking, and practicing divine service: **Do this in remembrance of me**" <note>original Latin: *Ut hoc facite, in mei commemorationem*</note>, as Luther writes in his <gloss>marginal note on this passage</gloss>. To mention the names of idols is not forbidden here as a simple matter of fact; for Moses himself and the prophets mentioned them in their sermons against pagan idolatry. Rather, the prohibition means that we should not mention the names of idols religiously—that is, we should neither honor nor fear them. This is explained in the following verse 25: "You shall not worship their gods, nor serve them." Our poets and rhetoricians act against this divine command when they believe they have beautifully adorned their writings by citing the names of pagan idols, or even praising and calling upon them. **Let Christians see here how finely they adorn their poems, in which they sometimes invoke the fictitious gods of the Gentiles—Jupiter, Apollo, etc.** <note>original Latin: *Viderint hic Christiani, quàm belle ornent sua poemata, in quibus quandoque Deos fictitios Gentium Jovem, Apollinem &c. invocant*; commentary by Lucas Osiander, a prominent Lutheran theologian</note>.

**II.** Because God commands the rooting out of pagan idols and abominations: Deuteronomy 7:5, 25 and 12:3. Therefore, one should not seek them out again. **Answer:** The divine command to root out idols was given so that one should not cling to or serve them, but not so that one should tell or write nothing about them. Rooting out and planting are opposites (Ecclesiastes 3:2), but rooting out and recounting what has been rooted out are not. Pagan religion is and remains rooted out, even if it is described in a historical manner and its abominations and horrors are presented. Furthermore, the refutation of paganism is a way of rooting it out; indeed, the mere account is a refutation.

**III.** Because in the fourth Carthaginian Council held in the year 398 by 214 bishops, Canon 16 forbade the reading of the books of the heathens: **That a Bishop shall not read the books of the Gentiles** <note>original Latin: *Ut Episcopus libros Gentium non legat*</note>, as cited in the <term>Magdeburg Centuries</term> <note>A massive 16th-century history of the Christian Church from a Lutheran perspective</note> Vol. 4, ch. 9, p. 874, and by Carranza in his *Summary of the Councils*, p. 169. **Answer:** Here, it is not private reading that is forbidden, but public reading in the church. As Philipp <note>Likely referring to Philipp Melanchthon</note> writes, in his time a monk in Tübingen supposedly read and explained <term>Aristotle's Ethics</term> <note>A foundational work of secular moral philosophy</note> publicly in the church.

**IV.** Because St. Jerome was reminded by God through a divine revelation not to read pagan books, as he himself testifies in his *Letter to Eustochium, on the Guarding of Virginity*, Vol. 1. **Answer:** Jerome himself admits in his *Apology against Rufinus* that it was a dream and a **mockery of the night** <note>original Latin: *ludibrium noctis*; a nocturnal illusion</note>. He intended by this to warn Eustochium against the excessive reading of pagan books, in which Jerome himself may have been too deeply immersed. They call it a **fabrication** <note>original Latin: *Figmentum vocant*</note> in the *Magdeburg Centuries*, Vol. IV, Church History, ch. 10, p. 1209.

Idolatry is of two kinds: a gross and a subtle idolatry. **Gross idolatry** is that which errs regarding the Person of **GOD**, where creatures are elevated to the throne of God and honored as divine instead of the one true God. Thus, the pagans deified the stars, deceased heroes, and evil spirits, and worshiped them as gods. This entire work deals with this gross idolatry of the pagans. Dr. Hunnius <note>Aegidius Hunnius (1550–1603), a prominent Lutheran theologian known for his defense of orthodoxy.</note> reckons the worship of deceased saints in the Papacy <note>Original: "Pabstthumb." A common term used by Protestant writers of this era to refer to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> as gross idolatry.

**Subtle idolatry** is that which errs in the service of God; while the one true **GOD** is indeed acknowledged, He is not honored and served as He commanded in His Word, according to Matthew 15:9. This occurs in the Papacy, where one wishes to honor and serve God through holy images. Likewise, it is a subtle idolatry when one prays and sings, confesses and takes communion with the mouth, while the heart remains unbelieving and unrepentant, as in Matthew 15:8. Similarly

# Cimbrian [History]

Noah <note>The biblical patriarch; in the 17th century, European history was often traced back to the sons of Noah</note>, coming out of Asia into Europe, caused the descendants of Japheth to move toward the north, first into Germany and further into this Cimbrian region <note>The peninsula of Jutland in modern-day Denmark</note>; from there, they sent their colonies into the northern kingdoms and populated them. *D. ## Chapter IV
# What our ancestors believed regarding the one true GOD and the other idols.

->Contents:<-

1. God has revealed Himself to the heathens through the external and internal Book of Nature.
2. The Cimbri <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic people from whom the author traces Northern ancestry.</note> believed in one single God.
3. As did the philosophers.
4. Likewise the heathens as a whole.
5. How our ancestors described the one true GOD.
6. They believed that the single, most high GOD sired other gods.

<column-break/>

7. And that these gods each have oversight over particular things.
8. The Romans and Greeks also believed this.
9. On the distinction between the heathen gods.
10. The Papacy <note>original: "Pabstthumb." The author is writing from a Protestant perspective, likely Lutheran, and compares Catholic saint-veneration to pagan polytheism.</note> has adopted this heathen idolatry.
11. As have the Valentinian heretics and the Turks <note>A common early modern reference to Muslims.</note>.

That it is known that GOD exists is manifest to them (the heathens): "For GOD has shown it to them," writes the Apostle to the Gentiles <note>original: "Heyden-Apostel," referring to St. Paul</note> in Romans 1:19. He shows that the knowledge of GOD was revealed to the heathens by GOD through the light or "Book of Nature," specifically: (1) through the **external Book of Nature**, described in the great architecture of the world, where all creatures bear witness to their Creator. "God’s invisible nature is perceived through His works, namely in the creation of the world," says the Apostle in the aforementioned place. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> agrees: "The invisible God," he says, "is seen from His works." <note>original: "Aristot. lib. 12. Metaph. cap. 6. & 7. Autor lib. de mundo, cap. 6." refers to Aristotle’s Metaphysics and the pseudo-Aristotelian work "On the Universe."</note> (2) Through the **internal Book of Nature**, written in our hearts, where human knowledge and conscience convince us that there is a GOD: Romans 2:15. In this, the worldly-wise heathens agree: that the knowledge of GOD is naturally implanted in all people. <note>original: "Cic. lib. 2. de Nat. Deorum num. 15. Seneca Epist. 117." Referring to Cicero's "On the Nature of the Gods" and Seneca’s "Moral Letters."</note>

The highest and greatest among all gods. This is testified by our ancestors in the *Edda* <note>The *Prose Edda*, a 13th-century collection of Norse mythology compiled by Snorri Sturluson.</note> Part 1, Fable 3, with these words: Who is the highest and oldest among all gods? Answer: The oldest among all gods is called: **All-Father!** This **GOD** lives in eternity, governs His entire kingdom, and understands or counsels for everything, what is great and small, high and low. He created Heaven and Earth. Of our Vandalic peoples <note>A reference to the Germanic tribes whom the author considers ancestors.</note>, Helmold <note>Helmold of Bosau, a 12th-century historian who chronicled the conversion of the Slavic and Germanic tribes.</note> writes: That they admit there is one single **GOD** who rules in heaven over the other gods, and that He is mighty above others, but cares only for heavenly matters, leaving earthly things to be commanded by the other idols: Helmold, Book 1, Chapter 84.

§. 3. In this, all pagan philosophers have agreed: that there was only one single true **GOD**. In this bickering and dispute, and manifold opinion, you may see that all laws and opinions agree that there is one single **GOD**, a King and Father of all things, to whom many other gods are joined, who are the sons of the highest God and, as it were, His colleagues. In this the Greeks agree with the barbarians, the inhabitants of the mainland with those of the islands, and the wise with the fools, writes Maximus Tyrius <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher who sought to harmonize different religious traditions.</note> in Dissertation 1. Whoever desires further information on this should read Micraelius <note>Johannes Micraelius (1597–1658), a German historian and theologian who wrote on the history of religions.</note>, Book 2 of the *Ethnophylacium* <note>original: "Ethnoph." — Micraelius's work on the religions of the world.</note>, Dialogue 3, Chapter 10, following page 18; he piles up the testimonies of the pagan poets and priests, of the Oriental and Occidental philosophers with all their sects and schools, as well as the European, Asian, and African peoples concerning the one true **GOD**. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential early Christian theologian.</note> in *The City of God* <note>original: "Civ. Dei"</note> Book 6, Chapter 1, recounts: That the philosophers recognized the one true **GOD** and rejected the multitude of gods; but out of fear of the common people, they did not dare to preach this publicly. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> in *Against Apion* <note>original: "cont. Apionem"</note> Book 2, page 852, writes: That Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Plato, and the Stoic philosophers taught correctly about the one single being of **GOD**; but because of the preconceived erroneous opinion of the common rabble (who firmly believed in the multitude of gods), they were afraid to present this doctrine publicly.

It appears that among our ancestors, some news remained from the Gospel preached in the Northern world by the Apostles or apostolic men regarding the great mystery: that **GOD** the Father begat His only-begotten Son from eternity. This mystery was not entirely unknown to the heathens; of this, Iamblichus writes in *On the Mysteries, chapter 39, page 154*: That the first **GOD** is a father of the first **God** whom he begets, who is His exemplar and pattern, and is called His son. Otherwise, this name of God, "All-Father," was common among the heathens. # Cimbrian
<meta>catchword: is</meta>

Heathens can be more conveniently divided into two groups according to the distinction between essential and non-essential things. In the first group are the idols which belong to the essential or self-standing things, and these are separated into different classes. The first class of gods is in the heavens, comprising the stars and comets; these are called Celestial Gods, among whom the sun and moon are the most prominent. The second class of idols is in the air; to this belong certain natural as well as supernatural *meteors* <note>In the historical sense, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including lightning, rainbows, and clouds.</note>, which might be called Air-Gods. The third class is on earth, which is varied: for here, first among men, is the family of heroes and heroines: such as **Thor**, **Othin** <note>Odin</note>, **Fro** <note>Freyr</note>, **Wagnofft** <note>Likely Vagnhofde, a giant or hero from Norse mythology.</note>, **Twisco** <note>Tuisto, the legendary ancestor of the Germanic peoples mentioned by Tacitus.</note>, **Ermenseul** <note>Irminsul, a sacred pillar-like object or deity of the Saxons.</note> etc. Likewise **Freya**, **Hertha**, **Weeda**, **Foste** etc. Similarly, the great gods and goddesses of the Greeks and Romans, whom **Ennius** <note>Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet.</note> included in these verses:

> ->Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,<-
> ->Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo,<-
<note>original Latin: "Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars, / Mercurius, Jovis, Neptunus, Vulcanus, Apollo"</note>

They are called *Dii Superi*, or Over-Earthly Gods. Secondly, there is the family of various irrational animals, such as snakes and dragons, and other beasts. Thirdly, the families of high mountains and trees, which were at the very least symbolic idols. The fourth class is in the water; here belong the so-called sirens and mermen, and other sea-wonders; these are called Water-Gods. The fifth class is the holy altar and sacrificial fire, and other unnatural or supernatural flames. The sixth class of gods is in Hell—that is, the evil spirits, from which all idolatry has its primary origin. These are the hellish idols, called *Dii inferi*, or Under-earthly Gods, under which names **Pluto** and **Proserpina** are otherwise usually understood. Indeed, the heathens have held the heavens, earth, air, water, fire, hell, and everything wondrous and supernaturally produced within these elements to be gods: **Prudentius**, Book 1, *Against Symmachus*, verse 297:

> ->Whatever the wonderful earth, sea, and sky bring forth,<-
> ->These they took for gods: the hills, seas, rivers, and flames.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quicquid humus, pelagus, coelum mirabile gignunt, / Id duxêre deos, colles, freta, flumina, flammas."</note>

# Cimbrian

<note>The term "Cimbrian" refers to the Cimbri, an ancient Germanic tribe. In this period, scholars often used "Cimbrian" as a broad label for the Northern or Germanic peoples and their ancient culture.</note>

The heathens can be more fittingly divided into two groups based on the distinction between essential and non-essential things. In the first group are the idols <note>The author uses the word *Götzen* (idols) to emphasize his view that these were false gods compared to the Christian God.</note> which belong to essential or independent things, and are separated into different classes.

The first class of gods is in the heavens; it includes the stars and comets, which are called **Heavenly Gods**, among which the **Sun** and **Moon** are the most prominent.

The second class of idols is in the air; to this belong certain natural as well as supernatural *meteors* <note>original: *Meteora*. In the 17th century, this term referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, which might be called **Air-Gods**.

The third class is on earth, which is diverse: for here, firstly among humans, is the family of heroes and heroines: such as **Thor**, **Othin** <note>Odin</note>, **Fro** <note>Freyr</note>, **Wagnofft**, **Twisco**, **Ermenseul** <note>Irminsul</note> etc. Likewise **Freya**, **Hertha**, **Meda**, **Foste**, etc. Likewise the great gods and goddesses of the Greeks and Romans, whom **Ennius** <note>An early Roman poet (c. 239–169 BC) who famously listed the twelve principal Roman deities.</note> included in these verses:

->*Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,*<-
->*Mercury, Jove, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo,*<-

These are called *Dii Superi* <note>original: "Dii Superi" — the gods above</note>, or **Upper-Earthly Gods**. Secondly, there is the family of various irrational animals, such as snakes and dragons, and other beasts. Thirdly, the families of high mountains and trees, which were at the very least symbolic idols.

The fourth class is in the water; here belong the so-called **Sirens** and mermen and other sea-wonders; these are called **Water-Gods**.

The fifth class is the holy altar and sacrificial fire, and other unnatural or supernatural flames.

The sixth class of gods is in Hell, that is, the evil spirits, from which all idolatry had its first origin. These are called the **Hellish Idols**, *Dii inferi* <note>original: "Dii inferi" — the gods below</note>, or **Under-earthly Gods**, under which names **Pluto** and **Proserpina** are usually understood. Indeed, the heathens considered the heavens, earth, air, water, fire, hell, and everything wondrous and supernatural produced within these elements to be gods: as **Prudentius** <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD) who wrote against paganism.</note> says in book 1 of *Against Symmachus*, verse 297:

> *Whatever the earth, the sea, the wondrous sky bring forth,*
> *They took as gods: the hills, the straits, the rivers, the flames.*
<note>original Latin: "Quicquid humus, pelagus, coelum mirabile gignunt, / Id duxêre deos, colles, freta, flumina, flammas."</note>

<header>Cimbrian</header>

There is no people among men so wild and barbaric that they should not know that one must have a God, even if they do not know what is fitting to have for a God, writes Cicero in Book 1 of *On the Laws*, Chapter 8, and Book 2 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, Number 15 <note>original Latin titles: "lib. 1. de Leg. cap. 8. & lib. 2. de Nat. Deor. num. 15." Cicero was a Roman statesman and philosopher whose works were standard texts for understanding natural theology</note>. Likewise, our ancestors under heathendom knew from the light of nature <term>light of nature: the idea that human reason alone, without divine revelation, can deduce certain truths like the existence of a creator</term> that there truly is a God who must be kept before one’s eyes. However, who and what this God is, they did not perceive from the light of nature. Therefore, they stumbled so greatly in the recognition of the true God that they took the creatures for gods instead of the Creator. In this, they followed their external senses and their rational arguments more than their internal ones. For when they saw the great lights of heaven—the sun and the moon—and considered their bright radiance, swift course, powerful influence, immense size, and heavenly throne, they regarded them as idols and assigned divine honor to them. Cilicius <note>likely a reference to a historical source or commentator</note> Book 1 of *B. D.*, Chapter 18.

§. 2. Of the Germans (to whom the incorporated Cimbrian peoples belong), the first Roman Emperor reports that they held the sun, the moon, and fire to be gods, which they saw before their eyes: Julius Caesar, Book 6 of the *Gallic War*, page 127 <note>original Latin: "J. Cæsar lib 6. Bell. Gall. p. 127." Caesar's account is one of the earliest written records of Germanic tribes</note>. From this, Philippus Cluverius <note>a prominent 17th-century geographer and historian</note> wishes to conclude that the Germans honored the one true God in a Trinity of persons under the image of the sun, the moon, and fire; and that they signified God the Father through the sun, God the Son through the moon, and God the Holy Spirit through the fire: Cluverius, Book 1 of *German Antiquities*, Chapter 29 <note>original Latin: "Cluver. lib. 1. Antiq. Germ. cap. 29."</note>. This would be a desirable thought, but it cannot be proven. The Emperor says that the Germans only respect those as gods whom they see before their eyes. Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian</note> writes of the Egyptians that they likewise honored these three gods—the sun, the moon, and fire—under the names Osiris, Isis, and Vulcan: Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 2. From this, one could just as validly conclude that the Egyptians honored the triune true God under said names, but it is without foundation. What fellowship or relationship does the sun, the moon, and fire have with the three persons of the Godhead more than other creatures which the Germans and other peoples also deified? Vossius, Book 1 of *Gentile Theology*, Chapter 37 <note>original Latin: "Vossius lib. 1. Theolog. Gent. cap. 37." Gerardus Vossius was a leading 17th-century scholar of classical religion</note>.

## §. 3.
The Cimbrian lands <note>likely referring to the Jutland peninsula and surrounding northern German territories</note> have been inhabited from time immemorial by the Goths, Saxons, and Wends; among all of them, the worship of the stars as idols was prevalent. For this reason, among them and all Germanic peoples, the last and first days of the week were named after the two great lights of heaven: Sunday and Monday. Regarding the Goths and Danes, this is recorded by Huitfeldt in the *Chronicle of the Kingdom of Denmark*, page 1 <note>original: "Witf. in Chron. M. p. 1." Arild Huitfeldt was a Danish historian</note>. King Canute the Great of Denmark, upon the introduction of Christianity, issued a decree that no one should worship the sun and the moon: cited by Geusius in *Human Victims*, chapter 20, page 445, from the *Political Laws of Canute the Great*, chapter 5 <note>original: "Victimæ humanæ... ex leg. Polit. Canuti M."</note>. How our Cimbrian Saxons honored the sun and the moon, and depicted the sun in male form and the moon in female form, is recounted by Worm in Book 1 of *Monuments*, chapter 4 <note>original: "Worm. lib. 1. Monument. cap. 4." Ole Worm was a famous Danish physician and antiquarian</note>, and Rossæus in Part 1 of *Religions of the World*, question 2, page 192 and following. The Vandal peoples were also devoted to this idolatry of the stars, as Peter von Dusburg writes concerning the Prussian Wends in Chapter 3 of the *Chronicle of Prussia*, chapter 5.

## §. 4.
The ancient Cimbri carried an ox's head in their coat of arms, as Plutarch writes in the *Life of Marius*. On the island of Gotland, various types of old coins, minted with a large ox's head, have been excavated; Strelou testifies to this in the preface of his *Guthlandic Chronicle* addressing the reader, and he further recalls that he himself possessed such excavated coins. Through this horned ox's head, they—in my opinion—represented their idol, the new moon, which is called a "two-horned light" by the poets because it first curves into the shape of horns, as Pliny says in Book 2 of *Natural History*, chapter 9 <note>original: "Plinius lib. 2. N. H. cap. 9."</note>. For the image of the moon was a horned ox's head, as Vossius notes in Book 2 of *Gentile Theology*, chapter 21. The goddess Isis is depicted with ox horns: Herodotus, Book 2, Number 46, page 114. However, Isis is the moon: Selden, *Syntagma* 1, chapter 3, page 53. Therefore, our Cimbrian Goths, or "Guthen," used to offer a sacrifice to the moon at the new light <note>the new moon</note>: Strelou in the *Gothic Chronicle*, page 12. It appears that this moon-sacrifice was an ox-head, for our ancestors were in the practice of sacrificing the heads of animals to their idols: Adam of Bremen in *On the Situation of Denmark and the Northern Realms*, page 153 <note>original: "Adamus B. de Situ Daniæ, & Reg. Sept. p. 153."</note>; Huitfeldt in the *Chronicle of the Kingdom of Denmark*, page 2. Likewise, Diodorus reports of the Egyptians that they fashioned horns upon the head of the image of the moon, and to the same a horned

### §. 7.
Not only the common people among the aforementioned heathens, but also their most distinguished philosophers have regarded these heavenly lights as gods. Likewise, Anaximander teaches (in Alessandro Alessandri, Book 6, Chapter 26, folio 383). Porphyry, in Book 2 of *On Sacrifices*, Chapter 1, reminds us that among the gods in the heavens, the Sun and Moon are the most distinguished. §. 8. Because of this idolatry, the mere names of certain cities still remain. Thus, Monsburg in the County of Cilli, the city of Monheim in Swabia, and the village of Mondorp on the Vistula are said to have originally received their names from the Moon <note>German: *Mond*</note>, as Schefferus indicates in *Upsalia*, Chapter 8. It is left to the kind reader’s consideration whether, among the following parish villages in the Kingdom of Denmark—Monsted, Solsted, Solberg, Soling, Solum, Solerup, Solröd, Solagger, etc.—some may have originally received their names from the worship of the Sun and Moon that was formerly practiced in these places during the era of paganism. It should be noted here that the Danish and all Northern peoples, like the Romans <note>original: "Lateiner" (Latins)</note>, call the Sun *Sol*.

## §. 12.
In the early church, Christians were falsely accused by the pagans of this same idolatry—as if they worshipped the sun—as Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)</note> testifies in his *Apology*, chapter 16. He added the reason for this false accusation with these words: "From this arose the suspicion, because it became known that we pray toward the region of the east." <note>original: "Inde suspicio, quod innotuerit, nos ad orientis regionem precari."</note> This suspicion, he says, arose because the pagans learned that we turn toward the rising of the sun during prayer. The reason why the first Christians turned toward the morning, or the rising sun, during the performance of prayer is attributed by the Church Fathers <note>The influential theologians of the early Christian Church</note>—among other reasons—to the lost earthly Paradise located in the East. They turned toward it in prayer and longed for the heavenly Paradise (which was foreshadowed by the earthly one): Basil, *Book on the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 1, page 189 and following; the author of *Questions to Antiochus* under the name of Athanasius, question 37; John of Damascus, book 4, *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 13; Pseudo-Clement, book 2, *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 61; Thomas Aquinas, part 2, question 84, article 13.

## §. 13.
The reasons which moved the pagans to consider the sun and moon as gods are, as Gerardus Joannes Vossius <note>A Dutch classical scholar and theologian (1577–1649)</note> notes: Firstly, their high heavenly throne and seat in the heavens, which was considered divine. Secondly, their immense size: for the sun, according to Ptolemy’s <note>An 2nd-century Greek mathematician and astronomer</note> calculation, is said to be 166 times larger than the earth, which itself is 5,400 German miles <note>A historical unit of distance; one German mile was approximately 7.5 kilometers</note> in size. Thirdly, its rapid course: for the sun is said to travel nearly two hundred and fifty thousand German miles <note>The original "drittehalb hundert tausend" is an archaic German fraction meaning two and a half hundred thousand</note> in the sky every hour. Fourthly, its powerful influence and effect on all elements and creatures through its bright radiance, penetrating heat and warmth, and other hidden powers, by which all things live and move to a certain measure. Fifthly, the constant distinction of times, days, and years: Vossius, book 2, *Theology of the Gentiles*, chapters 2 and 18. These reasons are touched upon by Aurelius Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348 – c. 413 AD)</note> in book 1, *Against Symmachus*, verse 310 and following.

...stars were living, rational beings: "All stars live, and possess rational souls, and are therefore indisputably gods." <note>original: "Sidera omnia vivere, atque rationales animas habere, & ideo sine controversia Deos esse."</note> The stars all live and have rational souls, and for that reason, they are undisputedly gods; so writes **Augustine** in *The City of God*, Book 4, Chapter 11, regarding the pagans. **Tanner** <note>Adam Tanner (1572–1632), a Jesuit professor of theology and mathematics</note> agrees with the pagans on this point, as he deems it proper to honor the stars with a holy religious service, provided that they live, possess reason, and exist in God's grace: *Tanner, Dissertation 4 on the Heavens.* The most prominent pagans—the Chaldeans, Persians, Egyptians, Arabs, the Greeks, and the Pythagorean, Platonic, Stoic, and Epicurean *philosophers*—are of this opinion: that the stars possess life and reason. Likewise, the Jewish Rabbis, as well as several among the ancient Church and school teachers, held this view: *as cited by the Conimbricenses in Aristotle's Book 2 on the Heavens, Chapter 1, Question 1; Alsted, Book 20 of the Encyclopedia, Chapter 2, § 5.* This opinion was so deeply rooted among the Greeks that even **Anaxagoras** was accused of godlessness <note>or "impiety"</note> by the Athenians and condemned to death because he held the sun to be a lifeless creature: *Diogenes Laërtius, Book 2 on the Lives of the Philosophers, Chapter 14, pages 87/89; Augustine, The City of God, Book 18, Chapter 41.* 

The (1) **reason** which brought the pagan philosophers to these thoughts, such that they attributed life and understanding to the stars, is their natural spatial movement. They believed that nothing could move naturally from one place to another unless they were living creatures. This argument persuaded **Aristotle** to the extent that he attributed the movement of the stars to angels. The (2) **reason** is the appearance of a human face in the body of the sun and the moon, about which **Plutarch** disputes in the book *On the Face in the Moon*, Volume 2, and *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book 2, Chapter 30, and the *Conimbricenses* in the previously cited work, Chapter 7, Question 4, Article 2. I have cited various opinions regarding this in: *Dissertation 3 on the Philosophy of Epicurus, Chapter 6, number 12.*

§. 17. That the sun and the moon were called by different names and religiously honored by various peoples—and that even within a single nation, their powers and properties were indicated by many names—is beyond all doubt. However, the claim that all pagan gods and goddesses belong to this category, and that the sun and moon are meant by all their names, is mere speculation <note>The original German uses "Deuteley," a dismissive term for a strained or over-elaborate interpretation.</note>. For one thing, it is certain that the pagans had many heroes and heroines who, after death, were counted among the gods and goddesses and honored in a divine manner—entities that are as different from the sun and moon as heaven is from earth. When the holy Church Fathers of the early church refuted pagan religion and demonstrated its folly by pointing to the multitude of their idols, the *pagan philosophers* invented this speculation to explain the many names of idols as referring to the sun and the moon and their various effects and qualities. **Seneca** <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman.</note>, on the other hand, goes further <note>literally "climbs higher"</note> and wants these names of idols explained as referring to the one true God. His names, he says, can be as many as his offices are varied. Our people (meaning the **Stoics**) believe that this God is Father *Liber, Hercules,* and *Mercury*: *Seneca, book 4, On Benefits, chapters 7 & 8.*

§. 18. As for what **Julius Caesar** writes about the Germans—that in addition to the sun and the moon, they also considered fire to be an idol—this is without doubt to be understood as a symbolic idol, through which they honored the sun as a fiery being, following the example of the Persians and Chaldeans. Subsequently, however, this symbolic idol became a literal one, so that fire was honored as an idol by almost all pagans, or at least by the common man: *Vossius, book 2, Gentile Theology <note>original Latin: "Theologia Gentilis," a study of pagan beliefs</note>, chapter 64.*

# Chapter VI
## On the Water-Idols of Our Ancestors.
### Contents:

<columns>2</columns>

1. From where this idolatry originated.
2. The Chaldeans and Egyptians dispute among themselves whether fire or water is the highest God.
3. On the dwelling, form, function, and names of these idols.
4. Niord—a sea-god—is the Roman Neptune.

5. Ranulle <note>Likely referring to the Norse goddess Rán.</note>—a sea-goddess—is the Greeks' Thetis and Amphitrite.
6. King Hadding in Denmark is said to have slain a sea-idol.

---

The situation with water was exactly the same as with fire: initially, it was also a symbolic idol under which the water-gods were honored, because—according to their superstition—they were said to have had their dwelling in the water. Eventually, among the common people, the water itself likewise became an actual idol. Thus the heathens held both elements, fire and water, to be gods and called them elemental gods <note>Original: "genial-Götter." In this historical context, "genial" refers to *genii* or spirits associated with the generative powers of nature.</note>: <term>Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 6, chapter 4</term> <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523) was a Neapolitan jurist who wrote extensively on ancient customs.</note>. Which the wise man punishes: <term>Wisdom of Solomon 13, verse 2</term> <note>This biblical text critiques those who "deemed either fire, or wind... or the great water, to be the gods which govern the world."</note>. This idolatry appears to have arisen because some held fire and others water to be the origin of all things, from which the world was created and into which the world would be dissolved upon its destruction: <term>Polydore Vergil, Book 1, On Inventors, chapter 2</term> <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555) was an Italian humanist priest who wrote on the origins of things.</note>. On this basis, the Scythian peoples sought to maintain against the Egyptians that their nation was older, because their land—on account of its coldness and higher elevation—was brought forth first before all others, either from fire or from water: <term>Justin, Book 2, chapter 1</term> <note>The Roman historian Justinus here refers to a debate over whether the earth was once entirely covered by fire or water.</note>.

# Heathen Religion.

The Chaldeans carried their god—fire—about, and engaged in a contest with the gods of all other lands, with the condition that whoever won the victory should be believed by everyone to be the one true god. The gods of other countries were made of brass, gold, and silver, or of wood or stone, or whatever material they might be, all of which would undoubtedly be consumed by the fire. Therefore, it happened that fire held the upper hand in every place. When the priest of Canopus (in Egypt) heard of this, he devised a trick: it is customary in the land of Egypt to make earthen water jugs that are porous with many small holes all over, through which cloudy water flows to become clean and pure. This priest took one of these jugs, plugged the holes with wax, painted it from top to bottom in various colors, filled it with water, and set it up as an idol. He carefully placed and attached the severed head of an old statue (which is said to have been the ruler Menelaus <note>original: "Menelai"</note>) onto the top. After this, the Chaldeans arrived. The contest began: the fire was lit near this water jug, and the wax used to plug the holes melted. The fire was extinguished by the water flowing out of the jug. Thus, through the deception of the priest, Canopus (the Egyptian water god) was shown to be the conqueror of the Chaldeans. Because of this, the image of Canopus is made with small feet, a tucked-in neck, a swollen belly like a water jug, and a rounded back. Through this persuasion, Canopus was honored as a god who overcomes everything. Thus far, Ruffinus, Book 2, *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "Hist. Eccles."</note> (found in Eusebius, whose church history he continues; it is Book 11), Chapter 26. This story is also told by Suidas in his Lexicon under the entry <term>Canopus</term>. What this water god Canopus looked like is shown from Egyptian antiquities by Baptista Casalius, Book 1, *Concerning the Ancient Rites of the Egyptians* <note>original: "de Vet. Rit. Ægypt."</note>, Chapter 14, page 51.

§. 3. Our ancestors believed that there were certain idols in the water who, according to their superstition, held dominion over this element. Procopius writes about the Nordic peoples in Book 3, *Gothic History* <note>original: "Hist. Goth."</note>.

# Pagan Religion.

§. 5. Among the sea-goddesses, the most distinguished or well-known is named *Blakylle*, to whom the *Cimbri* <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic people from the Jutland peninsula</note> attributed the dominion of the sea. She may have received her name from the Scanian promontory *Kulle* (concerning this, see *Saxo Grammaticus, Book 10, in the Life of Harald Bluetooth, p. 185*) <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220) was a Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum</note> which is consecrated to this sea-goddess and honored by sailors with superstitious ceremonies and customs, as noted by *Wormius* <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a Danish physician and antiquary</note> and *Stephanius* <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish philologist</note>. This *Blakylle* may perhaps be the wife of *Njord* <note>A Norse god of the sea and wind</note>, who is called *Skadi* <note>original: "Schad"</note> in the *Edda*; she is the equivalent of the Romans’ and Greeks’ *Thetis* and *Amphitrite*, the wife of *Neptune*.

§. 6. Regarding King *Hadding* of Denmark, *Saxo* reports that while he was once bathing on the seashore in hot weather, a hideous sea-idol <note>A monstrous supernatural being or deity</note> tried to snatch him. He, however, is said to have defended himself, overcome this sea-idol, and finally killed it. Because of this, a prophetess announced to him the wrath of all the gods and the fury of the sea, because he had killed a god who had appeared in a foreign form; he is therefore called a "God-murderer" (see *Saxo, Book 1, in the Life of King Hadding, pp. 15 & 16*). Are these not extraordinary gods, who can be strangled by humans? Nevertheless, the pagans believed their idols were immortal and could not be killed according to their true essence and nature, but only in their assumed body and form in which they appeared to bring help or harm to men (see *Stephanius in his Notes on Saxo, p. 54*). *Saxo* points to this in the mentioned place, where he introduces the aforementioned prophetess speaking to King *Hadding* thus:

> Indeed, sacrilegious hands have slain one of the gods from above, 
> who was hidden in a foreign body. 
> Do you thus stand here as the killer of a life-giving deity?

->That is:<-

> Are you then present here as a murderer of a god,
> You who dared to lay your hands upon someone,
> and murdered that very one who, from the host of gods,
> was hidden before us in a foreign body?

Saxo here calls them—after the Greek and Roman manner of speaking—Satyrs, Fauns, Sylvans, Pans, etc.

§. 3. It serves our purpose to investigate these names of idols cited by Saxo and the distinctions between them. Initially, it should be known that the name Satyr is used broadly to include all field, forest, and mountain deities of the heathens who have either a human head or body. According to the differences in their form and the places where they appear, they receive different names. In this broad sense, Saxo uses this name for an idol when he calls Mimring a "Forest Satyr." In this way, Pan is called a "Mountain Satyr," Silenus a "Field Satyr," and Faunus and Sylvanus "Forest Satyrs." Furthermore, the name Satyr is used more precisely and held as a specific name when it is contrasted and distinguished from other forest and field gods, just as Saxo makes such a distinction in this last passage. Therefore, the Satyrs are called field gods, and they are commonly attributed animal heads—such as those of dogs, wolves, oxen, etc.—but human bodies and limbs. Among these Satyrs, some are called <term>Sileni</term>, <note>In classical mythology, Silenus was the tutor of Dionysus; here the author treats them as a class of senior spirits</note> who are said to be the oldest and most prominent among the Satyric field-idols: Camerarius Cent. 1. Hor. cap. 71. Vossius lib. 1. *On Idolatry* <note>original Latin: "Idololat."</note> cap. 21. Among these, some are called Fauns, who are said to be the most prominent among the Sylvans, just as the Sileni are among the field Satyrs. The wives of the Fauns are called <term>Fantuae</term> or <term>Fatuae</term>, <note>Prophetic goddesses often associated with Fauna</note> who are said to be forest-goddesses. Regarding their form, it is reported differently; some wish to assign them human heads but animal bodies and four feet. Ovid describes the Fauns thus: that they have horned human heads, but horned feet <note>meaning hooves</note> like horses. Regarding this mountain-god Pan, Castalius explains in his *Biblical Notes* (p. 361) the idol **Mipleßeth** <note>original: "Mipleßeth", from 1 Kings 15:13, usually interpreted as a shocking or "horrible" idol</note>: 1 Kings 15:13. Their form is depicted in various ways, but commonly so that they are said to have human heads and hands, but otherwise two goat feet and loins; this is how Alciatus (Emblem 97, p. 216) depicts **Pan**, and by this understands the nature of all things. Among the **Sylvans** <note>woodland deities</note> are counted the **Aquili** <note>from the Latin "aquila" for eagle</note>, which are said to be flying satyrs with human faces but eagle's wings and feet. The Egyptians are said to have worshipped such *Aquili*, as Baptista Casalius reminds us in Book 1 of *On Ancient Egyptian Rites* (Chapter 12, p. 42), where he also provides an illustration of them. One such *Aquilus* can be seen illustrated in the front of Olaus Magnus’s *Histories*. Similarly, Virgil describes the **Harpies** in his third book as having the faces of young women, but otherwise being shaped and natured like predatory birds. To this category belong the wood-goddesses who are called **Oreads** <note>mountain or wood nymphs</note> after the oak forests and trees where they appear (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 8, Fable 13). Among the satyrs are also the **Simi** <note>from the Latin "simus," meaning flat-nosed or snub-nosed</note>, who are so named when they appear with a flattened face like an ape. In the works of Lucian, **Silenus** is called *Simus* (Natalis Comes, *Mythology*, Book 5, Chapter 8; Stephanus in his notes on Saxo, Book 2, p. 66/67). Regarding the **Lamiae**—that is, the three Gorgon sisters—as well as the Larvae, Furies, etc., which do not belong here, one may read Hesiod and Pylades in the *Theogony*, as well as Natalis Comes.

§. 4. Such hideous wood- and field-demons are depicted on the **Golden Horn** found near Tønder in the year 1639. In the first circle stand three *Sylvans* who have human heads but animal bodies and four feet. In the third circle, two **Satyrs** are depicted who have animal heads but human bodies and hands; one has an axe and the other a sickle in his hands. Both open their muzzles wide against each other and threaten with their weapons. Beside them, a **Centaur** is also engraved, having a human head and hands, but otherwise the form of a four-legged animal. <note>The original text contains a typo "uud" for "und" (and).</note> That these represent the pagan idols of our ancestors, I have demonstrated in my work *The Golden Horn* (Part 2, Chapter 4), to which the kind reader is referred to seek further information; there, everything briefly composed here is handled in great detail.

§. 5. The most prominent pagan gods were depicted as **Satyrs**, or in a **satyr-like form**. Starting with Holy Scripture, it frequently mentions the Ammonite idol **Moloch**, who was honored by the Ammonites and the Jews in the form of a satyr. This **Moloch** or **Melech** <note>Hebrew for "King"</note>—otherwise also called **Adramelech** and **Anamelech** in Holy Scripture (*Selden, On the Syrian Gods, Book 2, chapter 9; Beyer in his Additions to Selden, p. 308; Schindler in his Lexicon, p. 1010*)—was depicted with an **ox’s head**, but otherwise with a human body and hands, made of copper and hollow inside. When the sacrifice was to begin, it was lit with fire from within, and small children were burned alive in its glowing arms (*Tarnovius on Hosea 14:2, p. 434; Schmidt on Matthew 5:22*).

Similarly, **Saturn** among the **Carthaginians** was also a copper figure, in whose glowing arms children were placed and burned (*Rossaeus, Part 3, On the Religions of the World, question 1, p. 121*). **Jupiter** in **Libya** was likewise honored in the form of a **satyr**, for he had a horned ram's head and a goat skin on his body (*Peucer, On Divination, section on Oracles, f. 93. a.*). **Bacchus** is also depicted with an ox’s head and clothed in a goat skin (*Natalis Comes, Mythology, book 5, chapter 13*). The idol **Apollo** is depicted in a **satyr-like** way by **Johann Herold** at the beginning of his third book on the pagan gods, attributed with a hideous animal head but a human body with hands and feet. 

Even the **Sun** was represented and honored under the image of a **satyr** (*Rossaeus, Part 4, On the Religions of the World, question 13, p. 180*). Likewise, the Egyptian **Anubis** was depicted with a dog’s head, but otherwise with a body in human form (*Battista Casali, On Egyptian Rites, chapter 21, p. 72*). In a similar **satyr-like**, or rather devilish manner, the idol **Vitzliputzli** <note>original: "Vißlepußli"; a reference to the Aztec god Huitzilopochtli</note> is depicted among the Americans (*Olearius in his Notes on George Andersen’s Oriental Travels, book 1, chapter 31, p. 58*). The evil god **Deumo** among the Indians in **Narsinga** and **Calicut** (*Hondorff, Historical Theater, Part 1, p. 104*). The idol of the **Banyans** <note>A term used for Indian merchants or Hindu practitioners</note> in India (*Mandelslo, book 1, Indian Travels, chapter 37*). Indeed, most of the most prominent gods of the **Indians** are depicted in a hideous satyr-like form (*Erasmus Francisci, book 3, The Mirror, p. 1006*).

§. 8. The Romans learned this idolatry from the Greeks. As they sailed past *Antium*, the snake left the ship for the land and went into the temple of *Aesculapius*, remaining there for three days. §. 26. **Plato** distinguishes these household gods in this way: some are said to be **Lares** and others **Lemures**. The *Lares*, he says, are the souls of the pious, while the *Lemures* or **Larvae** are the souls of the wicked which appear after death: see **Augustine** (*City of God*, Book 9, Chapter 11) and **Alexandro ab Alexandro** (Book 6, Chapter 4). The **Papacy** <note>original: *Pabstthumb*; the author is writing from a Protestant perspective, likely critiquing Catholic views on Purgatory and ghosts.</note> agrees with Plato regarding the supposed appearance of souls after death, about which **Thyreus** and other Papists have written entire books. In truth, these were devilish phantoms which the blind heathens regarded as gods.

Among the **Germans**, they are named **Cobalden** [Kobolds], **Chimcken**, and **Woltercken**. Among the **Northern peoples**, they are called **Nis-Pucken** <note>Likely referring to the Nisse or Tomte of Scandinavian folklore combined with the term Puck.</note>. Among the **Romans**, they were called **Lares** because they dwelled in houses; **Praestites** because of their supposed presence; **Larvae** because of their nocturnal appearance; and **Lemures** when they made a Great Racket. In the works of **Maro** <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note>, they are called **Ancestral Gods** or **Native Penates** <note>original Latin: *Dii patrii, Penates Patrii*</note>—meaning paternal or fatherland-gods—though **Salmuth** explains this differently in the aforementioned place: *Compare Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book 3, Chapter 4; Rossinus; Alexander ab Alexandro, f. 324. a.* Otherwise, they are called **Familiar Spirits** <note>original Latin: *Spiritus familiares*</note>, **House-Spirits**, or **House-Guardians**.

§. 28. There are varying reports regarding how many of these household gods existed. The poets tell of only two, fathered by **Mercury** and **Lara** <note>In Roman myth, the Lares were the children of Mercury and the nymph Lara.</note>: **Natalis Comes**, *Mythology, Book 4, Chapter 4.* The Egyptians believed in four household gods, or rather four types and lineages of them, calling them **Daemon**, **Tyche**, **Heros**, and **Anachis** <note>original Greek-derived terms: *Dymon, Tychis, Heros, Anachis*; representing Fate, Fortune, the Heroic spirit, and Necessity/Constraint.</note>: **Alexander ab Alexandro**, *Book 6, Chapter 4, f. 325. a.* Generally, it was believed there were as many household gods as there were houses, especially the houses of the pious. For the heathens held that their household gods did not dwell in all houses, but only appeared in those where the inhabitants were pious, pleasing to them, and lived according to their will.

§. 29. In whichever house they desired to dwell, they declared their will to the master of the house in the following manner: they would gather a pile of wood shavings and fill the milk pails with milk, but then smear them with all kinds of animal dung. If the master of the house noticed this and yet ate or drank the milk defiled by the dung with his household servants, and did not clear away or scatter the pile of shavings, it was taken as a sign that they wished to remain in that house: **Pontanus** in his *Notes on Danish History, page 810.* Thus, Satan is an unclean spirit who takes pleasure and delight in uncleanness.

§. 30. To these household gods may also be added those domestic animals which the heathens elevated to the rank of gods. # Pagan Religion

[He]liopolis had an ox, and in the city of Memphis, a cow was held as an idol: Alessandro degli Alessandri, Book 1, Chapter 29, folio 49b and Book 6, Chapter 26, folio 383a. I leave it to the Christian reader’s consideration whether this author might have stumbled over the names of the cities, and that it should instead be said that a cow was divinely honored at Heliopolis, and an ox at Memphis. This Egyptian ox-god bore the name Apis, or Serapis, which is the word for an ox in the Egyptian language. He is said to have been black over his entire body, but with a square white spot on his forehead, the figure of an eagle on his back, and a peculiar mark on his tongue. He had his temple in Memphis and—according to claims—was conceived by a cow struck by lightning and flashes of light: Herodotus, Book 3, number 76, page 187. His mark on the right side is a white spot, a knot under the tongue, and horns like the new moon. When he reached a certain age, he was drowned in a well, and another ox was sought with great lamentation; this new ox was brought to Memphis and installed there in his temple by the priests: Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 8, Chapter 46; Solinus, Chapter 46. He is a black ox marked with certain (white) spots, unlike other oxen in his tongue and tail; he is said to have been conceived not naturally but by a heavenly fire: Pomponius Mela, *On the Geography of the World*, Book 1, Chapter 5, page 19. Augustine reports that a king named Apis ruled in Egypt, who after his death was honored as a god in the form of an ox, which is venerated in almost all Egyptian temples: Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 5. <note>See also the commentaries of Juan Luis Vives and Leonardus Coquaeus on this passage.</note> Similarly, Suidas mentions that a wealthy man, or king, named Apis, sustained the Egyptians at Memphis during a <term>famine</term> <note>original: "Theurung," referring to a period of great scarcity and high food prices</note>; therefore, after his death, a temple was erected in his honor, and within it, an ox named after this king was kept as a symbol of agriculture. This author <note>Suidas</note> also notes that, according to some opinions, this Apis was actually <term>Joseph</term> <note>The biblical Joseph, son of Jacob, who became a high official in Egypt and saved the land from famine</note>, who provided the Egyptians with sustenance during the famine: Suidas, in the *Lexicon*, under the entry Apis or Serapis. Rufinus mentions the very same thing in almost the same words:

> Some maintain that the image was formed in honor of our Joseph, because of the distribution of grain with which he came to the aid of the Egyptians during the time of famine; others say it is found in the ancient histories of the Greeks that a certain father Apis... <note>original: "Quidam in honorem nostri Josephi formatum perhibent simulachrum, ob divisionem frumenti, qvô famis tempore subvenit Ægyptiis, Alii reperitum in historiis Græcorum veteribus ferunt; Apin quendam patrem"</note>

### Cimbrian

...[he was] the father of a household, or a king established at Memphis in Egypt, who, when grain failed at Alexandria during a time of famine, abundantly provided food to the citizens from his own stores. When he died, they established a temple in his honor at Memphis, in which an ox is nourished as a sign of the best farmer; having certain distinctive colors, he is called Apis after the king's name. But his *soron* <note>original: σορὸν</note>, that is, the tomb or coffin in which his body lay, was brought to Alexandria; from the combination of *Soron* and *Apis* they first called it *Sorapin*, and later by corruption, *Serapin*: Ruffinus, Book 2, *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 23. That this Apis was intended to represent Joseph, and was his image and memorial, is proven by Vossius in *Theology of the Gentiles*, Book 1, Chapter 29, through the following points:

(1) From the ancient tradition of the Egyptians, which the holy fathers Maternus and Ruffinus cite. 

(2) From the burial of Joseph, at which the Egyptians are said to have erected an image of an ox, as Augustine reminds us in *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*. 

(3) From the dream of King Pharaoh regarding the seven fat and seven lean cows, which was explained by Joseph as seven years of plenty and seven years of famine: Genesis, Book 1, Chapter 41, verse 14. 

(4) From the high honor and glory that King Pharaoh bestowed upon Joseph: Genesis, Book 1, Chapter 41, verse 37. 

(5) From the great kindness of Joseph, who provided all of Egypt with grain during the famine: Genesis, Book 1, Chapter 41, verse 53 and Chapter 47. This became so world-famous that even pagan historians recorded it: Justin, Book 36, Chapter 2. 

(6) From the labor of the ox, by which agriculture is maintained; the ox is called the "servant of Ceres" <note>Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture; original: *minister Cereris*</note> and the "animal of agriculture" <note>original: *animal agriculturæ*</note>: Varro, Book 2, *On Agriculture*, Chapter 5. 

(7) From the custom of the ancients, who honored with the symbol of an ox those who provided the people with grain during times of famine; for this reason, Minutius was honored by the Romans with a gilded ox: Livy, Book 4, Chapter 16. 

(8) From the word *Apis*, which has its origin in the Hebrew word *AB*, that is, "Father." Thus Pharaoh called Joseph *Abrech*, a "Father of the Land" <note>The term "Abrech" in Genesis 41:43 is traditionally interpreted as a cry of honor or "bow the knee," but here the author links it to the Hebrew "Ab" for father; original: *Abrech*</note>: Genesis, Book 1, Chapter 41, verse 34 <note>This likely refers to verse 43</note>. Joseph himself admits that God made him a "father to Pharaoh": Genesis, Book 1, Chapter 45, verse 8. *Serapis* or *Sorapis* therefore means as much as "Ox-Fathers." 

(9) From the grain-measure <note>The *modius*, a Roman dry measure, often depicted on the head of Serapis statues</note> depicted over the head of Apis or Serapis: Ruffinus, Book [?]. What an excellent temple this Apis or Serapis had in Alexandria in Egypt, and what strange and hid-

Pluto and his wife Proserpine, otherwise called Hecate, were death-idols among the pagans who were said to have had their residence in hell and there housed the dead: <note>original: "Nat. Comes lib. 2. Myth. cap. 9. & lib. 3. cap. 16." — Natalis Comes, Mythology, Book 2, Chapter 9 and Book 3, Chapter 16.</note> Regarding King Balder in Denmark, Saxo writes in the third book of his *Danish Histories* <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century historian famous for the Gesta Danorum.</note> on page 43, that Proserpine appeared to him in the night and announced that he should die on the following day. §. 2. These idols had other names among our ancestors; it would be wished that the aforementioned Saxo Grammaticus had given them their native Cimbrian-Gothic names; however, he keeps to the custom of "baptizing" the Nordic idols with Roman names. Stephanius, in his *Notes on Saxo* <note>original: "Stephanius in Not. ad Saxon. lib. 3. p. 96."</note> on book 3, page 96, reminds us that the Roman Proserpine is intended to be the Nordic goddess of hell, Hel or Hela. She is considered to be the daughter of the evil idol Loki; she is said to have been cast into hell by God and there conducts the government over the dead: <note>original: "Edda P. 1. fab. 28. & 44." — Referring to the Prose Edda, the primary source for Norse mythology.</note> This name for an idol has not yet been extinguished under Christianity. It is held that in the German and Danish languages, the place of damnation takes the names *Helle* and *Hel* from this goddess Hel.

Cimbrian [Pagan Religion]
82

...received. The common man, especially in North Cimbria <note>The northern part of the Jutland peninsula.</note> and the Duchy of Schleswig, is still held by the superstition that Hel <note>Originally the Norse goddess of the underworld, here personified as Death itself.</note> is Death itself, and indeed a true, independent being who, in times of plague, is said to ride around on a three-legged horse and strangle the children of men. When the plague and other contagious diseases spread, the common people say: "Hel is wandering about." When the dogs then bark and howl unusually at night, it is said: "Hel is among the dogs." Where the plague begins in a place, they say: "Hel has arrived there." Where the plague ceases in a place, they say: "Hel has been driven away from there." It is also firmly believed that Hel can be chased from one place to another. They cite examples of Hel being driven out of this or that town and village by certain people. They even name several daredevils who are said to have driven away Hel, or Death, in these quarters. When someone lies deathly ill, they say: "He has his <term>Helsoot</term> <note>From the German 'Sucht' or 'Seuche,' meaning a plague or fatal sickness attributed to Hel.</note>"; that is: his sickness inflicted by Hel, or Death. But when such a deathly ill person recovers, it is said: "He has settled with Hel"; or: "He has sacrificed something to Hel."

§. 3. Thus Death itself was an idol among the Greeks and Romans, fathered by Night: Hesiod in the *Theogony*, page 137. When Virgil writes in the eleventh book of the *Aeneid*: "Many bodies of oxen are sacrificed all around to Death"; <note>original: "Multa boum circa mactantur corpora Morti"</note> Servius reminds us in his commentary on this passage, page 1582, that Death was regarded as a goddess. See also Gyraldus, *History of the Gods*, Volume 1, page 47 and following; and Vossius, *Gentile Theology*, Book 3, chapter 20. The Indians, especially in the Empire of Indostan, have today among their eleven idols also a god of death, whom they call Siam: <note>Likely referring to Yama, the Hindu lord of death, sometimes referred to as 'Syam' or 'Chiam' in early modern European accounts.</note> Erasmus Francisci, *The Mirror*, Book 3, page 981. The Americans also have such a death-idol: Erasmus Francisci, in the same work, page 1060; Arnold in the *Additions to Roger on Heathenism*, chapter 38, page 955.

§. 4. Three death-goddesses are joined to Pluto, who are called the Parcae: <note>The Fates (Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos) who spin and cut the thread of life.</note> Rossinus, *Antiquities*, Book 2, chapter 15, who are said to determine the limit of every man's life: Natalis Comes, *Mythology*, Book 3, chapter 6. These same ones were not unknown to our ancestors: Saxo, Book 3, page 42.

->### Pagan Religion<-
->L 2<-

43. & *Book 6, page 102* calls these same figures sometimes *Parcae* <note>original: "Parcer"; the Fates of Roman mythology</note> and sometimes *Nymphs*. They were called *Norns* <note>original: "Nörner"</note> and were held to be the rulers over human life and death, fortune and misfortune: *Olaus Magnus, Book 3, Chapter 9.* The *Edda* <note>The Prose Edda, a 13th-century Icelandic manual of mythology.</note> *Part 1, Fable 15* describes them in the following manner: There come out of a heavenly hall three maidens, who are named thus: *Urd*, *Verthandi* <note>original: "Werand"</note>, and *Skuld* <note>original: "Schulde"</note>. These maidens determine a person's age (how long they shall live); we call them *Norns*. *Völuspá* <note>original: "Woluspa"; an Old Norse poem about the creation and end of the world.</note> *Numbers 20 & 21* agrees with this description of the *Parcae*. Both name these *Parcae* according to the distinction of the three times: For in Icelandic, *Urd* means the past; *Verthandi* the present; and *Skuld* the future. The Greeks called these three *Parcae* *Clotho*, *Lachesis*, and *Atropos*, and with these three names they pointed to the three times. *Aristotle* explains this in the *Book of the World* <note>original: "lib. de Mundo"</note> as follows: There are three *Parcae*, distinguished according to the three times, among whom one signifies past things, the second future things, and the third present things. For one among these *Parcae*, named *Atropos*, looks upon past things because what is past can in no way be reversed or called back. The other, who takes care for the future, is called *Lachesis*, because of the chance nature of natural things. *Clotho* completes present things: thus far *Aristotle*, or whoever else is the ancient author of the cited *Book of the World* found among the philosopher’s writings. Among the ancient Romans, they are called *Nona*, *Decima*, and *Morta*: *Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, Book 3, Chapter 16.* It is said these *Parcae* or *Norns* determine a person's age, how long they shall live, and when they shall die; one is said to spin the thread of human life, the second to wind it up, and the third to tear it off. Hereupon *Ursinus* <note>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583), a German theologian.</note> in *Volume 1 of Sacred Analysis, Book 4, Number 12* explains the saying of King Hezekiah <note>original: "Hiskias"</note> in *Isaiah 38, verse 12*, where he laments that his life is torn away from him as the thread is torn away from a weaver. These *Norns* come from the heavenly hall to indicate that our life's goal is determined in heaven. Otherwise, they are said to have revealed themselves in dark caves to show that the divine decrees are dark and hidden from mortal men: *Natalis Comes* <note>A 16th-century Italian mythologist.</note> *in the same place.* Thus the *Parcae* are said to have appeared to King Hother in Denmark in a cave.
