# Cimbrian <note>Referring to the Cimbri, an ancient Germanic people; here used generally for Northern or Germanic traditions.</note>

...have shown: *Saxo, Book 3 of the History of the Danes, in the Life of Hother, p. 42 seq. Compare Saxo, Book 6, in the Life of Fridlevus, p. 102.*

§. 5. The *Edda* <note>The Prose Edda, an Icelandic manual of mythology from the 13th century.</note> narrates at the aforementioned place that besides the three already listed, there are other Norns or *Parcae* <note>original: "Parcer"; the Fates of Roman mythology.</note> who are said to come to every human as soon as they are born into this world. The *Edda* distinguishes between good and evil Norns and reports that the former bring all good fortune, while the latter bring all misfortune to humanity. These might be called "Fortune Norns" to distinguish them from the first "Death Norns." *Edda Part 2, Number 18, under the title "Of Odin’s Maidens"* mentions two Norns whom it names *Nipt* and *Dys*. By these are understood the good and evil *Genius* <note>original: "Genius"; in Roman religion, a protective spirit assigned to a person at birth.</note>, who come to a person at the hour of birth, one to bring good and the other evil: *Iamblichus, On the Mysteries, chapter 43; Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 6 [of the Genial Days], chapter 4.*

§. 6. The *Edda* also mentions the War Norns, whom it calls *Valkyries* <note>original: "Valkyrer"</note>, and names fourteen of them, whom the war-god *Odin* <note>original: "Othin"</note> is said to dispatch to all battles to choose those who are to be slain in war and to direct the victory wherever they wish: *Edda, Part 1, Fable 31.* *Völuspá* <note>original: "Woluspa"; the 'Prophecy of the Seeress,' an Old Norse poem.</note> *Number 30* also treats these Valkyries or "War-Fates." They are called *Valkyries* from the "choosing of the slain" <note>The term is derived from Old Norse 'valr' (the slain) and 'kyrja' (chooser).</note> in war. It was believed that they were meant to invite the souls of the slain in war to Odin’s residence, called *Valhalla* <note>original: "Valhall"</note>: *Resenius in the Notes to Völuspá, as cited; Stephanus in the Notes to Saxo, Book 3, p. 88.* *Saxo* <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a Danish historian.</note> relates at the beginning of his third book that these War Norns appeared to King *Hother* in Denmark and revealed to him how wars are conducted through their direction, and how they are invisibly present at the slaughters; how they provide help and assistance to their friends and, as they please, bring about fortune and misfortune. He calls them Forest Maidens and *Nymphs*, and adds that they presented King Hother with a garment resistant to cuts and stabs, and at the same time discovered for him how he might prevail over his enemy, King *Balder*, in war: *Saxo, Book 3, in the Life of King Hother, pp. 39, 42, 43.*

The Cimbrian-Gothic and all Nordic peoples in the three northern <note>literally "midnight," an archaic term used to denote the North</note> kingdoms had three principal idols, who are named **Thor**, **Wodan**, and **Freya**. Adam of Bremen <note>An 11th-century German chronicler and geographer</note> describes them as follows: The most powerful among the three idols is Thor; he rules in the air, over thunder and lightning, wind, rain, and fair weather, as well as the fruits and produce of the earth. The second is called Wodan (or Odin), that is, "the strong one"; he reigns over war and grants courage to men against their enemies. The third is Fricco (or Freya), who bestows peace and pleasure upon mortal men. In times of pestilence and famine, they sacrificed to Thor; in times of war, to Wodan; at weddings, to Fricco: *Adam of Bremen, On the Geography of Denmark and the Northern Realms, p. 143.* <note>original Latin: "de Situ Daniæ, & Reg. Sept."</note> These three idols, through sorcery, so blinded the people that they attained divine names in Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, and were honored with sacrifices and idolatry: *Saxo Grammaticus, Book 6, History of the Danes, in the Life of King Frotho IV, p. 103.* <note>Saxo was a 12th-century Danish historian</note> These three are called the great gods: *Schefferus, in his work on Uppsala, chapter 9, p. 117.* The principal gods: *Johannes Magnus, Book 1, chapter 10.* The gods of the first veneration: *Olaus Magnus, Book 3, chapter 3.* <note>Johannes and Olaus Magnus were 16th-century Swedish brothers and historians</note> These three idols are described by Olaus Magnus at the aforementioned place, as also by Stephanus—

Cimbrian

[Ste]phanius <note>original: "phan." refers to Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish historian known for his commentary on Saxo Grammaticus.</note> in his notes on Saxo [Grammaticus], Book 6 of the *History of the Danes*, page 139, describes them as follows: Thor sits in the middle upon a throne, clothed in a long belted robe, and adorned with a crown and scepter. Othin <note>Odin</note> stands to the right with a sword, helmet, and shield, otherwise fully armed about his body. To the left stands Freya, dressed in the Roman fashion, also armed with a sword and bow. These three gods were said to have stood not only in their temples, chapels, and groves, but also in the market squares of the cities: Helvadus <note>Niels Helvad (1564–1634), a Danish astronomer and historian.</note>, Book 3 of the *Encolpion*, folio 264. a. Perhaps they stood in the market squares depicted as reported by Verelius <note>Olof Verelius (1618–1682), a Swedish antiquarian.</note> in the *History of King Gothric and Rolf*, chapter 7: that all three gods sat crowned on three different steps of a throne, one above the other—specifically Thor at the very top, with Othin below him, and Freya at the bottom. Or rather, it may be that these idols were depicted differently in different places. Furthermore, these three northern idols, Thor, Othin, and Freya, were the same as Jupiter, Mars, and Venus among the Romans, and what <term>Bel, Gad, and Astaroth</term> <note>Ancient Near Eastern deities mentioned in the Bible; the author is drawing parallels between Norse mythology and biblical idolatry.</note> were among the Syrians in Holy Scripture.

§. 2. It appears that the Cimbrian-Gothic peoples, through the Gospel preached long ago by the Apostles or apostolic men, had some knowledge of the <term>Holy Trinity</term>; however, upon the re-establishment of paganism, they mixed this mystery with fables and made three idols out of the three persons of the Godhead, naming them Othin, Thor, and Freya: Compare Bang <note>Thomas Bang (1600–1661), a Danish theologian.</note>, *Ecclesiastical History of the Sweno-Goths*, book 6, chapter 8. Othin is called the <term>All-Father</term>, who begot his son Thor: *Edda*, Part 1, fable 7. This Thor is called a fighter of the <term>Midgard Serpent</term> <note>original: "Mitgardischen Schlangen"; in Norse mythology, the world-encircling serpent Jörmungandr.</note>: *Edda*, Part 2, number 4. He overcomes this hellish serpent but must lose his life in the process: *Edda*, Part 1, fable 48. This is the significance of <term>Thor's Hammer</term>, which was shaped like a cross: Worm <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), the famous Danish physician and antiquarian.</note>, Book 1 of *Monuments*, chapter 13.

§. 3. The supreme god of all northern peoples was Thor. Everything that may be said and believed regarding the one true GOD, the Nordic peoples said and believed regarding their Thor, writes Schefferus <note>Johannes Schefferus (1621–1679), author of "Upsalia", a study of Swedish antiquities.</note> in his *Upsalia*, in the sixth chapter. Among such gods, writes Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish ecclesiastic and writer.</note>, Thor was the first and most powerful; he sat in the middle of the hall, upon a cushion, and was worshipped, to whose [honor...]

on those both sides stood two other gods, namely Othin <note>Odin</note> and Friggo <note>Frigg</note>. This Thor, it is said, has his seat in the air, makes thunder and lightning, wind, rain, and fair weather. He gives the grain along with all fruits and drives away the plague. He is depicted with a crown, scepter, and twelve stars around him. They believed that nothing in the world could be compared to his magnanimity. He always has his day in the week and the first month in the year (called Thor’s-Day and Thor’s-Month): <note>original: "Olaus M. lib. 3. cap. 3." refers to Olaus Magnus, the 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian.</note> I am of the opinion that Thor's-Month is not the first month of the year, but rather April, which the peasants among us call *Thorn*. The twelve stars signify the twelve signs of the zodiac and the twelve months of the year; or, if there are to be seven stars, they signify the seven planets or the seven days of the week, as Schefferus <note>Johannes Schefferus (1621–1679), a humanist scholar.</note> reminds us in the aforementioned place.

This Thor is the most powerful and highest among the gods: <note>original: "Ericus Upsal. l. d." refers to the previously cited location in Ericus Olai’s work.</note> He overcomes everything that lives: <note>original: "Edda P. 1. fab. 7." refers to the Prose Edda, a primary source for Norse mythology.</note> He is the most noble and strongest among all gods; his hall is called <term>Bilskirnir</term> <note>Old Norse for "lightning-bright," the residence of Thor.</note>, containing 540 floors. # Cimbrian

Saxo, in Book 6 of the *History of the Danes*, in the *Life of King Frotho IV*, page 103, <note>original: "Saxo lib. 6. Hist. Dan. in Vita R. Froth. IV. p. 103." refers to the medieval chronicler Saxo Grammaticus.</note> wishes to cast doubt upon this, but without basis. The description, depiction, and appointment of these two idols agree; in Holy Scripture, he is called Bell and Baal. <note>original: "Seldenus Synt. 2. de DIS Syris, cap. 1. p. 195/ 214." refers to John Selden's work on Syrian deities.</note> Some believe that **Thor** is the last syllable of the name **Jupiter**, created as an example through <term>aphaeresis</term> <note>The linguistic process of dropping the first syllable of a word.</note>—just as from Margaret comes Gret; from Catharine, Trin; from Christine, Stin; from Adolph, Olff; from Johannes, Hans; and from Euphrates, Phrat. Others believe that Jupiter was called **Thur** among the Asiatic peoples. Schefferus, in the place often mentioned, writes from the *Alexandrian Chronicle* that among the Assyrians, Belus was called **Thura**; Belus, however, is the Assyrian Jupiter and is called by the surname Jupiter Belus. <note>original: "Conf. Selden. l. d." Consult Selden in the place cited.</note> Likewise, Thor is called **Thur** by Dudo in Book 1 of the *History of the Normans* (as shown by Vossius in *On Idolatry*, Book 1, Chapter 35). The Scythian **Tharan**, mentioned by Lucan in Book 1 of the *Pharsalia*, page 22, was understood by the Scythians to mean Jupiter: <note>original: "Sulpitius & Beroaldus in Comment. ad Lucan. l. d." refers to scholarly commentaries on the Roman poet Lucan.</note> In the British language, he is also called **Taran**: <note>original: "Scheffer. Upsal. cap. 6." refers to Johannes Schefferus's work on Uppsala.</note> Thus, this idol is named after thunder, which the Danish and British peoples call *Taren* and *Taran*.

Cluver, in Book 1 of *German Antiquities*, Chapter 26, page 227, reports that Jupiter was named **Taran**—and according to different dialects, **Toran**, **Tonar**, **Donar**, **Tordan**, or **Tonder**—among the Celtic (that is, British, Spanish, Gallic, Illyrian, and German) as well as Asiatic peoples. These names are attributed to Thor because of the thunder over which he is said to rule, as indicated by the thunderbolt in his hand. Similarly, Jupiter is surnamed by the Greeks as *brontaios* <note>original: "βρονταῖος", meaning "the Thunderer"</note> and by the Latins as *Tonans* <note>original: "Tonans", meaning "the Thundering One"</note>, which is to say, a god who thunders. From this, the good city of **Tondern**—or as our people in this Duchy of Schleswig say, **Tonner**—may have taken its name, and the thunder-god Thor may have had his sacrifices and idolatrous worship there. That this idol Thor was also honored in a divine manner in these two Duchies <note>Schleswig and Holstein</note> shall be shown below in its proper place, God willing. The ancient Germans called the god of heaven by no other name than **Thorn**, as Grotius writes in the *Prolegomena to Procopius’s Gothic Wars*. Various cities and villages in the Kingdom of Denmark are said to take their names from these idols, as Dr. Wormius <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a Danish physician and antiquary.</note>

### Pagan Religion.

As shown in Book 1 of the *Danish Fasti*, Chapter 15. <note>original: "libr. 1. Fast. Dan. cap. 15." refers to Olaus Worm’s *Fasti Danici*, a study of Danish chronology and antiquities.</note> To this belong the following church villages in the Diocese of Ribe: Torstet, Toring, Torup. In the Diocese of Aarhus: Toring, Torsberg, Torsagger, Torsleff, Torild. In the Diocese of Børglum: Torsee, Torsleff, Turup. In the Diocese of Odense or Funen: Thorslund, Turup, Toreby. In the Diocese of Zealand: Thorslund, Thureby, Torup. Schefferus, in the place often mentioned, writes that the towns of Torberg in Switzerland, Torlach or Turlach in the Margraviate of Torgau in Saxony, and the castle of Thorand there, derived their names from this idol; and that the marketplaces in the cities of the northern kingdoms <note>original: "mitternächtiger Königreichen" — literally "midnight kingdoms," a common early modern term for the Nordic countries.</note> are called "Tore" for this reason, as this Thor was their overseer. Doctor Worm, in the place recently mentioned, remembers various groves in the Kingdom of Denmark which were consecrated to this Thor and named after him.

**§. 4.** The second chief deity of the northern kingdoms was **Othin**—that is, "the strong" (these are the words of Olaus Magnus); he is set over war and helps men against their enemies, standing at the right hand of the god Thor. This Othin is depicted armed and held in such superstition as Mars was among the Romans, and his day (of the week) was also kept in eternal memory of his name. <note>Referring to Wednesday, derived from "Woden," another form of Odin.</note> While still alive, he attained the title of deity throughout all Europe, for there was no one like him in the art of war. The Goths always appeased him with blood sacrifices, such as the death of prisoners, believing that one could not more appropriately placate the commander of war than with human blood. These were called *Drotner* or *Drutner* (otherwise known as Druids). <note>The author reflects an early modern theory linking the Norse *Drottnar* (lords/priests) with the Celtic Druids.</note> Othin, or Oden, was a powerful and warlike lord; he waged war far and wide across the world and overcame many lands and kingdoms. He was victorious and never lost a battle, but always carried away the victory. Because of this, his people believed that in every encounter he held victory sent down from heaven. Whenever he sent his people out to war or other service, he would lay his hands upon their heads and bless them, which they regarded as a sign of good fortune. When they were in need or danger, whether by water or by land, they called upon his name and expected to receive help from him; thus, he was all their comfort.

Othin had two brothers: one was named Wee <note>Vili</note> and the other Welir <note>Vé</note>, who looked after the land whenever Othin was absent at war. It once happened that he remained away for so long that his brothers believed he would never return; therefore, they divided the kingdom and took his wife Frigge <note>Frigg</note> for themselves. Soon after this, Othin returned home and took his wife back. He then moved against the Scythians <note>original: "Scyten"</note>, but eventually made peace with the Scythian and Asian peoples. This Mimer, a very clever man, was later beheaded; Othin embalmed his head and enchanted it so that it spoke and revealed hidden matters to him. Niord, his son Frey, and his daughter Freya, he counted among the Asian idols. <note>The text follows "Euhemerism," a historical theory that the pagan gods were actually great human kings from Asia who were later deified.</note> Freya first learned the art of sorcery among the Waner <note>Vanir</note>, a Scythian people.

*The Life of King Hadding* <note>Latin: "Vita R. Haddingi"</note>, pages 12 and following. The second under King Hother, the thirteenth king in Denmark: the same [author], book 3, in *The Life of King Hother*, page 44. The third under King Harald Wartooth <note>Original: "Harald Hyltetand." A legendary Danish king known for his "war-tooth" or prominent teeth.</note>, the 37th king in Denmark: the same, book 7, in *The Life of King Harald Wartooth*, page 138, and book 8, in the life of this Harald, page 146. From this, the well-regarded Schefferus <note>Johannes Schefferus (1621–1679), a prominent scholar who wrote "Upsalia," a history of the pagan temple at Uppsala.</note> wishes to conclude that three distinct Odins are cited by Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian.</note>. Here it should be noted that the Odin under King Harald Wartooth was not Odin himself, but his ghost, which appeared to the mentioned king, as the context in Saxo clearly indicates. Thus Snorri writes in Part 1 of the *Chronicle of Norway* <note>Latin: "Chron. Norvag."; this refers to the "Heimskringla" by Snorri Sturluson.</note>, number 1, page 8, that after his death, Odin is said to have revealed himself often during bloody times of war, according to the pagan superstition of our ancestors. Furthermore, it does not follow that there were two Odins simply because Saxo recounts that Odin lived under the eighth king, Hadding, and also under the thirteenth king, Hother, in Denmark. For this Odin could have reached so many years and lived under six kings in succession, as similar examples testify. The giant Starkad <note>Original: "Starckotter." A legendary hero in Norse mythology known for his immense strength and long life.</note> is said to have lived through three human lifespans and lived under thirteen kings in Denmark: Saxo, book 6, in *The Life of King Frotho IV*, and book 8, in *The Life of King Omund*. In the year of Christ 1593, Torkild Maßen died, the pastor of the church at Agerschou in the district of Haderslev; he lived for one hundred and five years and knew six kings in Denmark, namely: King Hans, King Christian II, King Frederick I, King Christian III, King Frederick II, and King Christian IV: Helvad, Part 2, *Chronicle of the Baltic* <note>Latin: "Chron. **Odin**: <note>Philipp Cluver, *Germania Antiqua*, book 1, chapter 26, p. 227.</note> Some wish to derive this name from *Wöden*—that is, raging and storming—and say he was so named because of his furious nature. Others want to trace this name from the old Cimbrian-Gothic word *Wode*, which means disaster and destruction, harm and danger; from this, the old proverb arose: "Go to Odin!" <note>Original: "Fahr zu Oden!"</note> which is a curse, where one wishes misfortune and ruin upon another. However, these words *Wöden* and *Wode* much more likely have their origin in the name **Wodan**, as he is said to be an evil god and a cause of all evil: <note>Compare Johannes Schefferus, *Upsalia*, chapter 7.</note> Cluver <note>Book 1, *Antiqua Germania*, chapter 26, p. 224.</note> opines that this Wodan was also otherwise called **Dan**, and that Denmark received its name from him.

The *Edda* <note>Part 2, number 2. However, this conclusion is not binding: for using sorcery, as King Gylffi of Sweden did, is one thing; teaching sorcery publicly and making a profession of it, as Odin first did in Sweden, is another. It is true that sorcery had been taught and learned privately <note>original: "privatim"</note> in Sweden before, otherwise King Gylffi would not have been able to use it; but Odin was the first to teach this black art <term>black art (schwartze Kunst): a common term for magic or necromancy</term> publicly, bring it into bloom, and establish schools of magic. ### §. 6.
We have thus far treated of the three highest idols of the Gothic peoples; there follows now their subordinate idols, of which <term>Olaus Magnus<note>A 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian famous for his descriptions of Northern peoples.</note></term> recounts three: namely, **Mitothin**, **Fro**, and **Bagnofft**; all three were famous sorcerers. **Mitothin** is depicted in the center with rays around his head; **Fro** to the right with a cap, both with raised hands; and to the left **Bagnofft**, armed with a sword in his hand and a plume of feathers on his head: <note>original: "Olaus M. lib. 3. cap. 4." — Translation: Olaus Magnus, *History of the Northern Peoples*, Book 3, chapter 4.</note>

(1) **Mitothin** means, according to his name, as much as "Othin's fellow-companion," and is titled the "Bishop of the Gods." Through sorcery, he earned for himself the name of an idol and made the decree that one should not sacrifice to the gods in common, but to each idol individually. He fled from Othin to the island of <term>Fyn<note>Also known as Funen, a major island in modern-day Denmark.</note></term>, where he was strangled by the inhabitants, and thus received the reward for his idolatry. From his dead carcass, such a poisonous stench arose that many died from it. Because of this, he was dug up, his head was struck off from the body, and his heart was pierced through: <note>original: "Saxo lib. 1. in vita Haddingi p. 13." — Translation: Saxo Grammaticus, *The Danish History*, Book 1, in the *Life of Hadding*.</note> In my opinion, this Mitothin is none other than the great sorcerer **Hollerus** <note>Also known as Ullr.</note>, who for a time was accepted into the order of the gods in place of the banished Othin and was called Othin for the sake of honor; but he was subsequently driven away by Othin and slain by the Danes: <note>original: "Saxo lib. 3. in vita Hotheri p. 45 / 46." — Translation: Saxo Grammaticus, Book 3, in the *Life of Hother*.</note> All circumstances—names, sorcery, flight, beginning, and end—agree, as does the deification.

§. 7. Additionally, they had private idols, which were not worshiped by everyone in common, but were honored specifically by certain people. It is suspected whether this Balder, or Bolder, gave the name and origin to the village of **Baldersleben**, located in this District of Apenrade: Helvadus <note>Nicolaus Helvadus, a Danish chronicler</note>, Book 3, *Encolpion*, folio 264. Our people call it **Balderslee** or **Bolderslee**, which is Bolder’s place and region. Near Oreting in Zealand, in the jurisdiction, there is a large stone, upon which this runic inscription stood:

<image-desc>A line of text written in runic characters.</image-desc>

->Because Disa's laws are worthy / they brought their pleas here.<-

->That is:<-

->Because Disa's laws are valuable / they brought their complaints to this place.<-

From this, it can be inferred that in former times, the assembly and law were held at this place, which for that reason was called **Lis-** or **Disting**: Wormius <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a Danish physician and antiquary who was a pioneer in the study of runes</note> Book 2, *Danish Monuments*, page 117 seq. & Book 1, *Danish Calendar*, chapter 15. Disa is intended to be taken for Thor's wife, as Dr. Worm indicates in the aforementioned place. Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian</note> Book 4, chapter 5, considers her to have been a Queen in Sweden. However, without doubt, the idol **Tuisco** is understood by this, whose name—according to the Danish manner of speaking and dialect—has been transformed into **Lisa** or **Disa**. For the Danish and Gothic peoples are accustomed to transforming the hard *T* of the Upper German names into a soft *D*. Therefore, where the Upper Saxons say: **Tag** [Day] / **Todt** [Death] / **Teufel** [Devil] / **Tragen** [Carry] / **Treiben** [Drive] / **Traum** [Dream] / **Tanz** [Dance] etc., in the Danish language it is: **Dag** / **Död** / **Diufel** / **Drage** / **Drive** / **Dröm** / **Danz** etc., in which the Lower Saxons certainly agree. But what need is there for long-windedness? Tuisco is called **Dis** or **Dise** by the Gallic people: "The father of the family was honored by both the Germanic peoples under the name of Tuisco and by the Gauls under the name of Dis" <note>original: "Familiæ patrem utrique populi Germani sub nomine Tuisconis Galli sub nomine Ditis honorarunt," Caesar, Book 6, Gallic Wars</note>. This Tuisco was considered a god of justice and was divinely honored by our ancestors in this Duchy of **Schleswig**, as will be made clear in the next chapter. He is said to have been the first King of the Germans, who established an excellent system of governance <term>Policey-Ordnung</term> <note>In this period, "Policey" referred broadly to civil administration, social order, and public regulation rather than just a modern police force</note> among his people, and strictly maintained—and commanded to be maintained—law and justice: Compare Pareus <note>Johann Philipp Pareus, a 17th-century historian</note> Vol. 1, *Universal History*, page 242 seq.

Regarding the Cimbrian Saxons / who inhabited a large part of these two Duchies of Schleswig and Holstein / *Richard Verstegan* writes in *English Antiquities, chapter 3.* <note>original: "Antiqv. (2) On Monday they worshipped the Moon / in the form of a woman / with a short skirt and cap and long donkey-ears / along with a depiction of the Moon / upon her chest: The short skirt was meant to signify the short or swift course of the Moon / the two long donkey ears his <note>The original text switches gender pronouns for the moon here, common in Germanic languages where the moon is masculine (Der Mond).</note> two horns <note>referring to the crescent "horns" of the moon</note> / the cap or veil his hidden influence. (3) On Tuesday they prayed to the idol Tuisco / who was presented with a scepter in his hand / and clothed in the skin of a wild beast. He is considered a god of justice / therefore on his day the <term>Ding</term> <note>A historical Germanic governing assembly and law court.</note> and the law has been administered since ancient times / which for this reason is called *Dingstag* <note>Tuesday</note> / otherwise *Tistag* / but in former times was called *Twistag*. land. His scepter signifies his rule; his simple attire signifies justice, which is plain and right, without regard for the status of the person. (4) On Wednesday they served Wodan, who was a god of war, like the Roman Mars. He is depicted in armor, equipped with a helmet and breastplate, sword and shield. He is the Gothic Othin <note>Odin</note>, about whom we spoke in the preceding chapter. From this idol, Wednesday was called *Wodenstag*, and by contraction *Wonstag*. (5) On Thursday they called upon Thor, who is the Roman Jupiter; he is depicted in royal form, sitting on a throne with a crown and scepter and a thunderbolt, as was previously mentioned. He was an idol over thunder and lightning; he is therefore called Tonar or Tonnar, and his day is called Thursday, otherwise Thor's-Day. (6) On Friday, Freya was honored; she is depicted like a woman, but in the armed form of a man, with a sword and a bow and arrow, like the Roman Venus, about whom more was said above. From this idol, Friday is said to take its name. This Freya is supposed to have been the wife of Othin, as is generally believed. Others, however, claim that her husband was Istevon, the fourth king of the Germans: Alstedius in the *Chronicles* <note>original: "Chron." referring to Johann Heinrich Alsted</note>, title 21, page 197. Helvicus, *Chronological Theater* <note>original: "Theat. Chron."</note>, Section 3, under the heading *Concerning Germanic Kings* <note>original: "de German. Regibus"</note>. (7) On Saturday, they served the idol Sater, otherwise called Crodo, who is the Roman Saturn. Therefore Saturday received the name *Satertag* <note>Satur-day</note>. His image was that of an old man with a long coat, long beard and hair, with bare feet, standing on a fish; in his left hand he holds a wheel, and in his right a water pitcher filled with flowers. His long coat, beard, and hair signify the slowness of Saturn's movement, which extends over thirty years <note>A reference to the orbital period of the planet Saturn, which is approximately 29.5 years</note>. The wheel refers to the rotation of time; the water pitcher filled with flowers or roses points to his dominion over water and land, or as others suggest, to the proper time and the hope thereof. Hence the saying: "Time brings roses." The fish upon which this idol stands with bare feet depicts the slipperiness and instability of time. This idol Sater is named in Holy Scripture as Moloch or Melech by the Ammonites: 1 Kings 11:7. By the Syrians, Rimmon: 2 Kings 5:18. By the Assyrians, Adramelech (that is, the mighty Moloch): 2 Kings 17:31, and Baal: Judges 2:11, 13. Geusius, Part 1, *Human Sacrifices* <note>original: "Vict. Humanæ"</note>, chapter 5.

the nephew of Tuisco, the son of Mannus <note>In Germanic mythology, Tuisco and Mannus were regarded as the foundational ancestors of the Germanic peoples.</note>, as judged by Aventinus, Dresserus in *Part 1, Historical Introduction to the Third Millennium, p. 244*, and Alstedius in *Chronicle, Title 34, p. 227*. Or rather—which is more believable—the Duke Hermann, called *Arminius* <note>original: "Arminius"</note> by the Roman writers, the valiant war-hero of the Germans, who utterly defeated the Roman commander Quintilius Varus along with twenty thousand Romans near Paderborn in Westphalia, as Pomarius in *Notes on the Old Saxon Chronicle, p. 23*, Vossius in *Book 2, Theology of the Gentiles, chapter 32*, and Schedius in *On the German Gods, Section 3, chapter 3*, rightly maintain; this is the most correct opinion. From this, the common folk made an idol and called it **Jodut**: *Old Saxon Chronicle, edited by Pomarius, pp. 243, 244*.

§. 2. The aforementioned Mr. Heinrich Walter mentions in the cited place that our Frisians had four distinct idols, which he describes thus:

> He says: "In particular, four idols were primarily honored and worshipped by the Frisians, named **Phoseta** (or Fosta), **Freda**, **Meda**, and **Weda**. Among these, Phoseta and Meda (who were goddesses) held several arrows in the right hand and a sheaf of grain in the left; Freda and Weda, however, had a shield upon their breast, a helmet on the head, were (for the most part) naked on their arms and legs, and had wings on their backs. From this, one may conclude that the former were worshipped for agriculture, and the latter for wars that occurred."

And on June 12th, in the year 1650, I myself saw the images of **Phoste** and **Wede** in St. Mary’s Church in Utrecht, alongside a large horn through which the people were summoned together by blowing for the idol-worship. Among these idols, however, **Phoseta** was the most prominent, being the same as <term>Vesta</term> <note>While Vesta is the Roman goddess of the hearth, the author here identifies her with the Germanic deity Foseti and describes her as the mother of Saturn, casting her as a goddess of the earth's fertility.</note>, the mother of Saturn; she was so named because she clothes the earth with flowers, herbs, and fruits, and she was honored the most in all the Frisian lands. Regarding the idol **Freda** among these, I find nothing else recorded; therefore, in my judgment, this is to be understood as the well-known **Freya** or **Frea**, as their names and armed depictions almost entirely agree. Some wish to consider **Weda** and **Meda** as a single idol; however, I find that both **Weda** and **Mede** had their distinct houses of worship <term>Götzen-Häuser: literally 'idol-houses' or pagan temples</term> in Friesland. **Phoseka**, who is called **Phosta** or **Fosta** for short <note>original Latin: *contractè*</note>, seems to have held the greatest honor among the Frisians, because her temples flourished in all Frisian provinces and islands, as we shall hear in the proper place, God willing! This Frisian **Fosta** is said to be the Roman **Vesta**; their names almost match, as does the depiction, for the Roman **Vesta** is the older one. The goddess **Tellus**, otherwise called **Rhea**, is depicted in the form of an old woman—Rossæus, part 4, *On the Religions of the World*, question 15, page 182—with ears of corn in her right hand—Vossius, book 2, *Theology of the Gentiles*, chapter 52. Her name is said to come from *Vestire* <note>Latin: 'to clothe'</note>, from the clothing of the earth with grass and herbs, flowers and plants, or from her firm-standing power, as Ovidius claims:

->The earth stands by its own force. By standing through force, she is called Vesta.<-
<note>original Latin: *Stat vi terra sua. Vi stando vesta vocatur.*</note>

In this regard, it should be remembered what Natalis Comes writes in book 8 of his *Mythology*, chapter 19: that there were two goddesses named **Vesta**, namely the Elder and the Younger Vesta. The former is said to be the mother of Saturn—or his wife, as others would have it—and the latter his daughter. By the former, one understands the Earth, but by the latter, Fire, as Natalis Comes indicates in the aforementioned place.

### Cimbrian

The land was for the most part taken over, so that the name of the Angles was eventually obscured and remained only in the small territory between the Flensburg Firth and the Schlei River. Danckwerth, in his *Description of the Lands of Schleswig and Holstein*, notes that the aforementioned Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian who wrote 'Germania'</note> explains that this goddess **Herthe** is understood to be the **Earth**. This explanation agrees with the name itself: for if the letter **H** is removed, we have the word **Erte**, or **Earth**. There are still several places and villages in this land called **Herthe**, **Hertethal**, and **Hertestet**, which, by all appearances, were named after this goddess. This **Herthe** was called **Isis** among the Egyptians, **Rhea** among the Greeks, and **Cybele** or **Berecynthea** among the Phrygians. To the Assyrians she was **Atargatis**, and to the Romans she was **Ops**, **Ceres**, **Vesta**, or **Tellus**—which is to say, the **Earth**—and was otherwise generally known as the **Mother of the Gods**.

> Who can doubt that the Mother of the Gods is considered to be the earth?
<note>original Latin: "Quis ambigat, Matrem Deûm terram haberi?"</note>

Macrobius, in book 1 of his *Saturnalia*, chapter 21, asks: "Who doubts," he intends to say, "that the Mother of the Gods is the Earth, or is held to be such?" She is said to be the wife of Caelus <note>the Roman god of the Sky</note> and the mother of all the gods. She was worshipped in the form of an old woman, had towers upon her head, a scepter in her right hand, and keys in her left. Her body was covered in a garment embroidered with grain and herbs, flowers and trees, and she sat upon a wagon drawn by lions or cows, as described in the following 25th chapter. Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a Dutch classical scholar</note> places ears of grain in this goddess's right hand and a drum in her left. Rossæus explains the depiction thus: That the Earth bears all towers and castles; that she brings forth grass, herbs, grain, flowers, and trees from her womb; and that she is an element that holds sovereignty, which is indicated by the scepter and the keys. The movement of her wagon signifies the movement not of the Earth itself, but of its inhabitants. The priest who steers this wagon—of whom we shall read in chapter 25—represents God's governance. On this matter, one may read Augustine’s *The City of God*, book 7, chapters 23 and 24, as well as the commentaries by Ludovicus Vives and Leonhardus Coqueus. See also Rosinus, book 2 of his *Antiquities*, chapter 4; Dempster in his notes on Rosinus; Vossius, book 2 of *Idolatry*, chapters 52 and 62; Rossæus, part 4 of *On the Religions of the World*, question 15, page 182 and following; Natalis Comes, book 9 of *Mythology*, chapter 5; and Clüver, book 1 of *German Antiquities*, chapter 27. It is said that **Herthe**, or **Isis**, invented how the soil should be tilled and sown, and for that reason was elevated into the order of the gods. Compare Rosinus, book 2 of *Antiquities*, chapter 22, and Dempster’s notes on this passage.

§. 4. **Tacitus**, in the aforementioned passage, relates that this goddess **Hertha** was honored on an island in the Ocean <note>original Latin: "Oceani"</note>, in a chaste—that is (as **Cluverius** and **Pontanus** explain), a holy—forest, near a secret water, with special ceremonies, which shall be dealt with, God willing, in the 25th chapter. **Philippus Cluverius**, in the place just mentioned, is of the opinion that **Tacitus** intended the island of **Rügen** here. Meyer** in *Chorographic Maps* <note>original Latin: "Mapp. Chorograph."</note> Table 19. That this **Foste** is **Hertha** herself has already been mentioned. With **Tacitus's** holy forest, where this goddess was worshipped, it agrees remarkably well that in the year 800, a woodland named **Hielgen-Walde** <note>Holy Woods</note> stood on **Heligoland**, as **Johann Meyer** indicates in his aforementioned regional map. With **Tacitus's** consecrated water, with which the idol of **Hertha** was washed, it agrees that in ancient times there was a holy spring on this island, where those who desecrated this hallowed spring were punished with death, as the anonymous author testifies in the *Life of Willibrord* <note>Saint Willibrord was an 8th-century missionary known as the "Apostle to the Frisians"</note> in the tenth chapter. **Tacitus** writes that the **Angles** worship this goddess. Holſat."</note> chapter 13, p. 152. seq. # Chapter XIII
## Concerning the Pagan Idols
### of the Cimbrian Wends.

-> Contents: <-

1. Our Wends had a good and an evil god.
2. And also other idols, such as: **Prove**, **Siva**, and **Ridegast**.
3. Likewise **Swantevit**, who

<column-break/>

was their foremost god.
4. And **Flins**.
5. Believed that there is only one unique God, but that other gods are <unclear>subjected</unclear> to him.

---

The Vandalic peoples <note>Wandalische Völcker: This refers to the Slavic tribes, often called Wends by German writers of this period</note>, who inhabited the **Wagria** region of **Holstein** and the entire southern stretch of the **Baltic Sea**, had a good and an evil god. They believed that all good fortune comes from the good god, and all misfortune from the evil god; the latter they call **Zornboch** <note>original: "Zornboch," likely a variant of Chernobog, the "Black God"</note>, a black god, but the former **Belboch** <note>original: "Belboch," likely Belobog, the "White God"</note>, a white god: **Helmold**, book 1, chapter 53; **Albert Cranz**, *Wandalia*, book 3, chapter 37; **Schedius**, *On the German Gods* <note>original Latin: "de DIS Germon."</note>, section 3, chapter 13.

**Plutarch** describes how this opinion regarding a good and an evil god belonged to most of the oldest philosophers. §. 5. Nevertheless, the Wendish peoples believed that there was one single God, but they maintained that this single God ruled only over heavenly matters. They believed the other gods sprang from his essence and blood, and each was appointed to a specific office to look after things beneath the heavens. The more closely these idols were related to the "God of gods," the greater and more excellent they were said to be. Among these idols, some were over the fields, some over the forests, some over the water, some over sorrow, and some over pleasure and joy: *Helmold, book 1, chapter 48.* <note>Helmold of Bosau, a 12th-century chronicler of the Slavs</note> What these Vandal gods were called by name was shown above in the fourth chapter. ---

Among the worldly-wise <note>A literal translation of "weltweisen," a common early modern term for philosophers</note> heathens, it was a matter of dispute whether the world has existed from eternity, or whether it was created in time. Regarding the first origin of mankind, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> writes that there are two different opinions held by the most highly esteemed naturalists and historians. Some, who hold that the world is without beginning or end, declare that the human race has existed from eternity, without any beginning of generation <note>original: "generation"</note>. Others, on the contrary, who consider that the world was both brought forth and is subject to destruction, confirm that humans as well as the world took their origin at a certain time: *Diodorus Siculus, book 1, chapter 6, page 6.*

§. 2. Our ancestors, the Cimbrians and all the Northern <note>original: "Mitternächtige," literally "midnight" peoples, a term for those living in the far North</note> peoples, were of this latter opinion: that the world was created. The oldest among all the gods is called: **All-Father!** who created heaven and earth, and the air, and all their properties, and what is greatest of all, made man and gave him an ever-living and imperishable soul: so writes the *Edda* <note>The primary collection of Old Norse poems and myths</note>, Part 1, fable 3. In the following sections, this is mixed with poetic myths, such as: fable 4, on the origin of all things; fable 5, on the creation of the first human from stones; fable 6, on the creation of the world from the dead body of the giant **Ymir** <note>original: "Imers"</note>; fable 7, regarding...

## Chapter XV.
### What our ancestors believed regarding the governance of the world.

->Contents:<-

1. Various philosophers have denied God’s providence.
2. Our ancestors believed in God’s providence.
3. As did the Platonic and Stoic philosophers and the poets.
4. Our ancestors were of the opinion that
<column-break/>
the Most High God rules alone in heaven, and has entrusted the government of the elemental world to other idols.
5. The heathens in general are given to this error.
6. As are also the pagan philosophers.

---

Many among the heathens believed that there is no providence <term>providence: the protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</term> or government of God in the world, but that everything happens by chance and accident, and depends on blind fortune. This was the common doctrine of the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, who taught that the gods exist but do not involve themselves in human affairs.</note>, according to the testimony of Plutarch, book 2, *Sentiments of the Philosophers*, chapter 3; Lactantius, book 3, *Divine Institutes*, chapter 17; Eusebius, book 15, *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 4; Seneca, book 4, *On Benefits*, chapter 19; and Josephus, book 10, *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 12; more regarding this can be found in my third dissertation *On the Natural Philosophy of Epicurus* <note>original: "de Philosophia Epicuri Naturali"</note>, chapter 2, paragraph 3 and following. Likewise, Pliny, in the seventh chapter of his second book, considers it a mockery and a laughingstock that God should take care of us humans, believing that the divine nature would be defiled by such a thing. Therefore, he would have everything in the world attributed to blind, fickle fortune. Plutarch agrees entirely with this in the seventh chapter of his first book of *Sentiments of the Philosophers*, seeking to accuse Plato and Anaxagoras of an error because they attributed the creation and government of the world to God. Such heathens are even found among the people of God, who deny God’s providence, as seen in Psalm 10, verses 1 and 13, and Psalm 94, verse 7.

§. 2. On the other hand, the Cimbri <note>A term used here to refer generally to the ancient Germanic and Northern European ancestors.</note> believed in God’s providence: God lives for eternity, He governs His kingdom, and rules all things, whether great or small, above or below, as the *Edda* <note>The primary source for Norse mythology.</note> writes in Part 1, Fable 3. Regarding Aristotle, Laërtius writes in his *Life of Aristotle*, page 283, and Plutarch...

...Plutarch, Book 2, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapter 3; Eusebius, Book 13, *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 7; and Clement of Alexandria, Book 5, *Miscellanies*, page 275, that he alone ascribed the governance of the heaven and the stars to **God’s Providence**, but excluded the **elemental** world <term>elemental world: the physical world below the moon, composed of the four elements of earth, air, fire, and water</term> from it. Others have indeed granted God's governance over the elements, but not over other **elemental** creatures. However, concerning our ancestors, the *Edda* <note>The Prose or Poetic Edda, the primary source for Norse mythology.</note> writes that all creatures—not only the great ones, such as the elements, but also the small **elemental** creatures; not only the creatures above in heaven, like the stars, but also those below on earth and in the water—are subject to **God’s Providence** and governance.

§. 3. The **Platonic philosophers** recognized this through the light of nature; **Plato in the *Epinomis*** writes that **God** cares for the greatest and the most insignificant things in the world. The **Platonic philosopher Plotinus** holds that **God’s Providence** extends from heaven down to the lowest things on earth: according to **Augustine, Book 10, *The City of God*, chapter 14**. The **Stoic philosophers** have placed the entire world, and all things in the world, under **God’s Providence**: according to **Diogenes Laertius in his *Life of Zeno*, page 450**. What the pilot is to a ship, what the driver is to a wagon, what the lead singer is to a dance, what the law of the authorities is to a city, and what the field marshal is to an army—that is **GOD** in the world; so writes the ancient author of the *Book on the World* <note>original: "Buch von der Welt," referring to *De Mundo*, a treatise once attributed to Aristotle but likely written later.</note>, found among the writings of **Aristotle** in the sixth chapter. The **poets** agree; **Horace, Book 1, *Odes*, Ode 12**, describes the highest **God** as he who governs the actions of gods and men, the sea and the earth, and the world.

§. 4. Regarding our Wagrian Wends <term>Wagrian Wends: a Slavic people living in the Middle Ages in what is now eastern Holstein, Germany</term>, **Helmold** writes that they believe in a single **God**; but they imagine that this single **God** rules the heavenly realm alone, while other gods, having sprung from his essence and blood, are appointed each to their certain office to oversee everything that is under heaven. Among these idols, some were over the fields, some over the forests, some over the water, some over sadness, and some over pleasure and joy: **Helmold, Book 1, chapter 84**. It appears that the other **Cimbrian** and especially the **Gothic** peoples shared this error with the Wends, which is what the ***Edda*, Part 1, Fables 19 and following, and 30**, points toward.

Regarding the angels, the **Edda**, Part 1, fable 15, speaks as follows:
> There is a city in heaven called **Alfheim** <note>The realm of the Light Elves in Norse mythology; original: "Alffheymath"</note>; there dwells a people called the white **elves** <note>original: "Alffer"</note>; but the black **elves** dwell below in the earth, who are unlike the others, both in deed and in appearance. The white **elves** are brighter than the sun, but the black ones are blacker than pitch.

This refers to the good and evil angels, as **Dr. Resenius** <note>Peder Hansen Resen (1625–1688), a Danish scholar who published the first printed edition of the Prose Edda in 1665.</note> writes in his *Notes on this passage* <note>original: "Not. ad h.l." / Notis ad hunc locum</note>. Here, the good and evil **elves** or angels are distinguished (1) by their external form: the good angels are called white **elves**, while the evil ones are called black **elves**. It was believed that good angels would reveal themselves in white form, and the evil in black form. The **Holy Scripture** also testifies to the revelation of holy angels in white form: **Mark 16:5, John 20:12, Acts 1:10**, where the white garments indicate holiness and innocence: **Matthew 17:2, Revelation 1:14, 3:4, 5, 18, 7:9, 13**. Evil spirits, on the other hand, are depicted as black, and their nature is called the black art <note>A common historical term for necromancy or malevolent magic.</note>: **Wisdom of Solomon 17:7**. the Papacy <note>original: "Pabstthumb"</note> has adopted this idolatry, in all its circumstances, from the heathens and introduced it into the Church of **God**, as *Doctor Hunnius* <note>Aegidius Hunnius (1550–1603), a prominent Lutheran theologian known for his critiques of the Catholic Church.</note> shows in the fourth chapter of his book on the *Apostasy of the Roman Church*.

§. 2. Furthermore, the idolatry of the heathens consisted in their various sacrifices. Immediately after the Fall, our first parents began their divine service with sacrifice and passed it on to their children: *Genesis 4:3–4*, and through such sacrifice prefigured Christ’s sacrifice on the Cross: *Hebrews 8:3, 5; 9:9, 23.* <note>The original text uses "iix" for 8 and "ix" for 9.</note> Noah renewed this sacrifice after the Great Flood and commanded it to his sons: *Genesis 8:20.* Among Shem’s descendants, and especially in the lineage of *Arphaxad*, the sacrifice was maintained in an unadulterated form until *Moses*, who, by God’s command, explained the manner and fashion of sacrificing and recorded it in writing in his third book <note>The Book of Leviticus.</note>. Among the descendants of the other two sons of *Noah* <note>Ham and Japheth.</note>, the wretched *Satan* corrupted the sacrifice, so that it was offered not to the one true **God**, but to creatures—indeed, to the Devil himself—disguised under all sorts of idol-names; what the heathens sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils: *1 Corinthians 10:20.* Therefore, the sacrifice of the heathens is called an ungodly sacrifice: *Wisdom 12:5*, because it was not brought to the true **God**, nor ordained by Him. *Satan* also attempted this corruption of sacrifice among the people of **God**, and at times succeeded; the prophets lament this, saying that the Jews sacrificed to devils, and even dedicated their children as sacrifices to devils: *Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 106:37–38; Jeremiah 32:35.*

§. 3. The Northern Peoples <note>original: "Mitternächtigen Völcker," literally "Midnight Peoples," a common early modern term for the Scandinavians and Northern Germanic tribes.</note> initially used to sacrifice to their idols in common and without distinction. This lasted among them until, before the birth of Christ, a sorcerer <note>original: "Teufel-Künstler," literally a "devil-artist."</note> named *Mitothin* <note>A figure from Norse legend mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus; he was said to have usurped Odin's place and introduced new religious rites.</note> persuaded the people that one must sacrifice to the idols individually, and bring specific sacrifices to each particular idol: *Saxo, Book 1 of the History of the Danes, p. 13; Olaus Magnus, Book 3, ch. 4.* They also distinguished the sacrifices according to the various feast days; thus the sacrifices became so many and manifold that, due to the great quantity, one could hardly distinguish them. Among the Greeks, there were fifty-eight kinds of sacrifices: *Cornelius Agrippa, Book 3 of Occult Philosophy, ch. 59.* The Egyptians had six hundred and sixty-six types of sacrifice: *Peucer, on Divination, section on Extispicy, leaf 184a; Saubert, on Sacrifice, ch. 1, p. 17.*

§. 4. Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on vegetarianism and ritual.</note> opines that in the beginning, animals were not sacrificed, but rather herbs and fruits; subsequently, however, trees as well as spices were offered: *Porphyry, Book 2 of On Sacrifices <note>original: "de Sacrif."</note>, chapter 1.* Holy Scripture testifies that the first humans sacrificed both the fruits of the field and sheep: *Genesis 4:3, 4.* It was also customary to sacrifice cakes, wine, and milk: *Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist.</note>, Book 2, chapter 22.* Our ancestors sacrificed all kinds of animals, such as: oxen and sheep: *Helmold <note>Helmold of Bosau, a 12th-century chronicler of the Slavs.</note>, Book 1, chapter 53.* Also humans, horses, dogs, and roosters: *Thietmar of Merseburg <note>An 11th-century chronicler.</note>, Book 1 of his Annals, page 10.* and occasionally other birds: *Johannes Petri, Part 1, page 17.* as well as goats: *Pontanus in his Notes on the History of Denmark, page 809.* which the Cimbrian Lombards were accustomed to sacrifice: *Baronius in his Annals for the year 579, number 12.* On high feast days, it was customary to sacrifice nine different kinds of animals, and among them humans as well: *Adam of Bremen <note>An 11th-century geographer and historian.</note>, Book on the Geography of Denmark <note>original: "de Situ Daniæ"</note>, page 153.* and *Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish writer.</note>, Book 3, chapter 7.* Pigs were also sacrificed: *Bangius, Book 5 of the Ecclesiastical History of the Swedes and Goths, chapter 15.* The Wendish <note>A historical name for West Slavic people living near Germanic settlements.</note> peoples also offered cakes and wine to their idols: *Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, author of Gesta Danorum.</note>, Book 14 of the History of Denmark, page 320.*

§ 6. The ceremonies attending the sacrifice were diverse, according to the differences between various peoples; however, in this regard, our ancestors agreed with other European nations. (1) That before the sacrifice, the libation <note>A ritual pouring of a liquid as an offering to a deity.</note> occurred, where the priest tasted a little of the wine or other drink from a cup or horn, and gave those standing around a taste, and thereafter poured the same upon the head of the animal that was to be sacrificed. Afterward, the hair between the horns was plucked from the sacrificial animal and thrown into the fire; this they called *the first offerings* <note>original: "libamina prima"</note>. (2) That during the sacrifice, the animal was brought forward by the sacrificial attendants with its head wreathed in oak leaves, struck upon the forehead with an axe or club, and stabbed with a knife. The blood was caught in vessels, the body opened, and the entrails diligently searched by the soothsayer <note>Often referred to as a "haruspex," a diviner who reads omens in the organs of animals.</note>; finally, it was cut into pieces, and one piece thereof was rolled in flour and burned upon the altar; the Romans called this *to sacrifice successfully* <note>original: "Litare"</note>. (3) That after the sacrifice, a sacrificial meal was held, where the remaining meat was boiled and roasted and consumed by those present. During this, songs of praise and thanks were sung and dances performed to honor the gods: *Cluverius, Book 1 of Ancient Germany, chapter 35. Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 4, chapter 17. Rosinus, Book 3 of Antiquities, chapter 33. M. Beyer in the Additions to Selden's On the Syrian Gods <note>original: "de Diis Syris"</note>, chapter 23, page 173 and following. <unclear>Laurentius</unclear>, Book 3 of the Synopsis of Universal Learning <note>original: "Polymath. Synop."</note>, 5. Saubert, On Sacrifices <note>original: "de Sacrif."</note>, chapters 18 & 19. Casalius, On the Profane Rites of the Romans <note>original: "de Prof. Roman Ritibus"</note>, chapter 15, page 149 and following.*

§. 7. This must be further explained from our antiquities. Before the sacrifice, the first libation occurred, where first the priest and then those present tasted a little of the drink—which in wine-growing lands was commonly wine, but in these northern <note>literally: "midnight"</note> lands was mead <note>An alcoholic drink made by fermenting honey with water.</note>. The Athenians also offered libations of mead or water mixed with honey. To the subterranean idols, they offered water; to Mercury, wine mixed with water and blood. During this libation, one did not only pour something upon the head of the animal that was to be slaughtered and sacrificed, but some of it was also poured upon the altar, or table, or hearth-fire, or upon the ground, or into the sea, to honor the gods. At meals in general, such a libation occurred where some of the food was thrown into the fire, just as some of the drink was poured upon the ground—

This libation <note>original: "Libation"; a ritual pouring of a liquid as an offering</note> was made from a bowl or cup, but among our ancestors, it was made from a horn. It is to be noted that in these Northern lands in ancient times, drinking vessels were commonly horns, which were called cups and bowls; from this, the Greeks derived their names for cups. To illuminate this, the following story serves: When the Gutes or Goths departed from this land and took the island named after them, Gothland, under their military leader Tilvar, it is said that he made an offering to their presumed god, the Moon in its new light. Beforehand, however, he filled a horn with mead <note>original: "Meet"; a fermented honey wine popular in ancient Northern Europe</note>, tasted it, and then poured some from the horn onto the earth, meanwhile thanking the gods with a quiet prayer for a lucky journey and successful business. Afterwards, he is said to have handed this horn to his son and the others standing nearby, who performed the libation with the same ceremonies, one after the other: Strelov in the *Chronicle of Gothland*, page 12. Furthermore, there was another libation made from sacrificial blood; for when the animal dedicated for sacrifice was slaughtered, the blood was collected, which the priest tasted and then poured onto the altar: Saubertus in *On Sacrifices*, chapter 25, page 658; Laurentius Polymath, book 3, Synopsis 3. Likewise, our Wagrian-Wendish <note>The Wagrians were a Slavic people living in what is now Holstein, Germany</note> priests were accustomed to tasting the blood of the sacrifice so that they might hear the oracle more powerfully and so that their gods might appear at the offering: Helmoldus, book 1, chapter 53. When Duke Hasting wished to go to sea with the royal Prince Bjorn, the son of King Ragnar in Denmark, to wage war in foreign lands, he first slaughtered human sacrifices for a lucky journey and—what is even more abhorrent—drank the blood with his followers: Huitfeldt's *Chronicle*, page 111. This blood-drinking is undoubtedly to be understood as the libation, which was sometimes performed with human blood mixed with wine: *The Magdeburg Centuries* <note>A massive 16th-century Protestant history of the Christian Church</note>, volume 4, *History of the Church*, chapter 15, page 1531, which...

### §. 8.
During the offering, the altars, the priests, the sacrificial livestock, and the vessels belonging to the sacrifice were crowned, or rather wreathed, as *Natalis Comes* shows in *Mythology* <note>original: "Mythol."</note>, Book 1, chapter 10, pages 24 and 25. When Paul healed a man born lame at Lystra, the inhabitants believed the gods had come down from heaven; the priest of Jupiter, however, whose temple was before their city, brought oxen and wreaths to the gate and wanted to offer sacrifice along with the people: *Acts of the Apostles* <note>original: "Apost. Gesch."</note>, chapter 14, verse 12. Some interpreters of the Holy Scripture explain this as follows: that only the oxen, dedicated for the slaughter-offering, were decorated with the wreaths, and they argue that it is an oratorical figure of speech called a *hendiadys* <term>Hendyaden: a figure of speech where two words connected by "and" express a single complex idea, e.g., "cups and gold" for "golden cups"</term>, and these "oxen and wreaths" are intended to mean "wreathed oxen": *Beza*, *Piscator*, *Erasmus Schmidius* in *Notes on this passage* <note>original: "Annotat. ad h. l."</note>. However, these sacrificial wreaths are not to be understood as referring to the oxen-wreaths alone, but also to the altar-wreaths as well as the priest-wreaths, with which the altars and priests, as well as the slaughter-offering, were adorned. It was customary to decorate the sacrificial livestock with wreaths, and also likely the church doors, the altars, and the churchyards: *Ernestine Bible on this passage* <note>original: "Biblia Ernestina ad h. l."</note>. The Druids (as our pagan priests were called) performed no sacrifice without oak leaves: *Alexander ab Alexandro*, Book 4, chapter 17, folio 223a. This author explains in the words immediately preceding that crowns or green wreaths were used in the sacrifice and idol-worship; he took this from Pliny, who adds that the priest, dressed in a white robe, climbed the oak tree and cut off a small branch with a golden sickle, which was caught in a white robe, and that the sacrifice then commenced: *Pliny*, Book 6, chapter 44. These are commonly called "sacrificial crowns," but they were actually green wreaths prepared from the green foliage of trees, which differed according to the variety of the idols to whom the sacrifice was made: namely, those of Bacchus were of ivy, regarding which see *2 Maccabees 6, verse 7*; those of Venus were of myrtle; those of Hercules were of poplar; those of Apollo were of laurel branches; those of Plu... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely referring to Pluto</note>

# Cimbrian Practices

However, this is not to be understood as applying to each and every slaughter-offering <term>Schlacht-Opffer; an animal sacrifice intended for ritual consumption or appeasement</term>, but rather specifically to the offering made to the water-idols: *In the sacred rites of the sea gods, the blood of the victims was collected in bowls; they were not struck with an axe but were slit at the throat with knives* <note>original Latin: "In Sacris Deorum marinorum Sanguis victimarum colligebatur, in crateres, nec percutiebantur securi, sed cultris jugulabantur"</note>: *M. Beyer* in his additions to *Selden, On the Syrian Gods*, chapter 23. It is beyond dispute that the slaughter-offering was stabbed, but beforehand it was struck upon the forehead with an axe or a club. That the Cimbri <note>an ancient Germanic or Celtic tribe who threatened the Roman Republic in the late 2nd century BCE</note> performed this is attested by *Dudo* in book 1 of his *History of the Normans*, where he describes how the Goths and Danes dedicated oxen for sacrifice to the god Thor, striking them with a terrible blow to the forehead. His words are: *A pair of oxen were struck once and hard on the head; and with the brain of each shattered by a single, powerful, well-chosen blow, they were laid out upon the ground, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Juga boum una vice duriter icebantur, in capite, collisôque unicuique singulari ictu forte electo cerebrô, sternebantur in tellurem &c."</note> The entire context of this cited Norman historian is referenced in the following 24th chapter, under the first section.

§. 10. The sacrificial blood was handled in various ways. First, it was caught in specially designated tubs made of brass, as the Cimbrian priestesses were accustomed to do, according to *Strabo*, book 7, page 294. After the priest had tasted it from a horn, part was poured onto the altar, as mentioned, and part was poured beneath the altars: *Wormius*, book 1 of *Danish Monuments*, chapter 3. With this sacrificial blood, the walls and benches were smeared using a sponge: *Ibid.*, chapter 4, page 28. Similarly, *Snorri Sturluson* <note>a famous Icelandic historian and poet</note> relates that in Trondheim, Norway, various types of livestock, including horses, were slaughtered for sacrifice at a festival in the idol-temple; the sacrificial blood was collected in vessels and then smeared on all the walls, both inside and out, with a brush or sponge: *Snorri*, part 3 of the *Chronicle of Norway*, number 3, page 75. Furthermore, the sacrificial blood was used to sprinkle the bystanders, the idol and its throne, or the nearby groves and sacred trees: *Schefferus, On Uppsala*, chapter 11, page 139 and following. In Gaul, humans were slaughtered for sacrifice, and the surrounding people were sprinkled with this sacrificial blood: *Camerarius, First Century of Historical Meditations*, chapter 59. This author further relates that in the New World, the Caribbean Caribs are accustomed to smear their idols with human blood, according to the testimony of *Benzoni*, book 2 of the *History of the New World*, chapter 6. # Heathen Religion

...from the sacrificial blood <note>original: "Schlacht-Opffer herfliessendem Blut"</note> flowing out, the priestesses prophesied, as *Strabo* writes in the seventh book, page 294, regarding the Cimbrian <note>an ancient Germanic tribe</note> priestesses. It was considered a good omen if the blood was pleasant to look upon and flowed abundantly from the sacrificial victim; conversely, it was a bad omen if the blood was unsightly and refused to flow freely: *Peucer, On Divination, under the heading "On Extispicy"* <note>the practice of divining the future from the entrails or blood of sacrificed animals</note>, *folio 187.*

§. 11. Among the slaughtered animals, the heads were primarily offered: *Adam of Bremen, On the Geography of Denmark, page 144, and book 4 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 12.* Similarly, the Cimbrian Lombards <note>a Germanic people who famously migrated into Italy</note>, who moved out of this land, were also accustomed to sacrificing the heads of animals in Italy, and especially goat heads: *Hedio, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 19; Baronius, Annals, year 579, number 12.* Just as the head is the highest and most noble limb, where the five senses have their seat, so they believed that this part, above all other limbs, was most fitting as an offering to the gods. The Chinese <note>original: "Sineser"</note> sacrifice pig heads: *Arnoldus in his additions to Rogerius, On Gentilism, chapter 8, page 564.* The Indians <note>likely referring to the peoples of the East Indies</note> offer goat heads: *Rogerius, part 2, The Open Door to Hidden Heathenism, chapter 15, page 392.* Likewise, they offer pig and deer heads: *Olearius in his notes on Mandelslo’s Indian Travels, book 3, page 216.* Among the Egyptians, it was the custom that they threw the head of the slaughtered animal into the water during the sacrifice, with the wish: **That all their misfortune should fall upon this head**: *Alexander ab Alexandro, book 4, chapter 17.*

It was customary to carry the heads around on poles before the sacrifice. Thus, in the year 1066, during the fourth Wendish persecution, the Wends <note>a group of Slavic tribes living in what is now northeastern Germany</note> struck off the head of Bishop John in Mecklenburg, displaying it on a pole as a sign of victory, and then sacrificed it to their idol **Ridegast** <note>a major West Slavic deity of war and hospitality</note>: *Adam of Bremen, book 4, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 12; Helmold, book 1, chapter 23; Albert of Stade, in his Chronicle for the year 1066, page 131.* In the same way, the Philistines struck off the head of the deceased King Saul, displayed it along with his weapons throughout the land, and then sacrificed it to their idols: *1 Samuel 31, verses 8 and 9.* When our ancestors undertook a military expedition, horses were sacrificed; their heads were struck off, placed upon poles, their mouths propped wide open with pieces of wood, and thus carried before the main body of the army: *Olaus Magnus, book 3, chapter 8.*

§. 13. At the slaughtering of the sacrifice, a specially consecrated knife was used, which was employed for no other purpose than the offering. Such a large, broad knife was found on the **Golden Horn** <note>a famous archaeological discovery in 1639 near Tønder, Denmark, consisting of two gold horns decorated with figures</note> near Tønder in 1639; it is engraved with the image of one man about to slaughter another for sacrifice, as discussed in my *Golden Horn, Part 2, chapter 6, §. 5.* Such sacrificial knives among the Greeks and Romans were large and long; their blades were of steel, their handles of ivory <note>original: "Helffenbein"</note>, their fittings of silver, and the nails that fastened the ivory to both sides were made of Cyprian bronze. With this knife the sacrifice was slaughtered, and by all appearances, the head was cut off with it (*Scheffer, in Upsalia, chapter 16, page 292,* considers that the head was hacked off with an axe). One was not permitted to touch the entrails with one's hands before the divination <note>term: "Wahrsagung," the act of foretelling the future through rituals</note>, but had to examine and learn everything using the aforementioned knife: *Peucer, book on the same, page 185; Alexander ab Alexandro, book 4, chapter 17; Camerarius, First Century of Historical Hours, chapter 58.*

# Heathen Religion.

Other priestesses opened the body and prophesied victory and the outcome of war from the entrails: <margin>*Strabo, Book 7, page 294.*</margin> An illustration of this can be seen on the frequently mentioned **Golden Horn** <note>Referring to the Golden Horns of Gallehus, famous 5th-century archaeological finds</note>, where in the third circle a female figure has a man before her to slaughter him as a sacrifice; she has a large knife in her hand and opens the belly with it using four long cuts. Regarding this, I have noted in my book on the Golden Horn at the stated place that two types of sacrifice were in use among the heathens, as *Macrobius* <note>A Roman provincial and author from the 5th century</note> reminds us. The first, he says, is when the will of God is sought from the entrails of the slaughtered victim; he calls this a **Consultative Sacrifice** <note>original: "Hostiam Consultatoriam"</note>, a sacrifice for seeking counsel. The other is that which, without seeking the divine will, is killed as a simple matter and offered to the gods; he calls this an **Animal Sacrifice** <note>original: "Hostiam Animalem," referring here to the physical life or soul of the creature</note>: <margin>*Macrobius, Book 3 of the Saturnalia, chapter 5.*</margin>

§. 15. In the places where the **idol-houses** <note>original: "Götzen-Häuser," a term used by Christian writers to describe pagan temples</note> once stood, "houses of God" [churches] were built upon the introduction of the Christian religion, where such springs bubble forth or streams flow past, as I have noted at various churches.

§. 16. The **sacrificial fire** had to be no ordinary fire, but struck with a flint stone and lit upon the altar, and the sacrifice was to be burned with it: <margin>*Wormius, Book 1 of Monuments, chapter 3, page 7.*</margin> This sacrificial fire had to be lit with **oak wood**: <margin>*Hartknoch, Dissertation 10, Prussian Matters, number 2.*</margin> This wood was otherwise consecrated to the idols in this land, as will be understood in its proper place concerning the **Cimbrian Groves** <note>The Cimbri were an ancient people of the Jutland peninsula; "groves" refers to their sacred natural sanctuaries</note>, God willing. Among other peoples, oak wood was likewise used for the sacrificial fire: <margin>*Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 4, chapter 17; Rosinus, Book 3 of Antiquities, chapter 33; Laurentius, Book 6 of The Polymath, under the entry "Fire" page 449.*</margin> Among the Greeks and Romans, the wood for the sacrificial fire differed according to the distinction of the gods, and for this purpose specific wood-cutters were appointed. Thus, **Bacchus** had fig-wood or the vine; **Venus** had myrtle-wood; **Jupiter** had oak-wood; **Mars** had ash-wood; **Hercules** had poplar or medlar-wood; **Sylvanus** had alder-wood; **Pluto** had cypress; **Cybele** had fir; and **Minerva** had olive-wood dedicated for the sacrificial fire: <margin>*Natalis Comes, Book 1 of Mythology, chapter 10, page 28 M.; M. Beyer in Additions to Selden’s "On the Syrian Gods," chapter 29.*</margin> Furthermore, one **prophesied** from the sacrificial fire; where it burned steadily and clearly, and its flames rose straight upwards and consumed the sacrifice entirely, it was said to be a good sign; otherwise, it was considered an evil omen: <margin>*Peucerus, On Divination, section on "Divination from Entrails," page 192 and following.*</margin>

Beyer in the aforementioned work, chapter 23; Casalius, Book on Roman Rites, chapter 15, page 161 and following.*</margin> Over twenty types of songs in honor of the gods...

# Pagan Religion

...sung and recorded in Laurentius, Book 4 of the *Polymath*, Synopsis 17. Stephanius relates in his *Notes on the Preface to Saxo* <note>Referring to the historian Saxo Grammaticus</note>, page 11 and following, of many and various types of songs common among our ancestors, among which there were undoubtedly some that were sung during sacrifices and **idol-worship**. Regarding this, Adam of Bremen [Adamus B.] says in *On the Situation of Denmark*, page 144: "The dirges <note>original: *Næniæ*</note> that are usually performed in such libation rituals are manifold and unseemly <note>original: *inhonestæ*</note>." This is to say that during the sacrifice (at Uppsala in Sweden) various **fool-songs** <term>Narren-Lieder: a dismissive term used by Christian chroniclers for pagan hymns they considered nonsensical or obscene</term> were performed. The word *Nænia* properly signifies a funeral song or a song of praise for a dead person sung to the pipe during a funeral procession: Festus Pompeius, *On the Signification of Words*, under the letter N, page 112. Such funeral songs among the Romans were commonly foolish songs: Rosinus, Book 2 of *Antiquities*, chapter 19, page 390. Therefore, *Nænia* is commonly taken to mean fool-songs and "rag-songs" <term>Lumpen-Lieder: low-quality, vulgar, or trivial songs</term>. Thus our **Vandalic** <note>The author uses "Vandalic" to refer generally to the ancient Germanic and Slavic tribes of Northern Europe</note> peoples, to honor their idols, are said to have raised songs of praise and thanks during the sacrifice. Concerning the **Prussian Wends** <term>Preuß-Wenden: Slavic-speaking people of the Prussian region</term>, Johannes Meletius reports that they brought their sacrifice to the idol **Pergrub** <note>Pergrubius, a Baltic/Slavic deity associated with spring and agriculture</note> with this song of praise:

> You drive away the winter: You bring back the spring and the dawn. Through you the fields and gardens turn green: Through you the forests bloom, etc.

Johannes Meletius in his *Letter to Georg Sabinus, on the Religion and Sacrifices of the Ancient Prussians*, which is found at the end of Michael Neander’s *Geography*, and in Pontanus’s *Notes on Danish History*.

§. 18. During the sacrifice, the priest called upon the gods so that they might graciously accept it; for no sacrifice happened without prayer: Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 4, chapter 17, folio 224 b. Of our **Druids**, Pliny relates in the 16th Book, the twenty-fourth chapter, that they were accustomed to pray during the offering that God would let this gift be a source of happiness and success for those who brought it. Our **Wendish** priests were in the habit of calling upon their idol **Swantevit** <note>Sventevit, the four-headed chief god of the Slavic Rugians</note> during the sacrifice for goods and riches, and victory over their enemies, as well as for a rich harvest: Saxo, Book 14 of *Danish History*, in the *Life of King Waldemar I*, page 320. The prayer of the Prussian Wends to their idol **Puscheit** <note>Puschkaitis, a Prussian deity of the earth who lived under elder trees</note> is mentioned by Johannes Meletius in the aforementioned place. This prayer of the pagans will be treated in detail in the following 28th chapter.
