# Cimbrian 

§. 19. After the completion of the sacrifice, a sacred meal was held; a portion of the sacrifice—and primarily the head—was brought to the gods and commonly burned upon the altar. The remainder was consumed at this festive meal, where the people ate and drank heartily, while also dancing and playing games: *Helmold, Book 1, Chapter 53; Johannes Peter, Part 1 of the Chronicle, page 17.* <note>Helmold of Bosau was a 12th-century chronicler of the Slavs; Johannes Peter refers to a later historian citing these customs.</note> Where these were private sacrificial meals, they were held at home with good friends; however, if it was a common, public sacrifice, the sacrificial meal took place in the **house of idols** <term>Götzen-Hause: a disparaging term used by Christian authors for a pagan temple</term>: *Saubertus, On Sacrifices, Chapter 26, page 678 and following.* Concerning these communal idol-feasts, more shall be reported—with God's help—regarding the pagan festival times of our ancestors in the following 29th Chapter.

§. 20. The final cause <note>The philosophical "purpose" or "intent"</note> why the heathens sacrificed in such a manner, as has been said, is explained by **Porphyry** <note>original: *Porphyrius*; a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> as follows: "For three reasons," he says, "must one sacrifice: that we might **venerate** <note>original: *veneriren*</note> the gods, that we might show them gratitude, and that we might ask of them what is necessary for us and turn away evil": *Porphyry, Book 2, On Sacrifice, Chapter 1.* <note>Actually referring to Porphyry’s *On Abstinence from Animal Food*</note> These reasons for sacrifice identified by Porphyry are also noted by **Iamblichus** in *On the Mysteries, Chapter 33, page 113*, though he also undertakes to demonstrate at length other various reasons, utilities, and effects of sacrifice. Our ancestors agree with Porphyry regarding these stated reasons for sacrifice. Their primary intention was to honor their idols and to thank them for blessings received. Therefore, the greater their sacrifice was, the greater the honor and gratitude they believed they were showing their gods. To that end, after achieving a victory, they were accustomed to sacrifice to their gods out of gratitude, using both a portion of the booty and the prisoners of war; *Saxo, Book 14, In the Life of King Waldemar I, page 320; Helmold, Book 1, Chapter 23.* <note>Saxo Grammaticus was a medieval Danish historian.</note> According to the decree of **Odin** <note>original: *Othins*</note>, our ancestors sacrificed three times a year: once at the beginning of winter for a prosperous year; secondly, in the middle of winter for a fruitful year; and thirdly, in the summer for the achievement of victory: *Snorri, Part 1 of the Norwegian Chronicle, number 1, page 7.* <note>original: *Snoro*; referring to Snorri Sturluson’s *Heimskringla*</note> Likewise, when famine, high prices, and other **scourges of the land** <term>Land-Straffen: literally "land-punishments," interpreted as divine judgements like plague or drought</term> were at hand, they sacrificed specifically to their gods to avert such scourges: *Snorri, at the place cited above, number 9, page 13.* Thus Iamblichus writes in the aforementioned place that without the effect of sacrifice, we cannot be delivered from pestilence, famine, and high prices.

## §. 20. 
What we have heard so far concerning the sacrifices of our ancestors, they received for the most part through tradition from the holy **Patriarchs** and the people of God, as is shown by a comparison with God's sacrificial laws in the **Third Book of Moses** <note>The Book of Leviticus</note>. Here, the following were prescribed for the people of God:

(1) Various **types of sacrifices**, which differed according to the type of sacrificial animals, the people offering them, the times of sacrifice, the sacrificial debts <term>Opffer-Schulden: referring to guilt or trespass offerings required for specific sins</term>, etc.

(2) All kinds of things to sacrifice, such as: oxen, cows, calves, sheep, lambs, bucks, goats, and birds. Also, cakes and wine: Leviticus 1:11 <note>original: *III. Mos. I. v. 11.*</note>.

(3) To pour the **sacrificial blood** before the Lord onto the base of the altar: Leviticus 4:6; to smear it upon certain limbs of the person: Leviticus 8:23–24; 14:14; and to brush the doorposts and thresholds with the blood of the **Passover Lamb** <note>original: *Osterlambs*</note>: Exodus 12:22–23 <note>original: *II. Mos. XII.*</note>.

(4) To sacrifice the heads of the animals: Leviticus 1:8, 12, 15; 8:20; 9:13; but beforehand to "lift" and "wave" them: Exodus 29:27. This was done in a cross-shape by lifting back and forth toward the four corners of the world, as **Lyranus** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), an influential Franciscan biblical scholar</note> explains.

(5) To wash the sacrifice beforehand: Leviticus 1:9; 8:21.

(6) To burn the sacrifice with the **eternal fire** upon the altar: Leviticus 6:13; and to ignite no **strange fire** <term>frembd Feur: unauthorized or "profane" fire, as in the biblical story of Nadab and Abihu</term>: Leviticus 10:1.

(7) During the festival sacrifice, to strike up magnificent **vocal and instrumental music** with all kinds of songs of praise and resonant instruments: Numbers 10:10 <note>original: *IV. Mos. x.*</note>; 2 Chronicles 35:15–16.

(8) To hold a meal after the completion of the sacrifice. The sacrifice—especially the **thank offering**—is divided into three parts: one part is sacrificed to the Lord, the second part is enjoyed by the priests, and the third part is consumed in a holy place by those who brought the sacrifice: Leviticus 6 and 7.

(9) To adorn the priest with a **holy crown**: Exodus 29:6; 39:30.

(10) To sacrifice for the purpose of being reconciled with God and cleansed of sins: Leviticus 5:10, with respect and outlook toward the **Lord Christ**: Hebrews 9 and 10. Also, that they might thank God for His benefits, which is why it is called a **thank offering**: Leviticus 7.

There, in almost all villages, people tie straw bundles to long poles, light them, and hold them high aloft, and in many places they dance and jump nearby until late into the night. ### Limburgish

...a silver altar was carried before him, while the Persian Sages sang a song (to honor the sun): *Curtius, book 3, chapter 3.* <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus was a Roman historian who wrote a biography of Alexander the Great.</note> This author mentions in the cited place that above the tent of King **Darius**, an image of the sun was set in **crystal** and shone; and that a great horse of the sun followed the holy fire, which was perhaps sacrificed to the sun; for among the Persians, horses were sacred to the sun: *Justinus, book 1, chapter 10*, and dedicated for sacrifice; just as King **Cyrus** sacrificed horses to the sun: *Xenophon, book 8, Cyropaedia.* The sun had its own special priests appointed over the holy fire. One such priestess of the sun was the Persian Queen **Aspasia**: *Justinus, book 10, chapter 2.* **Alexander** the Great ordered the Persians to extinguish this holy fire during the funeral procession of **Hephaestion** <note>Alexander's closest companion and general</note>: *Diodorus Siculus, book 17, chapter 114.*

The idol-houses in which the holy fire burned were called <term>Pyrea</term> <note>Derived from the Greek word "pyr" for fire; the author explains them as "fire-places."</note>. When Bishop **Audas** destroyed such a *Pyreum* and refused to rebuild it, the Persian King **Isdigerdes** <note>Yazdegerd I, who reigned in the early 5th century.</note> not only had this bishop killed but also had all Christian churches in his entire realm torn down and cruelly persecuted the Christians themselves, a persecution which lasted thirty years: *Cassiodorus, book 10, Tripartite History, chapter 30; Theodoret, book 5, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 38.*

The aforementioned author tells a remarkable story regarding this: When **Maruthas**, a bishop in **Mesopotamia**, was sent by the Roman Emperor to the said Persian King, and this king was very well-disposed toward the bishop, the Persian <term>Magi</term> <note>The priestly class of ancient Persia, known for their knowledge of astronomy and fire rituals.</note> feared their king might become a Christian. Therefore, they made a pit in their *Pyreo*, or idol-house, beneath the altar where the holy fire burned, and hid a man in it who was trained for a villainous trick. Now, when the king enters the idol-house to worship the fire, the man hidden in the vault beneath the altar cries out: The king should be cast out, because he honored a Christian priest. At first, the king was greatly dismayed by this, believing it to be a divine voice; but following the advice of Bishop **Maruthas**, he had the area beneath the altar searched and thus discovered the deception. Consequently, the Persian *Magi* were punished, and the Christians were allowed by the king to build churches in his realm and to proclaim the Christian faith: *Cassiodorus, book 10, Tripartite History, chapter 8; Socrates, book 7, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 8.*

# Pagan Religion

The Persians call this idol-fire <term>Orimasda</term> <note>A corruption of *Ahura Mazda*, the supreme deity in Zoroastrianism, often associated with light and fire.</note>; they carried it around daily on certain festival days upon a white horse with great pomp, followed by the King, the Princes of the Realm, and a great multitude of people: *Luther in his Latin Commentary on Genesis 11, folio 147b; Peucer in "On Divination," folio 192.* <note>Martin Luther was the German leader of the Reformation; Caspar Peucer was a 16th-century German scholar and physician.</note> Nowadays, the inhabitants of the great Persian city **Spahan** (which likely refers to the royal residence **Isfahan**) are said to worship fire in an idolatrous manner, just as they do the sun: *Vossius, book 2, "Theology of the Gentiles," chapter 64.* <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius was a prominent 17th-century Dutch scholar.</note> This is also done by the modern **Persians** in the city of **Jazoy** <note>Likely Yazd, a historic center of Zoroastrianism in Iran.</note>, where they tend the holy fire in their temple on Mount **Albors** <note>The Alborz mountain range.</note>; according to their vain claims, it is said to have burned there for three and a half thousand years: *Arnold in his "Additions to Roger’s On Heathenism," chapter 26, page 859.* **Olearius** <note>Adam Olearius was a 17th-century German scholar and diplomat who traveled to Persia.</note> mentions this idol-fire in book 4, "Persian Journey," chapter 20, page 447, adding that it had been abolished in his time. He calls the mountain **Elburs**, which is said to be part of the great **Caucasus** range. In several places in Persia, this holy fire is said to be kept in a pit before the altar; children are purified in it according to pagan custom, while the dead are burned there; and those who have made a vow are said to throw themselves into it alive of their own free will, as the aforementioned **Arnold** cites in the same place from the travel book of **Rabbi Benjamin**. <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented the Middle East.</note>

### [Fire Worship in India and Ceylon]

...or space together, they light a fire of cleaned wood in an earthen vessel, sit around it, and pray. The priest, however, stands by the fire, chatters of many things, and occasionally throws fragrant wood, frankincense, benzoin <note>A balsamic resin from trees in East Asia, used in perfumes and incense.</note>, and fragrant oils into the fire. He, as well as all those sitting around, has his mouth covered with a cotton cloth so that their breath—which they consider unclean compared to the holy fire—does not blow upon the flame. They do not tolerate, whenever they can prevent it, anyone pouring water into the fire. # Pagan Religion

...preserved. If through their negligence the eternal fire were to go out, it was considered an evil omen, which was meant to signify nothing good for the Romans. Any Vestal Priestess who was responsible for this extinguishing of the fire was severely beaten by the High Priest <note>The *Pontifex Maximus*, the chief high priest of the Roman state religion.</note>. The extinguished holy fire was not relit with other common fire; instead, a triangular vessel made of bronze <note>original: "Erz"</note> was placed in the sun with dry tinder, and in this way the fire was caught through the reflection of the sun’s rays. Before and until this relighting occurred, all was quiet and mournful in the city; all business, trade, and commerce were suspended in the meantime: *Rosinus, Book 3, Roman Antiquities, chapter 19; Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 5, chapter 12.* The Roman Emperors had the holy fire carried before them, just like the Persian kings: *Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 1, chapter 28.*

**§. 12.** The Romans took this <term>idolatry</term><note>The worship of idols or excessive devotion to something other than the Christian God.</note> from the Greeks, who maintained the holy fire continually in the Delphic Temple and had appointed unmarried women <note>original: "ehlose Weiber"; likely referring to widows or women past the age of marriage who tended the Prytaneum fire.</note> to guard it. If it happened that this fire went out, it had to be relit through the rays of the sun: *Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 5, chapter 12.* Thus, the oldest *Philosophers* in Greece attributed a divinity to fire and wished to derive the origin of all things from it: *Magdeburg Centuries, Volume 2, Church History, chapter 15, page 252.*

**§. 13.** In the New World, the *Americans* <note>A 17th-century term for the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.</note> worship the sun and maintain a perpetual holy fire for that purpose, for which certain priests are appointed: *Erasmus Francisci, Book 3, "The Guiding Mirror" <note>original: "Speculum"</note>, page 1057.* The inhabitants in *Virginia* dance around the fire, in which their devotion consists: *Alexander Ross, Part 3, "Religions of the World," question 13, page 132.* The *Brazilians* hold fire as highly sacred and commonly carry it with them as a protection against the Devil, who, according to their superstition, is said to be terrified of fire: *Erasmus Francisci, as cited above, page 1003; Alexander Ross, as cited above, question 23, page 145.*

**§. 14.** Thus, the idolatry of the sun and stars primarily consisted of maintaining a perpetual fire in their honor; this idolatry is said to have been first introduced by the first Assyrian Emperor, *Nimrod*, who forced the people into the divine worship of fire: *Alexandrian Chronicle, page 64; Lyndwood, Book 3, Dialogues, chapter 3, folio 37.* For this reason, it is called *Nimrodian* idolatry: *Luther, Latin Commentary on Genesis.*

### Cimbrian

The words of this ancient Teacher of the Church are: This passage shows that the Jews were enslaved to every kind of idolatry and superstition at all times, so much so that in veneration of the Sun, which they believed to be a God according to the custom of the nations, they placed chariots and horses beneath the image they had made, and this in the courtyards of the Lord's temple. Therefore, the local inhabitants are accustomed to bring their sick to this river and to dip them halfway into the water, so that they may be purified of sins. This stream has been held as a universal <term>Idol<gloss>Abgott; in this context, an object of divine worship or a false god from the perspective of the Christian author.</gloss></term> not only by the Indians but also by other heathen peoples, who placed such trust in it that they believed they could be cleansed of sins by any water whatsoever, provided they only think of the river Ganges and say:

# Cimbrian Antiquities

...other field herbs and fruits; likewise, columns of honor, artistically crafted, were dedicated to them: Camerarius, Century 1, *Historical Meditations* <note>original: "Hor. cap. 71" referring to *Horae Subsecivae* (Leisure Hours).</note>, chapter 71.

§. 2. Their sacrifices and idol worship varied; people offered the first fruits of apples and grapes to the **Satyrs** <note>Nature spirits of the woods and mountains, often depicted with goat-like features.</note>, goats to the **Fauns**, milk to the **Sylvans** <note>Deities of the forests; from the Latin "silva" meaning woods.</note>, and milk and honey to **Pan**: Natalis Comes, book 5, *Mythology*, chapter 6 and following. Otherwise, at other times or in other places, it was customary to sacrifice a lamb to the Fauns, a pig or goat to Sylvan, and a badger to Pan: Rossæus, Part 4, *On the Religions of the World*, question 5, page 166; Laurentius, book 3, *Synopsis of Polymathy* 3, page 196.

§. 3. In Rome, on the 15th of February, a special festival called **Lupercal** <note>The Lupercalia, an ancient Roman festival focused on purification and fertility.</note> was held for the idol Pan. The priests of this idol were called **Luperci**, who celebrated this feast naked. The shepherds sacrificed naked during this festival; the young men who attended were also naked and bare, and they all danced, leaped, and played together. Even the most prominent people and the Roman Emperors took part in this festival, for Pan was the most significant idol in Rome. During this feast, goats and dogs were sacrificed to him, and this sacrifice was performed in a cave. The Pan-priests, the Luperci, hung the hides of the slaughtered goats around themselves, jumped about, and struck those they encountered with leather straps. This festival was celebrated so that the livestock might be protected from wolves and that women might become fertile. To that end, barren women ran toward the Pan-priests and allowed themselves to be struck with the leather straps, believing that they would thereby become fertile: Fenestella, book 1, *On Roman Priests*, chapter 1; Pomponius Laetus, book 2, *On Roman Priests*, chapter 1.

Mos. XVII. v. 7." (The Third Book of Moses).</note>. The children of Israel are punished for this idolatry, having sacrificed to the field-devils: **Deuteronomy 32:17** <note>original: "v. Mos. Our ancestors held house-snakes and Kobolds <note>Legendary house spirits or goblins in German folklore, often believed to help with chores or guard the home.</note> to be House Gods, as was reported above in the eighth chapter. They performed their prayers before the house-snakes. An image of this idolatry is presented to us on the Golden Horn <note>Referring to the Golden Horns of Gallehus, famous archaeological finds from 1639 in Denmark, which featured intricate carvings of mythological scenes.</note> found in the year 1639 near Tønder; there, in the first circle, one can see in three places how snakes were worshiped by people with raised hands and bent knees, as is explained in my *Golden Horn*, Part 2, Chapter 2.

§. 2. The Prussian Wends, Lithuanians, and Samogitians <note>People from Samogitia, a cultural region in present-day Lithuania.</note> have their house idols. They are accustomed to inviting the snakes to a guest-feast once a year, where the priest lures the snakes out of their holes by the stove through his prayer. Now, when the snakes—upon the priest’s prayer—come straight out and to the table and taste the served food, they considered that a good omen; otherwise, however, it was to be an evil sign: *Camerarius*, Century 1, *Leisure Hours*, chapter 69 <note>original: "Camerar. cent. 1 Hor. cap. 69"</note>; *Pontanus* in *Notes on Danish History*, p. 810; *Hartknoch*, *Dissertation 10 on Prussian Matters*, thesis 4. *Balduinus*, in his *Commentary on 2 Corinthians 11, verse 3, page 714*, cites the story of Jerome of Prague <note>original: "Hieronymi Pragensis," a Bohemian scholar and reformer who traveled as a missionary to the Baltics.</note> regarding how he preached the Gospel in Lithuania and saw there that every father of the house kept a snake in the corner of his home and brought it both food and sacrifices. The very same thing is also testified by *Aubanus*, book 3, *On the Customs of All Nations*, chapter 7 <note>original: "Aubanus lib. 3. de Morib. G cap. 7," referring to the work of Johannes Boemus.</note>.

§. 3. People generally offered milk to snakes and nourished them with it, which was a widespread custom throughout the Northern world: *Olaus Magnus, book 21, chapter 29.* The Prussian Wends <note>A historical term for Slavic peoples living in proximity to Germanic territories.</note> kept snakes in old, hollow oak trees and nourished them with milk; the women would go there at certain times and pray to the snakes for the purpose that their husbands might receive the strength to father children: *Hartknoch, as cited.*

§. 4. The most gruesome fact is that the Estonians and Livonians <note>People from regions in the modern-day Baltic states of Estonia and Latvia.</note> not only worshipped snakes and dragons but also sacrificed living humans to them; however, these victims had to be without any blemish or defect on their bodies: *Adam of Bremen, book on the Geography of Denmark, page 146.* In Poland, people daily sacrificed three head of cattle to a monstrous dragon, and yet even human lives were not spared: *Münster, book 4, Cosmography, chapter 48, page 1240; Franz, Part 4, History of Animals, chapter 5, page 863.*

§. 5. Regarding the snake-idolatry of the ancient heretics, who were called Ophites <note>From the Greek *ophis*, meaning "snake."</note> but otherwise known as Gnostics, this was discussed above in the eighth chapter. These people regarded the serpent of Paradise as Christ, and therefore, in the practice of the Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note>, they used snakes which were summoned by the priest’s conjuring from caves onto the nearby altar. There, the snakes tasted or licked the sacramental bread. For they believed that the bread was then blessed, and they partook of it; meanwhile, they kissed and worshipped the snakes. To this point belong the testimonies of the Holy Fathers:

> They magnify the serpent to such an extent that they prefer it even to Christ himself. They bring it in to bless their Eucharist. <note>original Latin: "Serpentem magnificant in tantum, ut illum ipsi Christo præferant. Ipsum introducunt ad benedicenda Eucharistica sua, Tertullianus de Præscript. Hæred. cap. 47."</note>

> They keep a real snake, which they feed and venerate; when the priest chants, it comes out of its cave and climbs upon the altar placed near the cave, and it licks their offerings, and wrapping itself around them, it returns to the cave, as if they were sanctified by the serpent-Christ. <note>original Latin: "Habent verum colubrum, quem nutriunt, & venerantur, qui & incantante Sacerdote e spelunca egreditur, & ascendit super Altare innixum speluncæ, & oblationes eorum lambit, & involvens circa eas regreditur ad speluncam, quasi a serpente Christo sanctificatas, Augustinus de Hæresibus cap. 17."</note> They not only break the bread in which the serpent has entwined itself and hand it to those receiving it, but each person greets the serpent and kisses it on its mouth, whether because the serpent has been charmed into tameness by some trick or through some other operation of the Devil to deceive them, with the little animal behaving gently... <note>original Latin: "Non solum frangunt panes, in quibus serpens involutus est, & accipientibus tradunt , sed unusquisque salutat serpentem, & osculatur ex ore , sive per præstigias quasdam serpente ad mansuetudinem incantata , sive ex alia Diaboli operatione, ad hos decipiendos, ipso animalculo blandiente, a-"</note>

# Pagan Religion.

...they adore this, and give thanks <note>original: "dorant hunc, & gratiarum actiones dicunt"</note>: Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 37.

§. 6. The fire-hearths were the altars of the household gods; thus among the Romans, this phrase arose: *For altars and hearths* <note>original: "Pro aris & focis"</note>; to fight for one’s altars and hearths. The firstfruits of the harvest were sacrificed to them, and daily a portion of the evening meal was offered as a libation <note>A ritual pouring of a liquid, or in this case, a small offering of food into the fire</note>: Salmuth in Pancirollus, book 1, title 46, page 219. During meals, the household gods were the first to receive a libation. This libation was performed by throwing some food and drink into the fire: Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, chapter 21, folio 297 b; Saubertus, *On Sacrifices*, chapter 25. This is something the idolatrous Livonians <note>People from the Baltic region of Livonia</note> still do in our own times: Olearius, book 2, *Persian Journey*, chapter 9, page 109. Among the Romans, a festival called the *Lararia* <note>A festival dedicated to the Lares, the protective spirits of the household</note> was celebrated for the household gods on December 23rd: Rosinus, book 4, *Roman Antiquities*, chapter 16, page 650; Dresserus, *On Heathen Festivals*, page 247: "What is more sacred? What is more fortified by every religious scruple than the house of each individual citizen? Here are the altars: here are the Penates <note>The Roman gods of the household and the larder</note>: here the ceremonies of sacred religion are contained," Cicero, *Oration XXIX, For His Own House*.

§. 7. The <term>Genius</term> <note>A personal protective spirit believed by the Romans to accompany a person from birth until death</note> was specifically worshipped on birthdays and was regarded as a birth-god. He was honored with a drink-offering of wine, as Persius exhorted: *Pour pure wine for the Genius* <note>original: "Funde merum Genio"</note>; Leonhard Coquaeus in Augustine, book 7, *The City of God*, chapter 13, page 647. For this reason, the Genius is depicted as pouring wine from a bowl onto an altar: Herold, book 5, *On the Gods of the Nations*, near the beginning. People also swore oaths by the Genius, just as the Romans were accustomed to swearing by the Emperor’s Genius: Leonhard Coquaeus, as cited.

§. 8. Among the household gods, our ancestors also gave divine honors to cows and oxen, as was mentioned above in the 8th chapter under the 30th proposition. This divine worship was undoubtedly a form of symbolic idolatry and primarily consisted of religious adoration. Just as the Israelites did before their golden calf in Exodus 32:1, so the Cimbri <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic people who threatened the Roman Republic</note> are said to have performed their idolatry before a bronze image of an ox and to have sworn their oaths there. Plutarch alludes to this with these words: "The barbarians (Cimbri), having attacked the fortress that was across the Adige, captured it; [admiring] the bravery of the Romans, who had proven themselves the finest of men and had fought as was worthy of their fatherland..." <note>original: "Barbari (Cimbri) propugnaculum, quod erat trans Athesim aggressi ceperunt, Romanorumque virtutem, qui se optimos viros præstiterant, utque patria dignum fuerat, pugnaverant..."</note>

### Cimbrian History

...they admired them and, having given their word, dismissed them, **SWEARING BY THE BRONZE BULL** <note>original: "JURATO ÆNEO TAURO"</note>: Plutarch in *The Life of Marius*, chapter 13, page 60, volume 2. The Indians show cows and monkeys the kind of honor that belongs to no one but the true God; Tavernier <note>Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605–1689) was a French gem merchant and traveler whose accounts of India were highly influential in Europe</note>, in his *Travel Descriptions*, part 2, book 3, chapter 5, page 153 and chapter 7, page 157, relates that the Indians consider themselves blessed when they die with a cow's tail in their hand. And in another place, this author writes that the dying lie down beneath the hindquarters of the cow and watch for the cows to pass their water on them, for then they shall die blessed. The Banians <note>original: "Benjanen"; a term historically used by Europeans to refer to Hindu merchants or Hindus in general</note> in India make small cakes out of cow dung, and especially out of rice grains found within the cow dung, which their priests bless and regard as a holy relic <note>original: "Heiligthum"</note>, giving them to the sick to eat, as Volquart Iversen mentions in his *East Indian Travel Description*; he also relates that the Indians solemnly marry their oxen and cows when they are one year old through the following ceremonies: They are first led to the water with ropes and washed for a good while; meanwhile, the priest stands by the water, makes strange gestures with his hands, and cries out to them. During this time, a fire is lit by the water, into which the priest throws all sorts of spices. The beasts stand with their hind feet in the water and turn their heads toward him; he places new ropes around their necks, holds their muzzles together, and marks them on the forehead with a stroke of yellow paint, and lets them be led around the fire several times while he reads from a book with strange gestures. Then he throws fragrant things into a copper fire-pan filled with glowing ashes and incenses the joined <note>original: "copulirte"; meaning the ritually wedded pair</note> beasts under the head, belly, and tail, leads them five times around the fire with a mumbling voice, and holds tail to tail so that they touch. After the marriage is completed, these beasts are brought home accompanied by many men, women, and children, who are received with a wedding feast: Volquard Iversen, book 4, *Oriental Travels* <note>original: "Itiner. Orient."</note>, edited by the famous Olearius <note>Adam Olearius (1599–1671) was a German scholar and diplomat who published accounts of travel to Persia and India</note>, chapter 13, pages 207–208. In the notes to this passage, the famous Olearius cites an example from Sanson’s *Geography* <note>Nicolas Sanson (1600–1667), a pioneering French cartographer</note> that a Banian Indian spent ten or twelve thousand ducats <note>A significant fortune in gold coins, emphasizing the ritual's importance to the devotee</note> on a wedding for his cow married to the ox of his good friend. The aforementioned Volquard Iversen relates in the cited place that the Indian women watch for when such betrothed beasts pass water, which they [hold] as a holy relic...

### Chapter XXII.
# Of Sacrifices and Idolatry
## to the Deities of Hell and Death.

->Contents:<-

1. The sick have offered sacrifices to the deities of hell and death.
<column-break/>
2. These same deities were also consulted as oracles regarding the future fortune of children.

To offer sacrifices to the deities of hell and death was a custom especially during illnesses, both among our ancestors and other pagan peoples. Regarding those who became healthy again after suffering an illness, the common folk in North Jutland <note>original: "Nord-Cimberland"; the Cimbrian Peninsula corresponds to modern Jutland</note> are still accustomed to say: "He has reconciled himself with Hel" (which is what the Nordic peoples call Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld</note> and Proserpina <note>The Roman queen of the underworld</note>): "He has sacrificed something to Hel": "He has given Hel a bushel of oats <note>original: "Haber"</note> to feed her horse." This originates from paganism, as was indicated above in the ninth chapter. Likewise among the Greeks and Romans, those who had recovered from illness were accustomed to bring a sacrifice of black cattle to Pluto and his kindred deities of hell, which had to be done during the nighttime. Those who performed the sacrifice had to be clothed in black garments: Natale Conti <note>original: "Nat. Comes"; an influential 16th-century Italian mythographer</note>, *Mythology*, book 1, chapter 12. Compare Stephen's Notes on Saxo <note>Stephanus Johannis Stephanius, a 17th-century scholar who annotated Saxo Grammaticus</note>, book 1, page 54. Our ancestors brought such black sacrifices to the idol Freyr <note>original: "Fro"</note>: Saxo, book 1, *Life of King Hadding*, page 16.

§. 2. Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the "Gesta Danorum"</note> mentions that the Danish people were accustomed to consult the oracles of the Fates <note>original: "Parcer"; referring to the Parcae of Roman myth</note> (who were goddesses of death, called Norns <note>original: "Nörmer"</note> in this land) to ask how things would go for their children in the future. He further relates that King Fridleif <note>original: "Friedleff"</note> of Denmark is said to have done this for his son, for whom some among the Fates predicted good things, while others predicted evil: Saxo, book 6, *Life of King Fridleif*, page 102.

# Chapter XXIII.
# Of the Sacrifices and Idolatry
### of the Goths' Gods.

->Contents:<-

| | |
|----------|----------|
| 1. They sacrificed humans to their idol (Thor), as well as oxen and bread; of Thor’s hammer. | 3. Of the idolatry of Freya; her sacrifice was a sacred pig. |
| 2. To their war-idol Othin they sacrificed humans. | 4. Black livestock were sacrificed to the idol Fro. |

The gods of the Goths and Danes were: Thor, Othin, Frey, Fro, and These or Thiese, of whom we spoke in the preceding 10th chapter. To the idol Thor, not only livestock but also humans were sacrificed; this is attested by Dudo <note>Dudo of Saint-Quentin (c. 965–1043), a historian and dean who wrote one of the earliest histories of the Normans</note> in Book 1 of the *History of the Normans*. The Danes, he says, sacrificed to their god Thur not only of the large and small livestock, but they also slaughtered human blood for him, believing that this sacrifice was the most precious, which the priest ordained by lot. Alongside this, oxen were also slaughtered and struck to the ground with a terrible blow to the forehead; they smeared their heads with the blood, etc. The author's words read thus:

> In former times, those worshiping Thur, their god, used to sacrifice to him, to whom they slaughtered not some of the cattle or flocks, but the blood of humans, thinking it the most precious of all burnt offerings, with a sacrilegious priest preordaining this. Yokes of oxen were at one time violently struck on the head, and each one, having its brain crushed by a single blow by chance, was laid low on the earth; and the entrails were searched on the left side, namely the vein of the heart, from which the blood was drained, and according to their custom, they smeared their own heads [with it]. <note>original Latin: "Sacrificabant olim venerantes THUR, Deum suum, cui non aliquid pecudum, atque pecorum, sed sanguinem mactabant hominum, holocaustum omnium putantes pretiosissimum, Sacerdote sacrilego hoc prædestinante. Juga boum una vice diriter icebantur, in capite, collisoque unicuique singulari ictu forte electo cerebro sternebantur in tellurem, perquirebaturque levorsum fibra, cordis scil. vena, cujus exhausto sanguine, ex more suo, suorum capita linentes."</note>

In Jutland, in the lordship of Nord-Hold, there is a spring called Thor's Well <note>original: "Thors-Brunn"</note>, where in ancient times human sacrifices were said to have been slaughtered for this idol. Wormius <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a famous Danish physician and antiquary known for his collection of curiosities and study of runes</note> mentions this well in Book 5 of *Monuments*, page 285, reporting that a noble lord named Thor is said to have sacrificed his son to the gods at this well. Others wish to derive this well's name from the idol Thor—

§. 3. The idol **Sater** was worshiped on Saturday, which day received its name **Saturday** from him. # Cimbrian Antiquities

...slaughtered. Everything before the idol of **Sater** <note>Sater is the Saxon name for the god associated with Saturday, identified here with the Roman Saturn.</note> was filled with the noise or sound of flutes and drums so that the wailing of the slaughtered (children) could not be heard. <note>original Latin: "Scientes prudentesque suos ipsi liberos sacrificabant..." — Plutarch, *On Superstition*.</note> Knowing and understanding what they did, they sacrificed their own children; those who had no offspring bought infants from the poor like lambs or young birds for this purpose. The mother stood by without mourning or groaning; if she uttered a cry or wept, she was fined the price of the sacrifice, yet the infant was slaughtered nonetheless. Everything before the image was filled with the sound of pipes and drums so that the cries of the slaughtered could not be heard.

**Diodorus Siculus** writes in the aforementioned place—and from him, **Ludovicus Vives** in his *Commentary on Augustine’s City of God*, Book 7, Chapter 19, page 665—that among the Carthaginians, the idol of **Saturn** was made as a very large bronze colossus, hollow on the inside, with long curved arms and filled with fire, where children were burned alive. **Ludovicus Vives** also reminds us that the Spaniards, during their voyages to the New World, found an island named "Charles’s Island" after their king <note>Referring to King Charles V; the island is likely Cozumel or another Caribbean location described by early explorers.</note>, and discovered many hollow bronze idols there which were heated with fire from within, and children were burned there as sacrifices. **Zepperus** also mentions this in *Mosaic Laws*, Book 4, Chapter 4, page 265.

When **Alexander the Great** hard-pressed the city of **Tyre** in Phoenicia during a siege, the inhabitants deemed it necessary to sacrifice boys to **Saturn**, a practice the Carthaginians had learned from them as their ancestors: **Curtius**, Book 4, Chapter 3. The peoples in **Gaul** also offered humans as sacrifices to **Saturn**, as **Augustine** indicates in the aforementioned place. 

The Romans and Greeks also sacrificed humans to **Saturn** and held a festival in the winter month with lit candles, calling upon him for a fruitful year. At the sacrificial banquet, the masters had to serve their servants: <note>This refers to the Saturnalia, a winter festival where social roles were famously reversed.</note> **Dresser**, *On Festivals*, page 244; **Josephus Laurentius**, *Polymath*, Book 1, Dissertation 9, and Book 2, Dissertation 45, following **Macrobius**, *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Chapter 7, pages 276, 277. The Assyrians used to hold such a festival called **Sacran** <note>Also known as the Sacaea, a Babylonian/Assyrian festival of social reversal.</note> where the masters likewise had to perform services for their servants: **Selden**, *On the Syrian Gods*, Synthesis 2, Chapter 13; **Beyer** in his additions to this place, page 321.

It is said that the ancient Saxons, particularly those who were warriors, would ride alternately round and around before the **Irminsul** <term>Irminsul: A monumental pillar-like object, often a tree trunk, which the ancient Saxons worshipped as a symbol supporting the entire world.</term> on specific feast days, clad in armor and carrying a mace in their hands; they were required to kneel or bow before it in their armor. Concerning these twelve chief deities, **Johann Herold** <note>Johann Herold (1514–1567) was a Swiss-German humanist known for his works on Germanic mythology and history.</note> wrote six books, in which he describes at length their origins, names, images, sacrifices, idolatry, governance, offices, temples, feast days, etc. He shows how to each of these twelve deities was dedicated and assigned a particular month in the year; a particular sign of the heavens <note>A zodiac sign.</note>; a particular power of the elements; a particular limb of the human body; a particular animal on earth; a particular fish in the water; a particular tree in the forest; and particular metals and minerals in the earth.

§. 2. On **Heligoland** <note>original: "Heiligland," literally "Holy Land"</note> the goddess **Herthe** is honored, as was indicated in the preceding twelfth chapter, and humans were also sacrificed to her. **Tacitus** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian whose work *Germania* is a primary source for early Germanic tribes.</note> describes her idolatry in his book on Germany, in the following manner: The **Angles** <note>original: "Angler"</note> and the neighboring peoples honor Herthe, that is, Mother Earth, and believe that she is present among the children of men. There is a sacred grove on an island in the Ocean, and within it a consecrated wagon covered with a cloth, which no one is permitted to touch except the priest; when he perceives that the goddess is present in the sanctuary, he follows the wagon upon which the goddess travels, drawn by cows, with great veneration. When this occurs, a joyful festival is held, and the places which she dignifies with her arrival are kept as solemn holidays. For then they know nothing of war or war-gear, but only of peace and quiet. This lasts until the goddess Herthe no longer wishes to be among the company of mortal men, at which point the priest leads her back into the temple. Immediately after this, he washes the wagon, the cloth, and the idol in a hidden lake. The servants who assist in this are immediately drowned by the same lake. From this arises a secret terror and a holy ignorance of what it might be that only those who perish are allowed to see. The words of Tacitus run thus: 

The Angles worship **Hertha**, that is, Mother Earth <note>original: "Angli-Hertham, id est, terram matrem colunt"</note>, and they believe that she intervenes in human affairs and is carried among the peoples. They do not enter into wars, they do not take up arms; every iron tool is locked away; peace and quiet are then alone known and then alone loved, until the same priest returns the goddess to her temple, she having had her fill of the conversation of mortals. §. 3. It was indicated above that **Herthe** <note>The Germanic goddess Nerthus or Hertha, often identified with Mother Earth.</note> is the Mother of the Gods, **Rhea**. What **Tacitus** writes here concerning the <term>idolatry</term> <note>original: "Götzendienst," referring to non-Christian religious practices.</note> of Herthe practiced among the **Frisians** and neighboring peoples is likewise written regarding the worship of Rhea among the **Phrygians**, **Romans**, and **Greeks**. Her festival was celebrated annually in April, at which time her idol was led around on a special wagon drawn by lions or cows, and finally washed in the river **Almo**, which flows into the **Tiber**. The wagon, or the cows before the wagon, are strewn with fresh flowers. During this festival, the most precious and magnificent things were paraded in the city of Rome to honor the goddess; simultaneously, horns were blown, and pipes and drums were played and sung to, and some money was also offered to the goddess. # Chapter XXVI
## Concerning the Idolatry and Sacrifices
### of the Gods of the Wends.

->Contents:<-

1. On the sacrifices and <term>idolatry</term> <note>original: "Götzendienst," a term used by historical Christian writers to describe non-Christian religious practices.</note> of Swantevit.
2. Humans were also sacrificed to this idol.
3. On the sacrifices and idolatry of Prove.

The <term>Vandalic peoples</term> <note>The author refers here to the Wends (West Slavs), whom early modern historians often conflated with the ancient Vandals.</note> showed great honor to their idol, Swantevit. Once a year, after the harvest, all the people gathered before the idol's temple to celebrate a great festival, and therein to slaughter and sacrifice cattle and to hold an idolatrous feast. The day before the sacrifice and service, the priest had to diligently sweep the <term>church</term> <note>original: "Kirche." The author uses the Christian term for "church" to refer to the Slavic temple.</note>; however, while sweeping, he had to take care not to draw breath inside the church, so that the god might not be defiled by human breath. Therefore, the priest always had to stick his head out the door whenever he wished to catch his breath. On the following feast day, during the assembly of the people before the church door, the priest took the horn from the hand of the idol. This horn had been filled with wine the previous year, and from it, he would prophesy the fertility of the coming year. For if the wine in the horn had greatly decreased, it was taken as a sign of an infertile year; otherwise, they had reason to hope for a fruitful year. Thereupon, the priest poured the old wine out of the horn at the idol's feet and poured in fresh wine. He drank a toast to the idol and prayed that he would grant his people and their fatherland goods and riches, and victory over their enemies. Then he drank the horn of wine dry, filled it again, and placed it back into the hand of the idol. Round cakes, made of flour and <term>mead</term> <note>original: "Meet," a traditional fermented honey drink.</note>, were offered to the idol; these were as large as a man. The priest placed these large cakes between himself and the people and prayed for a rich harvest

§. 3. To their other idols, such as: **Prove** of Altenburg, **Siva** of Ratzeburg, and **Ridegast** <note>Also known as Radegast, a major West Slavic deity associated with hospitality, war, and the city of Rethra.</note>, the gods of the Meckelburgers, the Wends brought bloody sacrifices of Christian people, oxen, and sheep on public feast days. When the sacrifice was completed according to custom, the idol-feast began, during which they played music and danced: Helmold, Book 1, Chapter 53; Krantz, Book 3, *Wandalia*, Chapter 37. In **Wagerland** <note>Wagria, the northeastern region of Holstein, Germany.</note>, the Wends honored the idol **Prove**, who was worshipped in a forest east of the city of **Altenburg** <note>Now Oldenburg in Holstein.</note>. His image stood upon a large oak tree with many branches, so that everyone could see the idol; arranged in a circle around it stood a great multitude of other idols, some of which had two, some three, four, or more faces. Before this idol of Prove, an altar was built upon which they used to sacrifice to the god; it was surrounded by a high fence with two gates. No one was permitted to touch the tree except for the priest of the idol. On holidays, the common people were summoned by the priests into this idol-court; everyone came with wife, children, and servants—some brought oxen, some sheep, some birds, which they sacrificed to the idol. The priests of Prove were called **Mycke**: Krantz, Book 4, *Wandalia*, Chapter 11.

## Chapter XXVII
# Concerning the Abominable Human Sacrifices of our Ancestors.
### Table of Contents:

7. Thus **Jephtha** sacrificed his only daughter.
8. And the King of the **Moabites** his son.

10. **Fro** <note>Likely referring to the legendary Danish King Frotho or the Norse god Freyr.</note> is the first originator of this abomination among the Cimbrians.
11. How the Cimbrians conducted their human sacrifices.

Here our eyes might overflow, our hair stand on end, our ears ring, our tongue stick to the roof of our mouth, our heart tremble, our mind be astonished, and our limbs go numb, when we consider the abominable human sacrifices of our ancestors. In these rites, one human was slaughtered for another—a father his own child, or subjects their king or prince—just like a head of cattle, and offered up to the Devil. Here, the ancient Church Father **Lactantius** <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who critiqued pagan practices.</note> cries out: "O, what insanity! What more could the idols do to them (the heathens) when they are most enraged, than what they do when they wish to be merciful?" <note>original Latin: "O dementiam! Quid amplius facerent hostiles Dii, si essent iratissimi, quam faciunt cum volunt esse propitii?"</note>

**§. 4.** We wish to further investigate what this author records regarding the human sacrifices of the Americans. The Americans in Peru are most devoted to the gruesome practice of human sacrifice; they slice open the person’s belly up to the chest, tear out the living and warm heart, and sacrifice it to the Sun. Then they roast the body and devour it. Every ten years, they sacrificed many boys for the health and welfare of their *Juga* <note>The author likely uses "Juga" as a corruption of *Inca*, the title of the ruler of the Incan Empire.</note> or King. This terrifying sacrifice of young children happened especially if he was waging war, so that he might have better fortune and obtain victory. At the time of his coronation, over two hundred boys would be sacrificed, along with a significant number of those who were drawn from the monasteries for the service of the *Juga*: Arnold, in *Additions to Roger on Paganism*, Chapter 40, pages 986 and 992 following, from Acosta’s *History of the Indies*, Book 5, Chapter 19 following.

The Mexicans sacrificed up to twelve thousand children every year to the vile devils upon the altars. The entrails, along with the hearts—still living—were taken out, and the priests burned them upon glowing coals as a "pleasing aroma" to the devils. On the three "Sacrifice Islands," as they are called by the geographer, they sacrifice boys and girls to their idols: Arnold, in the place cited above, page 987. In New Spain <note>The colonial name for the territories centered on modern-day Mexico.</note>, children were sacrificed: first when the seeds began to sprout; likewise when the corn stood a foot above the earth; and again when it was two feet high. On certain feast days, they sacrificed a woman; on other holidays, a small boy and girl were drowned. The merchants had their own particular god and feast day, on which they slaughtered a man and sacrificed his heart to the Moon at midnight: Rossæus, Part 3, *On the Religions of the World*, Question 19, page 141 following. The place where the Jews sacrificed their children to *Moloch* was the beautiful Valley of *Benhinnon* <note>The Valley of the Son of Hinnom</note>, otherwise called *Tophet* and the *Valley of Slaughter*: *Jeremiah VII, v. 31, 32.* It was located right by *Jerusalem* toward the south <note>original: "gegen Mittag," literally "toward midday," a historical term for the south.</note>, surrounded by a pleasant forest through which the spring of *Siloah* flowed: *Bunting, Part 1, Itinerary of Holy Scripture, page 60.* *Benhinnon* means as much as a "wailing son" <note>Derived from the Hebrew *ben* (son) and *hinnon*, which the author associates here with lamentation.</note> / to indicate / that the Jewish sons there lamented with "Ah" and "Woe" during the burnt offering: *Crellius in the Biblical Concordance under the word Benhinnon*. §. 11. How our ancestors handled **human sacrifice** and previously prophesied of future things from their blood and entrails is recounted by **Strabo** <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian whose work provides a vital record of the ancient world.</note> in his seventh book, with the report that the **Cimbrian** <note>The Cimbri were an ancient people, likely of Germanic or Celtic origin, inhabiting the Jutland peninsula in modern-day Denmark.</note> priestesses brought the prisoners to a bronze cauldron, opened their throats with a sword or knife, and prophesied from the blood flowing into the aforementioned cauldron. Other priestesses opened the body and, from the inspection of the entrails, prophesied regarding victory and the outcome of the war. The author's words are: <note>original: "Sacerdotes divinationis peritæ captivis per caſtra, ſtriktis gladiis, occurrebant, quos ſternentes humi, ad craterem æneum protrahebant, amphoras circiter viginti capientem. Habebant autem pulpitum, quo agiliter aſcenſo ſuper craterem ſacerdotum una ſingulis in ſublime elevatis guttur incidebat, è ſanguine in craterem profuſo divinationem quandam captabant. Reliquæ (Sacerdotes) ventrem recludebant, extiſque inſpectis, victoriam ſuis vaticinabantur."</note> "The priestesses, skilled in <term>divination</term><note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note>, met the captives throughout the camp with drawn swords; throwing them to the ground, they dragged them to a bronze cauldron which held about twenty jars. They had a raised platform which a priestess would nimbly climb; standing over the cauldron, she would cut the throat of each victim as they were lifted up, and from the blood poured into the cauldron, they would seek a certain divination. The rest of the priestesses would open the belly and, having inspected the entrails, would prophesy victory for their people." Strabo, Book 7, p. 294. 

We found an illustration of this on the **Golden Horn** <note>The Golden Horns of Gallehus, discovered in 1639 and 1734 in Southern Jutland, were major archaeological finds from the Migration Period, though they were later stolen and melted down.</note> in 1639 near **Tønder** <note>original: "Tundern"</note>, where in the third circle a female figure (who is a priestess) has a person before her to slaughter for the sacrifice; she has a large knife in her hand and opens the belly with the same through four long cuts, as mentioned in my *Golden Horn*, Part 2, Chapter 6, Section 5. 

This manner of prophesying from the blood and entrails of sacrificed humans was practiced by the Greeks, Romans, Franks, Gauls, Thracians, and the two Roman Emperors **Heliogabalus** and **Julian**, and the tyrant **Maxentius**: Geusius, Part 1, *Victims of Human Sacrifice*, Chapter 21. Likewise the **Celtic**, Spanish or Lusitanian, and British peoples: Cluverius, Book 1, *Ancient Germany*, Chapter 35; as also the Scythian and Tartarian peoples: Delrio, Book 4, *Magical Disquisitions*, Chapter 2, Question 7, Section 1, p. 419. 

It was previously reported that the bare heads of both humans and animals were sacrificed to the gods: Adam of Bremen, *On the Geography of Denmark and the Northern Realms*, p. 144, and Book 4, *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 12. Of the ancient Cimbri, Aubanus writes in Book 3, *On the Customs of Nations*, Chapter 21, that they killed humans and animals and burned them together. It could be that they proceeded differently here with the so-called **consultative sacrifice** than with the vowed and silent sacrifice. During these sacrifices, the shed human blood was smeared onto the walls and the seating of the <term>idol-house</term> <note>original: "Götzenhaus," meaning a pagan temple or shrine.</note>. <note>original: Snorri Sturluson, Part 1, Norwegian Chronicle, number 9, in the Life of King Domaldi, page 13.</note>

Our ancestors offered their prayers not only during sacrifices but also at other times when necessity demanded it. # Cimbrian

§. 7. In this land, and especially in the northern part of this Duchy of Schleswig, a pagan <term>ejaculatory prayer</term> <note>original: "Stoß-Gebethlein," a short, intense prayer intended to be "hurled" toward heaven in a moment of crisis.</note> is still commonly used among both old and young in cases of misfortune, which sounds like this: **A jova tuta nei! Awiawoka nei!** These words are neither Tartar nor Thieves' Cant <note>original: "Rothwelsch," a secret cant or jargon used by vagrants and thieves in Germany since the 15th century.</note>, as some suppose; nor are they merely a string of interjections of exclamation and grief <note>original: "Interjectiones Exclamantis & Dolentis"</note>, as others believe. Rather, they have a specific meaning, which I explain thus: *O Jova tuta me, â via voca me* <note>original: "O Jova tuta me, â via voca me." Translated as: "O Jupiter protect me, call me from the way [or rescue me from the path]."</note>. It is not Ciceronian <note>Refined, classical Latin as written by the orator Cicero.</note>, but rather rough soldiers' Latin; it means: O Jupiter protect me, rescue me from violence. Now, one might wonder how and from where our ancestors came upon this Latin pagan prayer? It is believable that the ancient Cimbri <note>A Germanic or Celtic tribe that famously invaded the Roman Republic in the late 2nd century BC.</note> learned it from the Romans during their military campaigns in Italy. The Romans, who were severely distressed by the Cimbri and frequently defeated, called upon their god Jupiter for protection, as recorded by Florus (book 3, chapter 3), Livy (*Epitome*, book 65, page 640), and Paterculus (book 2, page 24) <note>These are standard Roman historians: Lucius Annaeus Florus, Livy (Titus Livius), and Velleius Paterculus.</note>. The Cimbri heard this but did not understand it, and therefore pronounced it in a corrupted way. When the surviving Cimbri returned home, they must have brought this Roman ejaculatory prayer back with them to their fatherland, where it was used as a proverb and passed down to their descendants until this very day. Helvaderus agrees with me on this (page 362, column a), though not in the explanation of the words, which he gives as: *Iova, tu de te ajebas, voca me* <note>Translated as: "Jupiter, you said of yourself, call me."</note>. However, this is quite nonsensical, for that is no prayer for distress or emergency, nor does it agree at all with the phonetics:

[clima]cteric festival, the Goths and Danes held every nine years in the month of January—directly after Epiphany <note>original: "H. Drey König," or Holy Three Kings.</note>—on the island of Zealand, at the ancient and long-destroyed royal residence of the city of Lejre <note>original: "Lethre oder Leire." This festival was observed with the highest solemnity by all the people throughout the entire kingdom, featuring many different sacrifices of both humans and livestock. There is a place in those parts, the capital of that kingdom, called Lejre on the island called Zealand; there, after nine years in the month of January—following the time we celebrate the Appearance of the Lord <note>original: "Theophaniam," or Epiphany.</note>—everyone gathers, and there they sacrifice to their gods 99 humans, and just as many horses, along with dogs and roosters, offered instead of hawks, believing for certain, as I have said, that these will appease the gods.* — *Thietmar of Merseburg, Book 1 of the Annals, regarding the life of Emperor Henry I, page 10.*

This author likely received this information from his cousin, Emperor Henry the Fowler, who waged war against the Kingdom of Denmark and thus had reliable reports of this abhorrent idolatry. The Greeks and Romans called such a sacrifice a <term>Hecatomb</term> <note>From the Greek 'hekaton' (hundred) and 'bous' (ox); a great public sacrifice.</note>: for when pestilence and contagious diseases raged, they sacrificed a hundred oxen, a hundred sheep, and a hundred pigs upon a hundred altars: *Alessandro Alessandri, Book 3, Chapter 22, folio 164a.*

*Adam of Bremen* <note>An 11th-century German chronicler and geographer.</note> also mentions this festival, which the Swedes are said to have celebrated every nine years at Uppsala. However, he does not agree on the description of the sacrifice, which, as he writes, consisted of all kinds of animals as well as male humans—specifically nine heads of each—which were sacrificed to the gods. Whether there were nine heads of every species and kind of animal, or only nine heads in total from all kinds of animals, is a matter of doubt. However, because the author relates that seventy-two victims of humans and dogs hung together in the groves at once, there is no doubt that nine heads of every kind of animal were sacrificed: *Schefferus in Upsalia, Chapter 16, page 293.* <note>Johannes Schefferus (1621–1679), author of "Upsalia," a history of the Swedish city.</note> From this, it can be concluded that nine human heads, nine horse heads, nine ox heads, nine sheep heads, nine goat heads, etc., were sacrificed. # Pagan Religion

[this] feast was held; Thietmar speaks of the sacrifice of the Danes, but Adam of Bremen <note>A medieval German chronicler (c. 1050–1081) whose work is one of the most important sources for the history and geography of Northern Europe.</note> speaks of the sacrifice of the Swedes. His words are:

*It is also customary that after nine years, a common festival of the provinces of Sweden is celebrated. For this solemnity, no one is granted immunity; kings and all peoples, both collectively and individually, send their gifts to Uppsala <note>The religious and political center of ancient Sweden, famous for its grand golden temple.</note>. And what is more cruel than any punishment: those who have embraced Christianity must buy their way out of participating in those ceremonies. The sacrifice is as follows: from every living creature that is male, nine heads are offered, and it is the custom to appease such gods (Thor, Wodan, and Fricco <note>The three primary deities at Uppsala: Thor (god of thunder), Wodan (Odin, god of war/wisdom), and Fricco (Freyr, god of fertility and peace).</note>) with their blood. The bodies, however, are hung in a grove which is adjacent to the temple. This grove is so sacred to the pagans that each individual tree is believed to be divine due to the death or the remains of those sacrificed. There, dogs hang alongside humans, and a certain Christian told me that he had seen seventy-two of their bodies hanging mixed together. Furthermore, the incantations <note>original: "næniæ," often referring to funeral dirges or ritual chants.</note> which are usually performed during these libation rites are manifold and unseemly, and therefore it is better to remain silent about them.* — Adam of Bremen, *On the Geography of Denmark and the Northern Kingdoms*, p. 144.

Ericus Upsalensis <note>Erik Olsson (d. 1486), a Swedish historian and priest.</note> mentions this in Book 1 of his *History of the Goths and Swedes*, p. 2. *In addition to these,* he says, *a certain general festival was established, to be celebrated with the utmost precision every nine years, to which the entire multitude of all the provinces of the Gothic nation was bound to come and offer gifts. At that time, living sacrifices were offered of both humans and beasts, with whose blood they appeased the gods. They hung the bodies in a nearby grove, believing the trees themselves to become divine and sacred through the death of those sacrificed, and they therefore paid them the highest honor.*

Albertus Crantz <note>A German historian (1448–1517) who wrote extensively on Northern European history.</note>, in the preface to his *Swedish Histories*, also mentions this nine-year festival and notes, moreover, that this feast was celebrated for nine days, and on each day nine kinds of animals—including a human—were sacrificed.

...after a grand festival, they devoted nine days to their sacrifice, performing it with great order and devotion. During these nine-day holidays, the designated number of sacrifices were butchered at the altar of the idols. Those people whom the lot chose for sacrifice were thrown alive into a spring that rose near the place of sacrifice. # Pagan Religion.

A festival was celebrated for sacrifices, which is called the **Disa-Sacrifice** <note>original: "Disa-Opffer." This refers to the *Dísablót*, a sacrificial festival held in honor of the female spirits or deities known as the Dísir.</note>: *Snorri, Part 1, Chronicle of Norway, number 22, page 23.* <note>The author refers to Snorri Sturluson’s *Heimskringla*.</note>

§. 5. The idol **Odin** is said to have ordained three festival and sacrifice times, so that people should come together three times a year and sacrifice to the gods; first, at **winter-time** for a good year and the growth of grain; second, in the **middle of winter**, for the fertility of the earth’s fruits; third, in **summer**, to obtain victory: *Snorri, Part 1, Chronicle of Norway, number 1, in "The Life of Odin," page 7.* It is especially noteworthy here that the ancient Nordic peoples divided the entire year into two parts, namely into summer and winter: *Dr. Worm, Book 1, Fasti, chapter 12* <note>Ole Worm was a 17th-century Danish physician and polymath who studied runestones and Norse chronology.</note> and they began winter immediately after the grain harvest in the beginning of autumn, but summer in the beginning of spring. Thus Snorri explains in *Part 3, Number 3, page 77*, where he says: That the first sacrificial festival was celebrated at the harvest, at the beginning of winter, which is autumn. Accordingly, the first festival was held in the autumn month immediately after the harvest; the second festival in the winter month; the third festival in spring. They sacrificed first at the harvest and welcomed the winter, then in the middle of winter, and for the third time in summer. And they maintained these sacrifices from all the districts in **Trondheim**, and twelve men were overseers over these sacrifices, writes *Snorri, Part 3, Chronicle of Norway, number 7, in "The Life of St. Olaf," page 240.* And shortly thereafter on *page 246* (which *in the edition by Worm is found in the Appendix, page 5*) he reports of **Sivard** that he kept the manner of pagan idolatry and sacrificed three times during the winter: namely, first at the beginning (of winter), then in the middle of winter, and finally in the spring. After he had accepted the Christian religion, however, he still kept this custom of holding feasts and inviting his friends as guests: at the harvest, at **Yule** (that is, Christmas), and at Easter. The first sacrificial festival was celebrated immediately after the harvest, in September, specifically to honor the idol **Thor**. *Snorri, Part 1, Chronicle of Norway, number 9, in "The Life of King Domald," page 13*, recounts that the Swedes, during a time of hunger and high prices, sacrificed many oxen at the harvest; in the second harvest of the following year, they sacrificed humans; but in the third harvest, they sacrificed their King **Domald**. He mentions in addition that the king was brought as a sacrifice to the idol **Odin** during this festival.

<header>Cimbrian [Customs]</header>

From which one might conclude that this festival belonged not to **Thor**, but rather to **Odin**. To this it must be answered that, because of the persistent period of famine and <term>scarcity</term><note>The original German "Theurung" refers to a time of "dearness" or high prices, almost always caused by crop failure and resulting in famine.</note>, something extraordinary occurred during this festival; for King **Domald** was not offered as a regular sacrifice, but rather as the cause of this harsh scarcity, brought as a punishment outside the usual order as a sacrifice to **Odin**. Similarly, King **Olaf** in **Sweden** was sacrificed to **Odin** both for the sake of victory and for the year's fertility: <note>original: "Idem l. d. num. 28. p. 30." — The same source [Snorri Sturluson's Ynglinga Saga] as cited previously, section 28, page 30.</note> It was therefore a thanksgiving festival, where the gods were thanked for the good harvest, and further prayers were made for a fruitful year and good grain growth. This belongs to the idol **Thor**, to whom one sacrificed during times of hunger and scarcity, as he was held to be a god of grain and all fruits, as was mentioned previously. 

The second sacrificial festival was held in **December** around **St. Lucia's Day**, held for seven days in honor of the goddess **Freya**, and was called **Yule**, from the revolution of the sun, which at that time reaches its so-called standstill <note>The winter solstice.</note> and begins to turn its running **Yule**, or wheel, closer toward us. This was their New Year's festival, at which they began the year and asked their gods for a good, new, and fruitful year, and distributed **Yule-gifts** or New Year's presents. 

At this festival, they sacrificed a fattened pig, which was held in great holiness and called the **Yule-pig**. Alongside this, they ate and drank heartily, believing that the more abundantly they kept this **Yule-festival**, the greater the **abundance** the new year would bring. They also played games and danced, which was called the **Yule-game**. From this, the **Christmas-play**, which is still customary in many places, has its origin; it is so deeply rooted that in many cases it could not be abolished even by the prohibition of high authorities. During this festival of **Freya**, young people also wooed, married, and held weddings. **In short**, everything was full of joy for the good beginning of the new year; that was their **Yule-joy**. 

The night immediately preceding this festival saw the start of this **Yule-joy**, where they played and danced throughout the entire night; it was called **Modrenatt**, or **Mother-Night**, to signify that she, like a mother, would give birth to the new year, considering that they held the night to be older than the day, and began and calculated time from the night. From this heathen festival, the **Christian-festival** immediately following it took the name **Yule** among the Goths

Then the priest exhorted the people that they should celebrate this sacrificial festival—established by their ancestors—with great devotion.

After this sermon, the priest slaughtered the goat and sprinkled and scattered its blood all around, but gave the meat to the women to cook. In the meantime, while the meat was cooking, the women baked cakes of rye flour and turned them back and forth frequently upon the hearth-fire. When the meat was finally cooked and the cakes were baked, the sacrificial feast <term>Götzenmahl</term> began, which was spent with barbaric gluttony and drinking throughout the entire day and the entire night, until they were quite mad and full, and vomited up what they had swallowed. Whatever remained of this sacrificial feast was buried. 

On **St. Gregory's Day**, they held a festival for the spring-god **Pergrub**, at which the priest took a drinking vessel filled with beer in his hand and praised the aforementioned god for how he drove away the winter, how he brought back the lovely spring, and how he made the forests green again. At the conclusion of this hymn of praise, he seized the drinking vessel with his teeth—without the help of his hands—drank it entirely dry, and, still holding it with his teeth, threw it backwards over his head. In this manner, all the people present had to drink one after another, just like the priest, and in doing so, they had to strike up a song of praise and thanksgiving in honor of **Pergrub**. Let us bring our offering to the moon: for we now see the very one who accompanied us on our voyage." Immediately, oxen and sheep were slaughtered for the sacrificial feast, and two horns of <term>Aurochs</term> <note>original: "Uhr-Ochsen" — the extinct wild ancestors of domestic cattle, prized for their massive horns.</note> were brought forth, which were encased in gold around the upper rim and used as drinking vessels. Tilvar takes these horns, filled with mead <note>original: "Meet" — a fermented honey wine.</note>, and tastes a little from them, while thanking the gods with quiet words for the successful journey and the discovery of the island, wishing himself and his people and lineage a prosperous future. Then he bows the horn toward the earth and pours some out of it <note>This is a libation, a common ritual pouring of a liquid as an offering to a deity or spirit.</note>. After this, a great drinking bout followed until late into the night, where they all became quite intoxicated and praised the new moon along with their leader, Tilvar. 

Even today, it is still the custom on Gotland to praise the new moon, and all work and undertakings such as plowing, sowing, etc., provided they are not begun during the new moon...

Whatever remained of this sacrificial feast was buried.

On the **Day of St. Gregory** <note>March 12th, traditionally associated with the beginning of spring.</note>, they held a festival for the spring-god **Pergrub**, at which the priest took a drinking vessel filled with beer in his hand and praised the aforementioned god: how he had driven away the winter, how he had brought back the lovely spring, and how he made the forests green. At the conclusion of this song of praise, he seized the drinking vessel with his teeth, without the help of his hands, drank it clean out, and, holding it with his teeth, threw it backward over his head. In this same manner, all the people present had to drink one after another, just like the priest, and in doing so, strike up a song of praise and thanksgiving in honor of Pergrub. Not only the new moon, but also the full moon was held sacred by the pagans, as *Herodotus* writes of the Egyptians in Book 2, number 48, page 118, and *Alessandro Alessandri* says of the Celtiberian people in Book 6, chapter 26, folio 383. # Heathen Religion

...because of this, they drank three cups, namely those of **Odin**, **Njörd**, and **Freyja**. In **Denmark** and **Sweden**, people drank the cups of **Thor**, **Odin**, and **Freyja**; specifically, they drank to **Thor** for a successful outcome in their endeavors, to **Odin** for victory, and to **Freyja** for peace and a "good year," as **Dr. Johannes Scheffer** <note>Johannes Schefferus (1621–1679), a renowned German-born professor at Uppsala University in Sweden</note> notes. From this, the custom is still maintained among the Northern peoples to say when drinking a toast: *Gott aar*, that is, "a good year." The leader drank the first cup empty and blessed it. To this blessing a special prayer was attached, which varied according to the specific god being honored. Following this, two other cups followed, namely the **Bragi-cup** <term>original: *Bragebecher*; a ceremonial toast often used to honor fallen heroes or to make solemn vows</term>, which was for the heroes slain in war, and the **Remembrance-cup** <term>original: *Meind-Becher*; related to the Old German 'Minne' or memory</term>, which was for deceased friends. See **Schefferus** in *Uppsala* <note>original: *Upsalia*</note>, chapter 10, pages 144 and 145; **Bangius**, *Ecclesiastical History of the Swedes and Goths* <note>original: *Hist. Eccles. Sueo-Goth.*</note>, Book 6, chapter 16; and compare **Worm**, *Monuments* <note>original: *Monument.*</note>, Book 1, chapter 5. The *Edda* <note>The primary source for Norse mythology, likely referring here to the Prose Edda by Snorri Sturluson</note>, Part 1, Fable 24, mentions an idol of the poets and of eloquence named **Bragi**; perhaps these *Bragi-cups* were drunk in his honor.

Likewise, the Latins and Romans kept various idol-cups at their sacrificial meals, such as those of **Jupiter, Juno, Mercury, Bacchus**, and the "Good Spirit" or ***Genius***, as well as cups for deceased heroes and friends. However, accounts differ on how these idol-cups were consumed; some believe the first cup was consecrated to **Jupiter** for the sake of health, the second cup to the **Good Spirit** or ***Genius*** for the sake of joy, and the third cup to **Bacchus** for the sake of pleasure. Afterwards, they are said to have drunk the cups of **Mercury** and **Juno**, which others place earlier in the sequence. Compare **Alexander ab Alexandro**, Book 5, chapter 22; **Dempster** in his notes on **Rosinus**, Book 5, *Antiquities*, chapter 30, page 871 onwards; **Laurentius**, Book 2, *Polymathy*, Dissertation 19; and **Saubert**, *On Sacrifices* <note>original: *de Sacrif.*</note>, chapter 26.

Holy Scripture mentions these idol-cups when the Apostle, in **1 Corinthians 10:21**, calls them the **cups of devils**. "You cannot," he says, "drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils at the same time." This means: you cannot simultaneously drink the cup of the Lord Christ in the Holy Communion and the cup or beaker of devils at the sacrificial meals of the heathens. The prophet **Isaiah** refers to this in chapter 65, verse 11, as "pouring out a drink offering to **Meni**" <note>Meni was an ancient Semitic god of Fate or Fortune; the text equates these libations with pagan toasts</note>. Such idol-cups had to be filled to the brim; the Northern peoples <note>original: *Mitternächtige Völcker*, literally "Midnight Peoples," referring to those of the far north</note> called this "carrying it full," as **Snorri Sturluson** indicates. **Johannes Schefferus**, in the previously mentioned...

Anyone who would not "match the drink" <note>original: "Bescheid thun," a social obligation to drink the same amount as a companion</note> was declared an enemy and sometimes beaten to death. # Cimbrian #

...[they begin to] dance, and thereafter exalt him <note>likely referring to a deity or a ritual leader</note> with prayers, and with curses mixed among them, until they, following the rhythm of the stringed instruments, heat themselves up so much in dancing that they become like madmen; so much so that some fall down to the ground, while the others meanwhile continue dancing, accompanied by bells and little bells that chime and ring to the music. As soon as one of them falls to the earth and the evil spirit has entered him, they change the tone, and their dance continues even more violently and madly; they say that at this same time the devils dance among them in bodily form, and are dressed like the priests. Now when this **Priest-Dance** <note>original: "Pfaffen-Tantz"</note> has lasted over four days, the nobility holds a feast and performs a sacrifice; then they play a very charming tone, and each of them takes a woman as he pleases to dance with her, yet in such a way that they do not touch each other with the hand, but rather they hold each other fast with a silk ribbon. They dance in a circle, and it is a delight to see this—though common, yet artistic—dance, because of the various steps they perform therein. When this has happened, the tone changes and goes somewhat lower, as if to rest, by means of special songs which they sing in praise of their deceased heroes, as their friends, whose bravery they celebrate with countless songs of praise, which are commonly fabricated: *Arnoldus in the Additions to Roger on Heathenism <note>original: "Addit. ad Roger. de Gentiliſmo"</note>, chapter 19, page 804 and following.* 

The **American Cannibals** or **Caribs** dance at their **Festival of Atonement** <note>original: "Verſühn-Feſt"</note> for a full fifteen days and are adorned with parrot feathers. In the middle of the dance-row stands their priest, wearing a long robe woven from similar feathers; he holds a long reed to his mouth in which a herb, like tobacco, is lit. He blows the smoke toward those dancing around him with these words: "Receive the spirit of bravery, so that you may overcome your enemies." Others are there who ring bells and sing a song of consolation to the effect of: namely, how their ancestors were brave heroes and have eaten very many of their enemies: *the same author in the same place, chapter 39, page 970 and following.*
