...to dance. On the other hand, there were few of those peoples who did not have such a practice in use. This is why the priests of the idol **Mars** were called **Salii** <note>original: "Salii"; from the Latin *salire*, meaning "to leap" or "to jump." These were the "Leaping Priests" of the Roman god of war.</note> and were held in very high regard by the Romans. In **Delos** <note>An island sacred to Apollo in Greek mythology.</note>, no divine service was performed in which dancing did not take place. It is also well known that no divine services were established by **Orpheus** and **Musaeus** <note>Legendary figures in Greek myth associated with music, poetry, and the founding of religious mysteries.</note> without dancing being ordained at the same time. This dance proceeded in such a manner: they began from the left side of the altar and danced toward the right hand, by which they intended to imitate the course of the heavens from sunrise to sunset. Then they turned from the right toward the left hand, and with this, they showed the course of the wandering stars or planets. This was likely what **Virgil** <note>The famous Roman poet, author of the *Aeneid*.</note> looked upon when he wrote:

> They renew the dances and gather in a circle around the altars. <note>original: "Instaurantque choros, mixtique altaria circum."</note>

Thus says the well-regarded author <note>Referring to Alexander ab Alexandro.</note>, who took most of this from **Alessandro Alessandri**, book 4, chapter 17, where it is recounted how they danced around the altar from left to right, and again from right to left on festival days, and sang along, and chimed with bells and cymbals, as was the custom among the heathens in general, and especially among the **Indians**, **Greeks**, and **Latins**. This festival dance is also attributed to the **Celtiberian people** <note>A group of Celts inhabiting the central-eastern Iberian Peninsula.</note> by the last-mentioned author in book 6, chapter 26. The aforementioned author makes mention of the priests of **Mars**, who are called **Salii**, so named from dancing because they danced and jumped through the city on their festival days and sang while doing so: **Fenestella**, book 1, *On the Roman Priesthood*, chapter 7; **Pomponius Laetus**, book 2, *On the Roman Priesthood*, chapter 17. Otherwise, the Romans, as well as the Greeks, had dedicated special holidays for playing and dancing, among which some were hallowed to the **Twelve Great Gods** in common, others to **Apollo**, others to **Jupiter**, others to **Mars**, others to **Consus** <note>An ancient Roman deity who protected grain and the harvest.</note>, others to **Ceres**, others to **Flora**, others to **Minerva**, others to **Juno**. *   **Games of Apollo** <note>original: "Apollinares"</note>
*   **Capitoline Games** <note>original: "Capitolini"</note>, that is, the **Games of Jove** <note>original: "Joviales"; honoring Jupiter.</note>

*   **Games of Ceres** <note>original: "Cereales"</note>

Such games and dance-festivals were held as a religious exercise of **idolatry** <note>original: "Götzendienst"; here meaning the worship of non-Christian gods.</note> in honor of the gods and for the welfare of the people. This is treated at length by **Rosinus** in *Roman Antiquities*, book 5, chapter 1 and following, through to chapter 24; compare also **Dempster's** *Commentary on Rosinus*. <note>Johannes Rosinus (1551–1626) was a German antiquary whose work on Roman customs was a standard reference, later edited by the Scottish scholar Thomas Dempster.</note> The **Spartans** had three dance choruses: In the first, the old men danced, who sang of their brave deeds and virtues. In the second chorus, the young men leaped, who boasted in song of their strength and undaunted courage. In the last chorus, the boys leaped, who promised great things for the future. <note>Cited from Benedictus Aretius, *Theological Problems*, topic 14, p. 176, and Johann Lauremberg, *History*, Century 1, 90.</note> Otherwise, special **war-dances** were customary among the ancient Romans and Greeks, in which they leaped about equipped with weapons. **Romulus** <note>The legendary founder of Rome.</note> is said to have ordained such war-dances. <note>Aretius, as cited above, pp. 170, 172.</note> It is said that the heathens learned this from the people of God in the **Old Testament**. **Zepperus** <note>Wilhelm Zepper (1550–1607), a Reformed theologian who wrote on Mosaic law.</note> writes that in the Old Testament, hardly any festival or divine service was held without dancing, and that this dancing during the performance of divine service even took place in the Temple to honor God. On the hills lying to the right and left, altars also once stood, dedicated to **Odin** and **Freya**, which have been destroyed over time. **§. 4.** Such altars, along with their hills, were of different kinds: for some were **funerary altars**, which stood over the graves of the dead and were dedicated to the deceased. Upon these, sacrifices were made for their annual commemoration, thereby testifying to the immortality of the soul and another life after this one: *Wormius, book 1 and chapter 6, page 35 and following; Helvad, book 3, Encolpion, folio 265.* <note>References to Ole Worm and Nicolaus Helvadus, scholars of Northern antiquities</note> The Greeks and Romans also had such grave-altars: *Kirchmann, book 4, On Roman Funerals, chapter 2; Josephus Laurentius, book 3, Synopsis of Varied Learning 1.* <note>original: "Polymathia Synopsis"</note> In contrast, our ancestors had general **idol-altars**, sanctified to the gods, where the entire district, town, or village community gathered to perform their sacrificial and idolatrous worship. The Danish Chancellor **Witfeld** <note>Arild Huitfeldt (1546–1609), Danish historian</note> makes such a distinction: that these **Church-hills** (as we call them now for the sake of distinction) upon which the idol-altars stood, extend in length between East and West; whereas the **Grave-hills** <note>Barrows or burial mounds</note>, upon which the funerary altars stood, extend in length between South and North, with their elongated stone circles: *Huitfeldt in the Chronicle of the Realm, page 1.* **Strelov** agrees with this in the *Gothic Chronicle, page 65 and following.* Such Church-hills, surrounded with stones and extending between East and West (of which I have seen few), have...

...be found in Holstein, especially in the District of Segeberg, near the <unclear>Kisel-Er-</unclear>bing, where such a **Pagan Church-Hill** <note>German: *Heydnischer Kirchberg*; likely a reference to a burial mound or megalithic site</note> is situated, sixty paces long and eleven paces wide. When pestilence and infectious diseases raged, the Romans and Greeks were accustomed to erect a hundred altars side by side and sacrifice upon them a hundred oxen, a hundred sheep, and a hundred pigs: *Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 3, Chapter 22, folio 164. a.* <note>Referring to the "Hecatomb," a massive public sacrifice</note>

**§. 5.** These pagan altars were surrounded not only with stones but also with green trees, which were consecrated to the idols and held in divine honor. Such sacrificial sites surrounded by trees, or even situated deep within the forests, are called **Groves** <note>German: *Hayne*</note>. Regarding our **Saxons**, **Adam of Bremen** writes in *History of the Church, Book 1, Chapter 6*: "They hallowed," he says, "groves and woods to their idols, and named them after their names." And in his *Book on the Geography of Denmark and the Northern Kingdoms, page 144* <note>original: "liber de Situ Daniae, & Regionum Septentrionalium"</note>, he relates that the groves were sacred to the pagans and the trees were considered divine. Therefore, **Pliny** in *Book 12, Chapter 1*, calls such groves "Tree-Idol-Temples." The Romans called these groves *Lucos* <note>Latin: sacred groves</note>, because the holy sacrificial fire shone there day and night: *Saubertus, On Sacrifices, Chapter 14, pages 326, 328.* These groves were regarded as the great sanctuaries of the entire land, which no man might desecrate or harm, much less cut down. If someone were to do so, they believed he had committed a hideous, mortal sin and was deserving of death. Near **Merseburg** in Saxony, the oak forest was an idol-grove consecrated to the forest god **Zuttiber** <note>A deity of the Polabian Slavs or Wends, often mentioned in regional Saxon chronicles</note>, in which no one was permitted to cut wood under penalty of death: *Brotuff, Book 1 of the Chronicles.*

# Cimbrian Antiquities

They honored a sacred oak tree, called **Jupiter's Oak** <note>The "Donar Oak" or "Thor's Oak," a sacred site of the Germanic Chatti tribe</note>, and attributed such power and holiness to it that they believed it was impossible for this tree to be chopped down. However, **Boniface**, the **Apostle to the Hessians** <note>Saint Boniface, c. 675–754, a missionary who spread Christianity in the Frankish Empire</note>, cut down this tree in the year 724 and built a chapel at **Geismar** from the wood. From there he moved to **Eichsfeld** <note>literally "Oak Field"</note> on the **Werra** (which place, without doubt, received its name from the holy oaks that stood there): *Fabronius, Part 1, History of the Ancient World, Book 1, Chapter 1, Number 4, Page 95, from the Annals of Baronius for the year 724.* In this regard, it should be remembered that among the **Celts**, Jupiter's idol-pillar was an oak tree: *Selden, Treatise 2, On the Syrian Gods, Chapter 2, Page 234.*

§ 11. From this it is evident that the **idol-groves** <term>Götzenhayne: groves of trees where pagan idols were worshipped</term> were oak trees, which were particularly hallowed to the gods: *Olaus Magnus, Book 16, Chapter 11.* Otherwise, every idol had its own specific hallowed trees: such as **Hercules**, the **poplar tree**; **Bacchus**, the **vine**; **Apollo**, the **laurel tree**; **Minerva**, the **olive tree**; **Venus**, the **myrtle tree**; **Jupiter**, the **medlar tree**; **Pallas**, the **palm tree**; **Rhea**, the **pine tree**; **Pluto**, the **cypress tree**: *Ravisius, Part 2, Offices, Page 243.* Oak trees, on the other hand, were dedicated to the idols in general, such as to **Jupiter**, **Bacchus**, **Ceres**, **Rhea**, etc., as **Natalis Comes** reminds us at the end of his work *On Mythology*. 

In the district of **Borsholm** in **Holstein**, there stood in olden times on the boundary between **Spreng** and **Blumenthal** an exceedingly beautiful and imposing oak tree called the **Schwerck Oak**, which the heathens are said to have held as holy and religious and to have venerated, as **Martin Coroneus** relates in his description of the antiquities of Borsholm. I consider that the **KirchEcken** <note>Church Oaks</note>, or Oaks, located in the district of **Trittau** near **Hamburg**, received their name from the **idol-oaks** that once stood there, just like the aforementioned places **Alteiche** <note>Old Oak</note> and **Eichfeld**. 

At **Romowe** <note>original: Romou; a central place of worship for Baltic pagans</note> in **Prussia**, there stood an **idol-oak**, six ells <note>roughly 12 to 15 feet</note> in circumference, which was green in both summer and winter; at the top it was very wide-spreading, and the branches and leaves were so thick together that no rain could fall through. It was held so holy that people hung its leaves around their necks as a **relic** <note>original: Heiligthum</note> and believed they would thereby be delivered from misfortune. This tree was dedicated to the three gods of the **Prussian Wends**, namely **Pickol**, **Perkūnas** <note>original: Perckun; the Baltic god of thunder</note>, and **Potrimpo** <note>original: Potrimp; the Baltic god of grain and fertility</note>, who were said to have lived in this tree. > **Do not cut down the juniper.**

But when he did not turn back from this, but intended to strike at it immediately, it was called out again:

> **I tell you, do not cut down this tree.**

Whereupon the servant, terrified, went away. Thus Satan still carries out his game among us Christians even now. To this point stands *Ovid, book 3, Loves, Elegy 1.*

For this Tree of Life would have served, before the Fall: (1) As a <term>Sacrament: a sacred rite or physical sign of grace</term> and sanctuary, to maintain an everlasting life; (2) As a <term>Medicament: a medicinal remedy</term> and pharmacy, to drive away death and the harbingers of death, namely diseases and weaknesses; (3) As an <term>Aliment: a source of food</term> for the nourishment of the body and life. # Cimbrian

> ...the appearance of Angels: to Christians, because even at that time He appeared to a pious man <note>Abraham</note>, He who in later times manifested Himself through the Virgin for the salvation of the human race. They honor that place each according to their own religion: some praying to the one God of all, others invoking Angels, and offering libations of wine, and sacrificing with incense or an ox, or a goat, or a sheep, or a rooster. For whatever each person held dear and good, having been carefully nourished throughout the entire year, they preserved according to their vow for the feast-banquet of that same site, both for themselves and for their households. For whatever each person held dear and good, having carefully nourished it throughout the whole year, they would reserve it according to their vow, both for themselves and for their households, for the feast of that same festival. Moreover, all honored that place—either to avoid the wrath of God so they might suffer no evil—they did not even have relations with their wives while they were there, although the women spent more time than usual on their adornment and feminine cleanliness for that feast, and moved about freely in public; nor did they behave lasciviously at other times, even though they shared tents commonly and promiscuously. In the time of the fair <note>original: "panegyrico," referring to a public assembly or festival</note>, no one drew water from it; for according to the law of the gentiles, some threw lit lamps into it, others poured in wine, others small cakes, others coins, ointments, and incense. <header>Cimbrian [Antiquities]</header>

ten the Cainites <note>The descendants of Cain, who in early modern theology were often credited with the invention of various arts, sciences, and—as suggested here—the origins of idolatry.</note> are said to have built idol-temples in honor of the sun and the stars, as Rabbi Maimonides writes in *On Idolatry* <note>original: "de Idololatria"</note> chapter 1, section 2. However, it does not seem likely to be the truth that the first world knew of temples: see Vossius in his *Notes on Maimonides*, in the aforementioned book.

§. 2. After God had commanded the construction of the **Tabernacle** <note>original: "Stiffts-Hütte"</note> as a chapel in the Arabian desert, and subsequently the great and magnificent **Temple at Jerusalem**: Exodus 25:1; 1 Kings 6; Satan brought it about that the heathens also erected churches and chapels in his honor: see the anonymous commentator <note>original: "Scholiast. Anonymus"</note> in Roger, Part 2, *Off. Th.* chapter 8, page 317.

§. 3. The first idol-temple after the Great Flood is said to have been that of Bel or Baal in Babylon. Herodotus describes this temple in Book I, number 33, pages 81 and 82, stating that it occupied a space of two stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 185 meters.</note> and had eight distinct towers. These were not placed beside one another, but rather set one on top of the other; the lowest tower was one stadium high and thick, while the uppermost tower contained the temple itself. Within it stood the idol of Bel, as well as his table, altar, chair, etc., all made of pure gold, which is valued at one thousand one hundred and eighty tons of gold <note>A "ton of gold" was a common early modern unit of account in Northern Europe, usually representing 100,000 thalers, rather than a measure of weight.</note>: see Christoph Matthias, Book I, *Theatrum Historicum*, pages 30 and 31. This high tower is without doubt the **Tower of Babel**, built by the descendants of Noah after the Flood, whose top was intended to reach into heaven: Genesis 11:14 <note>The biblical account of the Tower is found in Genesis 11:1–9; verse 14 refers to the lineage of Eber.</note>. This tower is generally held to be eight stadia high; however, Herodotus only says that the lowest tower was one stadium high, and he does not mention how high the other seven towers were. Jerome <note>original: "Hieronym."</note> in *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* <note>original: "quæst Ebr. ad Genes."</note> 11, relates that this tower was four thousand paces high, and that in his time, relics of it still remained there: cited by Stratmann in *Theatrum Historicum*, page 27.

§. 4. Initially, the Northern peoples erected **huts** for their idols, so that they might have protection during stormy weather and perform their idolatrous worship without inconvenience. They are therefore called **Shelter-gods** <note>original: "Schur-Götter"</note>, which are those idols that stood under huts: Olaus Wormius, Book I, *Danish Monuments* <note>original: "Monument. Dan."</note>, chapter 3. These idol-huts stood in their groves near the altars, where later their churches and chapels were erected. The Romans, on the other hand, had their *Lararia* or house-chapels, and within them their *Lares*, that is, household gods, as is reported of the Emperor [Alexander] Severus

This was the universal custom among the pagans: no one was permitted to lay a hand upon whoever took refuge in the houses of the idols and at the altars in times of need. Because the authorities in Athens acted against this and raged against those who had fled into the Temple of <term>Minerva</term> <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note>, all their descendants were punished for such a violation of religion: *Natalis Comes, Book 1 of "Mythology," chapter 10, page 30.* <term>Cicero</term> agrees with this, stating that the altars were an inviolable sanctuary: *Cicero, "Speech for Roscius the Actor," 3.* This is demonstrated at length by <term>Polydore Vergil</term> <note>An Italian humanist historian (c. 1470–1555) who wrote "On Discovery" (De Inventoribus Rerum).</note>; he says that after <term>Hercules</term> left this world, his grandsons (according to the testimony of *Servius* in *Book 8 of the Aeneid*), fearing the plots of those to whom their grandfather had caused much suffering, built for themselves in Athens the very first sanctuary—that is, a Temple of Mercy—from which no one could be taken away by force. He proves this from *Statius, Book 12 of the "Thebaid,"* and *Plutarch in the "Life of Theseus."* Furthermore, he relates how <term>Romulus</term> established a sanctuary so that he might obtain inhabitants to occupy the city of Rome, and how the Temple of Hercules in Egypt and the Temple of Apollo in Syria were also sanctuaries. §. 16. The temples, as well as the altars, were dedicated to specific gods and named after them. §. 17. Their idol-houses are highly sacred and held in great honor because of the presumed presence of their gods. This is proven with various examples by *Leonhard Coquæus in his commentary on Augustine's "The City of God," Book 1, chapter 2.* *Dempster, in the place cited, page 194.* It is noteworthy that the ancient **Goths**, who have their first origin in this <term>Northern region</term> <note>original: *Mitternächtigen Gegend*, literally "Midnight region," a common historical term for the North.</note>, spared the churches during war.

It was such prophetesses who prophesied from water to the German King **Ariovistus**—or **Ehrenvest** <note>The author suggests the German title *Ehrenvest* (Honorable/Steadfast in Honor), formerly reserved for Princes and Counts, derives from this king's name</note>—that he should not fight with the Romans <note>original: Plutarch in *Life of Julius Caesar*</note>. Our Cimbrian prophetesses are called *Alirunæ*, *Alrunæ*, or *Aliorunæ* in the writings of **Jordanes** <note>original: *On the Deeds of the Goths*, chapter 24</note> and **Paul the Deacon** <note>original: *On the History of the Lombards*, book 12, chapter 13</note>, as different editions read differently. 

These are two compound words, from "All" or "Old" and "**Runes**." The word "Runes" actually means to say or murmur something secretly, or into the ear. Furthermore, "to rune" also means to practice sorcery and to prophesy, because the practitioners of the black arts were accustomed to "rune" or speak and murmur secretly to themselves during their sorcery and prophesying. And because they misused the Cimbrian-Gothic letters for this purpose, these letters are therefore called **Rune-letters**. 

The meaning of the first part of the word is explained in various ways. **Saubertus** <note>original: *On Sacrifices*, chapter 8, p. 181</note> believes it should be *Alt-Runer*, that is, "**Old Prophetesses**." This agrees with Strabo, who reports that the Cimbrian prophetesses were old women. **Dr. Worm** <note>Ole Worm, Danish antiquarian</note> <note>original: *Fasti Danici* book 1, chapter 1</note> reads it as *Adel-Runer*, and claims they were so named for their noble status <term>Adelstand</term> and high rank. **Lysander** agrees with him in the preface to his *Danish History*. Others are of the opinion that they are called *All-Runer* because they prophesy "all" things, according to their imagination, whether it be even or odd; just as in Greek one is called *Pansophus* <note>original: *πανσόφος* (pansophos)</note> who knows everything, a title which belongs to God alone. To this belongs what **Laurentius** writes <note>original: *Centuria 3, Philological History*, 37</note>.

-># Pagan Religion<-

The historian **Aventinus** <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance humanist and historian</note> writes in his first yearbook, citing **Strabo** <note>Ancient Greek geographer (c. 63 BC – 24 AD)</note>, that formerly among the **Germans** (**Cimbri**) there were certain female persons called **All-Runes** <note>Also known as *Alrunes*; the name is derived from "all" and "runen" (to whisper or keep secrets)</note>, who were priestesses and prophetesses. From them, the men—when they went off to battle—learned of the beginning (or perhaps it should say the "outcome") of the war, and otherwise all manner of things to come. And as long as they had these **All-Runes** with them in their camps, all was well. 

These **All-Runes** walked with bare legs and feet, with grey hair hanging loose and tied up, and wore a white linen shirt <note>A simple, tunic-like garment</note> tied at the bottom, with a brass belt around the waist. When the men brought prisoners back from the conflict, these she-devils <note>original: *Teuffelinnen*</note> would fall upon them cruelly, slashing their throats with a sword and catching the blood in copper bowls, from which they then prophesied regarding future things. 

From these **All-Runes** has undoubtedly flowed the superstition which is still perceived today among many godless people, who take great care to have an **All-Rune** <note>Here referring to a mandrake figure or "Alraune"</note> in their house, believing that they will then have great luck and can know what shall happen to them. 

There are also vagabonds and deceivers to be found who carry such **All-Runes** about for sale. These are small idols, like little carved men or women with all their limbs, the head overgrown with long hair, and dressed in a small white shirt; in short, prepared in the same manner as the **All-Runes** of the ancient **Germans**. In truth, however, it is vain deceit and trickery <note>original: *Gauckeley*</note>. The root of the herb <term>Mandragorae</term> <note>The Mandrake plant, whose forked root was historically thought to resemble a human body</note> is naturally formed like a small naked human; these deceivers dig them out of the earth, wipe them off, and assist them with carving and finishing so that they look like a little man or woman, however they wish. Where the hair should be on the head, they stick in many grains of barley or other seeds, let them grow, and then dry them out somewhat so that they sit firmly and appear like natural hair. §. 4. Finally, they also had their sacrificial priests, whom the **Cimbri** <note>An ancient Germanic people</note> likewise called **Druids** (or rather, ***Druter***). **Stephanius** <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish historian</note> mentions this in his notes on **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, author of the *Gesta Danorum*</note>, Book 6, page 140. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> believes in Book 16, Chapter 44, that they take their name from the Greek *drys* <note>original: δρῦς</note>, which means an **oak**, because they always used oak leaves in their sacrifices and held this tree to be more sacred than others. However, because these ***Druter*** were not Greek but German priests, the origin of this word must be sought in Germany. It seems, therefore, to resemble the truth that they are so named from the Old Saxon words ***Dru*** or ***Tru*** and ***Glove*** <note>Related to the modern German *Glaube*, meaning faith or belief</note>, which they practiced in their office: **Saubertus** <note>Johannes Saubert the Elder (1592–1646), a German theologian</note>, *On Sacrifices*, chapter 7, page 155. From this comes the word ***Drut*** or ***Trut***, which means "trusted" or "dear," as when one says: "My dear friend" <note>original Low German: *Min truten Frund*</note>. The Goths say ***Tro*** or ***Dro***, from which comes the word ***Drotter***. **Aventinus** <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian historian</note>, in Book 1 of the *Annals of the Bavarians*, believes they are named after their first founder, who is said to have been called **Druid**. The first **Roman Emperor** <note>Referring to Julius Caesar, who provided one of the earliest descriptions of Druids in his *Gallic Wars*</note> describes these ***Druter*** thus: "They attend to divine service," he says, "arrange public and private sacrifices, and explain religion; a great crowd of young people comes to them for the sake of instruction..."

### Heathen Religion

...them, among whom they are held in great honor. They adjudicate public and private disputes. If a crime has been committed, or a murder <note>German: *Todtschlag*</note> has occurred, or if there is a dispute regarding an inheritance or boundaries, they judge the matter and decree rewards and punishments. Whoever, in a public or private capacity, does not abide by their judgment is placed under a ban <note>Excommunicated</note> and excluded from the sacrifices, which is the most severe punishment. Those who are thus under the ban are counted among the godless and the wicked; everyone avoids them and flees from their presence, so as not to approach them or speak with them, lest they be infected and come to harm. No legal right or honor is granted to them. Over all these Druids is a presiding leader, who holds the highest authority among them. When he dies, he is succeeded by the one who surpasses the others in dignity; but if many are equal in this regard, one is chosen by a vote. Sometimes they even take up arms and fight over this high position. They hold their assembly at certain times of the year in a specific consecrated place, where all who have disputes come to them and are obedient to their judicial decrees. They do not go to war, nor do they pay tribute <note>taxes</note> with the rest of the people, but are free from all burdens. Enticed by such great rewards, many enter this discipline <note>the Druidic way of life and training</note> voluntarily. Thus far from Julius Caesar, *Gallic Wars*, Book 6, page 123 and following.

§. 5. Here the Emperor <note>Referring to Julius Caesar</note> first describes the office of the priests: that they perform the sacrifices and the idol-worship, explain religion, instruct the young people, hold court, and place the disobedient under the ban. The office of the Vandal <note>A Germanic people</note> priests was to bring sacrifices to the gods; to instruct and teach the people in religion and idol-worship, and how one should live rightly according to the will of the gods; to pray to the gods for reconciliation and divine revelation; to bless the people and lead them with well-wishing; to explain what to do or leave undone in doubtful matters (this is properly the office of the soothsayer <term>Wahrsager</term>); to calculate the times; and to announce the feast days. See Hartknoch, *Prussian Affairs*, Dissertation 9, thesis 4. That the office of the Wendish <note>A Slavic people living in close proximity to Germanic tribes</note> priests consisted of these duties is shown by Saxo [Grammaticus], Book 14, in the *Life of King Waldemar I*, page 320.

Likewise, Anius was represented among the poets: **King Anius, a king of men and at the same time a priest of Phoebus**; <note>original: *Rex Anius, rex idemque hominum Phœbique Sacerdos* from Virgil’s Aeneid</note> that is: King Anius was a king over men and also a priest of the Sun. Augustus and the other Roman Emperors held it to be no less an honor to be called High Priest <term>Pontifex Maximus; the supreme head of the Roman state religion</term> than to be called Emperor. For these reasons, the priests wore crowns or wreaths, just as the Emperors did; some were crowned with laurel branches, like the priests of Apollo; some with poplar leaves, like the priests of Hercules; some with twigs of foreign heather-berries <note>possibly referring to myrtle, common in Mediterranean rituals</note>; some with ivy; some with oak leaves, etc.

The priests among the Romans were all free and exempt from contributions <note>taxes</note>, wars, and worldly duties. The High Priest in Rome, as Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian</note> testifies, has more privileges in one way or another than the Emperor, and was not required to give an account of his actions to either the Senate or the people. And Cicero, in his speech *For His Own House* to the Pontiffs <note>original: *Orat. pro domo ad Pontif.*</note>, acknowledges that the entire dignity and worth of a Republic—the preservation of all men, their lives, and their freedom—depends upon the religion of the gods and the High Priests. 

The great king of the Abyssinians <note>modern-day Ethiopia</note> still today wishes to be called Prester John <note>a legendary Christian patriarch and king</note>, although I am not unaware that some deny this. Among the Mahometans <note>Muslims</note>, no Musulman or "True Believer," as they call themselves, may assume the title of Lord, except for the Caliph or High Priest; and to cause even the slightest harm to the lowliest priest is there a hated and highly punishable crime. The priests of Mars, called *Salii* <note>the "leaping priests" known for their ritual dances</note> by the Romans, were of such status that no one was raised to such dignity unless he was a Patrician or a person of noble birth. In Tyre, the priests were dressed in purple and held the rank closest to the King. Among the Germans, in ancient times, no one had the power to punish major criminals except for the priests. The Tralli <note>an ancient people of the Balkans or Asia Minor</note> gave no one the privilege of living in a palace except for the king and the High Priest. ->Cimbrische<-

...chosen as one of the priests. **Mercury** was called **Trismegistus** <note>literally "Thrice-Greatest"</note>, because he served in three high offices, namely: as a **philosopher**, a **priest**, and a **king**. Among the Phoenicians, the priests of the Sun had the honor of wearing a long robe of gold and purple, and on their heads a golden crown set with precious stones. Similarly, the ancient Romans gave their priests the **privilege** of wearing crowns, which is why they were called **Stephanophori** <note>Greek for "wreath-bearers"</note>. In Rome, the **Flamen Dialis** <note>the high priest of Jupiter, the supreme Roman deity</note> had the honor that his simple word (**"Yes"**) was worth as much as a sworn oath; his very presence served as a sanctuary. If someone who had committed a crime took refuge with him, they were free from all punishment on that same day. He had the power to exercise the **authority** of a mayor <note>referring to the Roman office of Consul</note> and to wear a mayor’s clothing; no one else had the honor of being carried in a litter to the **Capitolium** <note>the Capitoline Hill, Rome's religious and political heart</note> except for the **Pontifex** <term>High Priest; the chief administrator of the Roman religious system</term> and the other priests. From this we see in what great **respect** and status they were held in ancient Rome; and no less, but rather much greater honor, have the priests and bishops in the "New Rome" <note>Christian Rome</note> received from Christian rulers. How highly the Great Turk <note>the Ottoman Sultan</note> **respects** his **Mufti** <term>the supreme legal and religious authority in the Islamic Ottoman Empire</term>, and in what honor and dignity the Christian **Patriarch** in **Constantinople** is held by him, is not hidden from those who have lived there or have read the histories. **In summary**: religion flourishes and withers with its priests and servants; it stands and falls, waxes and wanes, just as they do; like **Hippocrates’ twins** <note>a historical metaphor for things that are so closely linked they live and die together</note>, they live and die together. Thus far **Ross** <note>Alexander Ross (1591–1654), author of *Pansebeia: or, A View of all Religions in the World*</note>, page 15, on the religions of the world, second to last question, page 682 and following.

§ 7. Thirdly, the Emperor <note>Julius Caesar</note> reports that the **Druids** had a leader or High Priest over them. **Olaus Magnus** <note>a 16th-century Swedish historian and cleric</note>, in book 3, chapter 8, mentions the chief priests among his people, whom he otherwise calls bishops. Among the Prussian-Wends <note>the Slavic and Baltic tribes of the southern Baltic coast</note>, there was a High Priest over the clergy who, in their language, was called **Crive**, while the other priests who stood beneath him were called **Sigonoten**: according to **Duisburg**, part 3, *Chronicle of Prussia*, chapter 5, and **Waissel**, in his *Chronicle*.

# Cimbrian Priesthood

The Egyptian priests were provided with food and drink and were maintained with the necessary provisions for life: <note>original: Herodotus, book 2, number 46, p. 113</note>. Income in Egypt was divided into three parts; the first part was received by the priests: <note>original: Diodorus Siculus, book 1, chapter 73, p. 64</note>. Holy Scripture also testifies that they had their own lands from which they were to nourish themselves. But when these lands were not sufficient during the famine, Joseph provided them with maintenance: Genesis 47:22. <note>compare: Gerhard’s *Commentaries* on this passage, p. 799 and p. 801</note>. Otherwise, the pagan priests possessed **tithes** <term>a tax of one-tenth of produce or income</term> and the **firstfruits** <term>the first agricultural produce of a season, traditionally offered to a deity</term>: <note>original: Polydore Vergil, book 6, *On Inventors*, chapter 14, p. 588</note>. When the Persian King **Cyrus** overcame **Croesus**, the King of the Lydians, he offered a portion of the war-booty to Jupiter: <note>original: Herodotus, book 1, number 17, p. 46</note>. The Arabs were not permitted to sell any of their frankincense until they had given the tithes of it to their idol: <note>original: Pliny, book 12, chapter 14</note>. The Greeks gave tithes to **Apollo**, the Romans to **Hercules**, the Gauls to **Mars**, and the Arabs to **Sabin**: <note>original: Rebuffus, *Treatise on Tithes*, question 1, number 10</note>. When **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century Cardinal and historian</note> cites a great many examples of the pagans delivering tithes, he concludes with these words: *It is well known that among almost all peoples, as if by a certain impulse of nature, tithes were promised and given to the gods:* <note>original: Baronius, *Annals* for the year 57, number 74</note>. When **Romulus** <note>legendary founder of Rome</note> wished to organize his government properly, he divided the land into three parts: he assigned the first part to the priests, the second part to the public treasury, and the last part to the people, as **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** relates in his second book: <note>compare: Leonhard Coqueus's commentary on Augustine’s *City of God*, book 2, chapter 11</note>. To the idol **Bel in Babylon**, twelve **malters** <term>an old German dry measure for grain, roughly 150 liters</term> of wheat, forty sheep, and three **eymers** <term>a liquid measure, similar to a bucket or cask</term> of wine were sacrificed daily, which the priests consumed with their wives and children every day in the temple; this is mentioned in the appendix of the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament regarding Bel of Babylon. The Prophet Jeremiah refers to this in chapter 51, verse 44: *I have visited Bel in Babylon, and I have torn from his throat that which he had swallowed,* meaning by his priests: <note>original: *Biblia Ernestina* and Hulsemann on this passage</note>.

# Chapter XXXIII /
## On the Pagan Authorities of Our Ancestors.

->Contents:<-

1. Government was held by the kings.
2. Who were orderly elected.
3. The choice generally fell upon the royal and princely lineage.
4. The lower authorities were divided among the gentry into <term>Hoffdinger: archaic Scandinavian and Germanic court officials or district administrators</term> and <term>Heermänner: military commanders or leaders of a host</term>.
5. Among the Saxons, there were twelve regents.
<column-break/>
6. The kings had to hold <term>Imperial Diets: general assemblies of the estates or important leaders</term> when something important was to be decided.
7. They prescribed laws for their subjects. On the laws of war of King Frotho in Denmark.
8. And his civil laws.
9. On the places and types of judgment.
10. The regents and subjects were devoted to public plunder.

In this northern <note>original: "mitternächtigen," literally "midnight," a common early modern term for the North</note> world, as elsewhere, the pagans have had kings over them from time immemorial. <term>Saxo Grammaticus: a 12th-century Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum</term> relates in the first and second books that in this land among the Saxons, Wends, and Frisians, as well as in Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, kings ruled and waged great wars among themselves long before the birth of Christ. # Cimbrian Antiquities

Even after their conversion to the Christian faith, the **Franks** maintained the heathen, inhuman custom of offering themselves to combat for life and limb over minor causes and in almost every legal matter. By doing so, they sought to bring innocence and justice to light, as if the strong were always right and the weak were always wrong. Furthermore, he <note>Referring to the historian Christoph Lehmann (1581–1638), known for his chronicles of German cities.</note> recounts that during the questioning of witnesses, they held their swords by the pommel to signal that they were prepared to defend the witnessed truth with the sword. This was indeed the case; if neither party would concede to the other, a single combat was held in an open field between the two disputing parties. The defeated party and his supporters were then held to be perjurers and false witnesses; the loser’s right hand was cut off, while those on his side had to "ransom" their hands with money. Thus far **Lehmann**. This **law of combat** was customary among the most prominent European peoples, especially among the German **Franks**, **Burgundians**, **English**, **French**, **Spanish**, **Muscovites**, and **Lombards**, in both civil and criminal matters: **Stephan in notes on Saxo, book 5, page 120.** <note>Stephanus Johannis Stephanius, a 17th-century Danish scholar who provided extensive commentary on Saxo Grammaticus.</note> This heathen practice could not be entirely rooted out from among the knighthood to this day. Subsequently, this **Sword-Judgment** was abolished, and in its place the **trial of the glowing iron** was introduced. The accused had to grasp the iron with his bare hand and carry it for several paces. Depending on whether his hand was wounded or remained unharmed, he was declared guilty or innocent: **Saxo, book 10, page 189. Compare Stephan, notes on Saxo, book 5, page 120, and following; Worm, book 1, Monuments, chapter 11.** <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654) was a famous Danish physician and antiquarian who documented Norse monuments.</note>

His words are: "Horvendill, having exercised his rule for three years, had devoted himself to piracy with the highest worldly glory." <note>original Latin: "Horvendillus triennio tyrannide gesta per summam rerum gloriam pyraticæ incubuerat."</note> Similarly, **Snorri Sturluson** <note>The famous Icelandic historian and poet (1179–1241).</note> recounts this of the Nordic kings, noting that at that time piracy was considered an honorable war: **Snorri, Part 3, Norwegian Chronicle, page 121.** In this, the **Cimbrian peoples** followed their rulers, occupying themselves with piracy and sustaining themselves by it. §. 2. Parents did not usually marry off their children without their consent. The aforementioned King Frotho of Denmark <note>A legendary ruler of the Danes described by Saxo Grammaticus.</note> issued a decree <note>original: "Verordnung"</note> that children should not be forced into marriage, but should have the free power to marry whom they wished, even against their parents' knowledge and will: Saxo, Book [not specified]. This last point is considered Heathen <note>original: "Heydnisch"</note>, which the Papal Church has nevertheless sought to defend until now: namely, that a child's marriage vow should be legitimate even without parental consent: Council of Trent, Session 24, Decree 1, Chapter 1, cited in Soave Polano <note>original: "Svavispol.", a pseudonym for the historian Paolo Sarpi</note>, *History of the Council of Trent*, page 876; Coster, *Enchiridion*, Chapter 20, page 605; Bellarmine, Book 1, *On Matrimony*, Chapter 19.

§. 3. It is creditably said of the ancient **Cimbri** that they were supposed to have had no more than one spouse: Cilicius <note>Referring to the historian Heinrich Rantzau.</note>, Book [not specified]. This must be understood as referring to the **Cimbrian Saxons** and **Frisians** alone; for the **Wends** took as many wives as they could support, as Hartknoch writes regarding the **Prussian Wends** in his 12th Dissertation on *Prussian Matters*, Section 2. This practice was common in all three Northern Kingdoms <note>original: "Mitternächtigen Reiche", literally "Midnight Realms," an archaic term for Scandinavia</note>. Concerning the **Goths** and **Danes**, Witfeld’s *Chronicle* reports on page 111 that they had an ancient law allowing them to take many wives and to send out all sons except one to wage war in foreign lands. In **Sweden**, every man has two, three, or more wives according to his means; the most noble and wealthy married a far greater number of wives: Adam of Bremen, *Book on the Geography of Denmark and the Northern Kingdoms* <note>original: "lib. de Situ Daniæ & Reg. Sept."</note>, page 140. Marriage was conducted in the same way in **Norway**; the Norwegian King **Harald Fairhair** <note>original: "Harald Schönhaar"</note> had seven wives at the same time: Snorri Sturluson, Part 3, *Norwegian Chronicle*, number 1, page 50 and following. Similarly, King **Amleth** <note>The legendary figure who inspired Shakespeare's Hamlet.</note> in Jutland had two consorts at once: namely, the daughter of the King of England and the widowed Queen of Scotland: Saxo, Book 4, in the *Life of King Roric*, page 58. This practice of polygamy <note>original: "viel Weiber-Ehe"</note> was first introduced after the Great Flood by the godless Lamech of Cain’s lineage: Genesis 4:19. He was followed in this by the Asian, African, European, and American peoples, who maintained the custom of taking as many wives as they could support. This is written of the **Turks** by Lonicerus, Volume 1, *Turkish Chronicle*, Book 2, part 1, chapter 13, page 39. Of the **Tartars**: Aubanus, Book 2, *Of the Manners of All Nations* <note>original: "de M. G.", referring to De Moribus Gentium</note>, chapter 10, page 133. Of the **Persians**: Olearius, Book 5, *Persian Journey* <note>original: "Itiner. Pers."</note>, chapter 21. Of the **Indians**: Mandelslo, Book 1, *Oriental Journey*, chapters 23 and 35. Of the **Chinese**: Nieuhof, Part 2, *Journey to China*, chapter 4, page 280. Of the **Egyptians**: Schweigger, Book 3.

# Cimbrian Matters
<note>The "Cimbri" refers to an ancient Germanic people; the author uses this heading to discuss Northern Germanic history and customs.</note>

Ecclesiastical History, chapter 33. In our times, polygamy is defended by the Anabaptists: *Pontanus on Heresies, chapter 1.* By the David-Jorists <note>Followers of David Joris, a 16th-century radical reformer.</note> and the Libertines: *Hornbeek, Book 6, Controversies, page 413.* As well as by the modern Jews: *The same author, Book 2, Controversies, page 74.*

§. 4. Regarding marriages, the groom received no dowry <note>original: "Braut-Schatz"</note>; instead, he had to essentially buy the bride from her parents for a certain sum. *Marriages used to be for sale: Saxo Grammaticus, Book 3, in the Life of King Sivard I, page 154.* <note>original: "Venalia quondam solebant esse connubia"</note> King Frotho III, surnamed "the Great," issued a law in the Kingdom of Denmark—or rather, confirmed the old custom through a public law—that no one should marry a woman unless he had acquired her with money or money's worth. He believed such a marriage would be more stable and secure than others: *Saxo, Book 5, in the Life of King Frotho III, page 88.* For this reason, a man is called a "silly man" <note>original: "alber Mann". In this context, it refers to a man who is "simple" or "foolish" because he accepts a dowry, which was seen as a reversal of the traditional masculine role of providing the bride-price.</note> who receives goods and a dowry with his wife: *Havamal, number 69.* <note>The Havamal is a collection of Old Norse wisdom poems.</note> Thus, the Germans, Goths, Wends, Saxons, Franks, Norwegians, as well as the Romans, Greeks, Thracians, and Assyrians, maintained the custom of courting without a dowry and purchasing the bride for themselves: *Stephanus in his notes on Saxo, Book 5, page 122; Laurentius, Book 3, Synopsis of Polymathy 8, page 230.* When a maiden became of age among the Babylonians, she was brought to market and sold into marriage: *Herodotus, Book 1, number 14, page 36.* Among the Turks, it is still customary for the parents to give nothing to the daughter as a dowry; instead, they receive a sum of money from the groom, which is used for the bridal jewelry: *Lonicerus, Volume 1, Turkish Chronicle, Book 2, Part 1, chapter 13, page 91.* The same occurs among the Persians: *Olearius, Book 5, Persian Itinerary, chapter 22.* Among the Tartars: *Marco Polo <note>original: "Paulus Venet."</note>, Book 1, On the Eastern Kingdoms, chapters 55 and 62.* The inhabitants of China <note>original: "Sina"</note> must buy their wives for money and also have the power to sell them again: *Nieuhof, Part 2, Itinerary of China, chapter 4, pages 280 and following.* Among the Indians, the groom must give the parents a sum of money for his bride, which is intended as a reward for raising the daughter: *Mandelslo, Book 1, Indian Itinerary, chapter 36, and Book 2, chapter 19; J. Andersen, Book 1, Oriental Itinerary, chapter 31; Rogerius, Part 1, Open Door to Heathendom, chapter 11.* This custom is also kept by the Arabs: *Volateranus, Book 3, chapter 34.* The Egyptians: *Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 2, chapter 5.* The Moors: *Johannes Boemus <note>original: "Aubanus"</note>, Book 1, On the Manners of Nations, chapter 4.* The Brazilians in America: *Erasmus Francisci.*

§. 5. Thus, our ancestors looked purely upon virtue when it came to marriage. According to this Law of God, Duke Johann Adolf of Schleswig-Holstein issued a public mandate in the year 1608 that adulterers should be executed with the sword. The aforementioned King Frotho the Great of Denmark is said to have made the decree that adulterers and violent violators of virgins should lose their manhood <note>be castrated</note>, and otherwise defiled persons should be married by the perpetrators: Saxo, book 5, in the *Life of King Frotho III*, pages 85 and 88.

The deprivation of manhood was a common punishment for adultery among the Greeks, Romans, Poles, English, and Egyptians: Stephanius on the same; Laurentius, book 1, *Polymath*, Dissertation 28. The defiling of a virgin was an abomination to our ancestors. Therefore, when Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian</note> in book 5, page 89 and following, recounts the story of Hilda, the daughter of the King of Jutland—asking whether she had been defiled by her husband King Hithin of Norway before the betrothal—he adds that this was considered a gruesome deed among all peoples, which King Höcke then avenged upon his son-in-law with the sword.

### §. 7. ###
Just as second marriage <note>remarriage after the death of a spouse</note> was forbidden among various pagan peoples (as noted by Dr. Gerhard, *Theological Commonplaces, Volume 7, Laws of Marriage, Number 189*; Alberico Gentili, *On Marriages, Book 6, Chapter 22*; and Arnisaeus, *On the Right of Marriage, Chapter 5, Section 3*), it was likewise either not permitted or not customary among our ancestors (according to Cilicius, *On the German Benevolence, Book 1, Chapter 18*). In my opinion, this is to be understood as applying to the Saxons and Wends <note>A term historically used by Germans to describe West Slavic peoples</note>, and especially to their women. For among the Wends, surviving wives were required to die and be buried with their husbands (see William of Malmesbury and Hedio, *On the Life of John Peter, Part 1, Chronicle, page 18*; Solinus, *Chronicle, page 64*), which shall be further explained in its proper place, God willing. Otherwise, second marriages for both women and men were customary among the Goths and Danes, as demonstrated by *Saxo* <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a medieval Danish historian</note> with the example of King *Amleth's* <note>The legendary figure who inspired Shakespeare's Hamlet</note> mother and wife, both of whom remarried after the death of their lords and husbands (*Saxo, Book 3, in the Life of King Rorik, page 49; and Book 4, in the Life of King Viglet, page 59*).

### §. 8. ###
Among the Goths, it was the custom for the bridegroom and bride to place a naked <note>unsheathed</note> sword between them in the bed on the first night (*Edda, Part 1, Fable 73; Saxo, Book 9, in the Life of King Gorm III, page 179*). With this, they presumably had in mind the punishment for adultery. Among the Frisians, the bride had to step into the wedding house under an unsheathed sword, by which she was reminded to keep the marriage covenant faithfully with her husband; otherwise, as an adulteress, she would be judged by the sword, which is why it was called the "Marriage-Sword" (*Heimrich Walter, Book 1, Frisian Chronicle, Chapter 2*).

### §. 9. ###
Regarding the wedding customs of the Wendish peoples, particularly the Prussian-Wends and their neighbors the Lithuanians and Samogitians <note>A region in modern-day Lithuania</note>, *Johannes Miletius* writes as follows: Marriageable daughters wore small bells or tinklers on their belts, which was a sign that they wished to marry. Now, when a suitor appeared, he would have the girl snatched and carried away by his closest friends. After this abduction, he first approached the parents regarding the matter, and the formal promise followed. At the wedding, the bride was led three times around the hearth and then placed upon a chair where her feet were washed. With this foot-water, the marriage bed and all the household implements were sprinkled, as was every wedding...

§. 2. Nevertheless, some schools must have existed in the land, although they were in a poor state. For if people were able to read and write and compose epitaphs, there must have been schools where such things were learned. §. 3. To all appearances, the starting point in these schools would have been their pagan faith. For without such schools, their religion and idolatry could not have endured.

§. 5. They are commonly called Runic letters; however, it seems that this nickname arose from their misuse in all kinds of sorcery <note>original German: "Zaubereyen"</note>, and is thus to be understood *synecdochically* <note>using a part to represent the whole</note> or rather *catachrestically* <note>using a word in a forced or improper way</note>. But it does not follow from this that these letters should generally and properly be called Runic letters for that reason; however, I do not wish to quarrel with anyone on this point, but have only stated this *problematically* <note>as a proposition for debate</note> and leave it to the kind reader's consideration.

§. 6. In those times, people knew nothing of paper, but instead wrote on wood. For instance, Fengo, Duke of Schleswig, composed his correspondence to the King of Britain on wood: *Saxo, Book 3 of the History of the Danes, in the life of King Roric, page 52.* <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220) was a Danish historian whose "Gesta Danorum" is a primary source for early Estonian and Scandinavian history.</note> "That was once a famous type of writing-material," <note>original Latin: "Id celebre quondam genus chartarum erat"</note> writes this author. These were thin wooden boards into which the letters were carved: *Stephanius in his notes on this passage, page 100.* <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650) was a Danish philologist and historian.</note> Upon such boards or small tablets, Solon had his laws engraved: *Suidas in the Lexicon under the entry for Solon.* <note>Solon was an Athenian statesman often credited with laying the foundations for Greek democracy.</note> In the year 1525, a book made of wooden boards was found in a cave in Spain, inscribed with engraved Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters: *Camerarius, 3rd Century of Historical Meditations, chapter 14, page 47.* <note>Philipp Camerarius (1537–1624) was a German jurist and writer.</note> These writing-tablets were commonly made of ash-wood or boxwood: *Stephanius and also Salmuth in the commentary on Pancirollus, book 2, title 13.* This wooden boxwood tablet is mentioned by *Wormius in Book 2 of Fasti, chapter 4,* <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a Danish physician known for his collection of antiquities and runic studies.</note> where he also provides an illustration of it. Among the Greeks and Romans, these wooden boards were coated with wax, and the script was formed therein with an iron or bone stylus; these were called *Tabulæ, Codicilli, Pugillares* <note>Latin: "Tablets, small notebooks, or hand-tablets."</note> or writing-tablets: *Pancirollus & Salmuth, as cited above.* Otherwise, people also wrote on staffs, upon which the seasons of the year were recorded in writing; because of this, they were called Calendar-staffs <note>Also known as "clog almanacs," these were wooden sticks used as perpetual calendars in Northern Europe.</note>: *Olaus Magnus, book 16, chapter 20.* *Wormius* also illustrated these in *Fasti, book 2, chapter 2, and in his Museum, page 367.*

The Northern peoples <note>original: "Mitternächtige Völcker," literally "Midnight peoples," a common early modern term for Scandinavians or Arctic peoples.</note> also wrote upon stones and rocks. Regarding the Kings of Denmark, Harald Hytand and Ragnar Lodbrok, *Saxo* relates that they had their brave deeds recorded in writing upon rocks: *Saxo in the Preface to the History of the Danes, page 3, and book 9, page 173.* The Haraldic Runestone <note>original: "Runfels," a runic rock.</note> with its letters can still be seen today in Blekinge, and its likeness can be seen in *Stephanius’s notes on Saxo’s Preface, page 22.* Likewise, the brave Carthaginian war-hero Hannibal is said to have carved his passage over the Alps into the rock with letters as an eternal memorial; this inscription can still be read on a rock near the village of Barroum: *Paulus Jovius, book 15 of the Histories, page 168.* <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was an Italian physician and historian; the "Hannibal inscription" he mentions is now largely considered a curiosity of local legend rather than a verified Carthaginian artifact.</note> We have similar examples in Holy Scripture as well. God Himself wrote the Ten Commandments on stone tablets with His own hand: *Exodus 24, verse 12; 31, verse 18.* Moses commanded Joshua and the people of Israel: "You shall write all the words of this law upon stones, clearly and distinctly."

# Chapter XXXVI
## What our ancestors believed regarding divine punishments and tribulations.

->Table of Contents:<-

<columns>2</columns>

4. How a person should conduct themselves during private tribulations.

They believed that land-plagues and other tribulations did not strike humanity by chance or accident, but were ordained by the gods. For they were of the opinion that both good and bad fortune, good and evil, came from the providence of the gods. Our Wendish peoples <note>original: "Wandalischen Völcker," referring to the Slavic and Germanic tribes of the Baltic region</note> believed in both a good and an evil god, and supposed that all good came from the former, but all evil from the latter: Helmold, Book 1, chapter 53; Krantz, Book 3, *Vandalia*, chapter 37. Likewise, our ancestors had their good and evil Norns, or Fates <note>original: "Parcer," referring to the Parcae of Roman myth</note>, to whom they attributed all the good and evil that they encountered throughout their entire lives: *Edda*, Part 1, Fable 15; Olaus Magnus, Book 3, chapter 9.

§. 2. They believed that the principal cause of divine punishments and plagues was the contempt and neglect of idolatry <note>The author uses "Götzendienst" (idolatry) to describe the ancient pagan worship from a later Christian perspective.</note>: *Magdeburg Centuries*, Century 4, *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 15, page 1500; Clausen, in *Description of Norway*, chapter 33, page 161. When King Eric the Younger began to reign in Denmark, his people (no doubt his priests) made him believe that the gods were enraged and would inflict every misfortune upon the land because the old worship had ceased and a foreign service <note>meaning Christianity</note> had been introduced: Rimbert, in *The Life of Ansgar*, chapter 28; Gualdo in *The Life of Ansgar*, chapter 71. Regarding King Olaf <note>likely Olof Trätälja</note> in Sweden, it is told that he was reluctant to sacrifice to and serve the gods; when a time of famine occurred in the land, the Swedes attributed the cause of this scarcity to their King Olaf, because of his contempt for the sacrifice

How the heathens were to conduct themselves during private tribulations is taught by the Icelandic book called the *Hávamál* <note>A collection of Old Norse poems containing advice for living and wisdom attributed to the god Odin.</note>, through the following sayings which agree with the Word of God: (1) You shall not reveal your misfortune to wicked people. (2) You shall have sorrow with the sorrowful. (3) You shall not rejoice over another’s misfortune. (4) Do not quarrel with wicked people, but rather yield to them when they rage: *Hávamál*, numbers 105, sequence 114.

§. 5. Regarding the tribulations of the righteous, the heathen Seneca writes in his book titled *On Providence* <note>original: *de Providentia*</note>; however, he does not write as a heathen, but as if he had been raised in the Church of God and had studied the Holy Scriptures. He writes that nothing evil happens to the righteous, that all adversities are exercises in virtue, and that God has a fatherly heart toward the righteous and loves them dearly, exercising them through all manner of adversity so they may be strengthened in goodness. He claims that he who has never been in misfortune is truly wretched; that God visits the most pious either with weakness or other adversities; and that God loves those whom He tests and exercises through tribulations. Just as trees are more firmly rooted in the earth through the buffeting of the wind, so are the righteous strengthened in goodness through trials. The words of this wise man are worthy of being placed here:

> Seneca, from the book: *Why misfortunes happen to good men, though Providence exists.*
> No evil can happen to a good man. He considers all adversities to be exercises. Chapter 2.

I judge you miserable because you have never been miserable. Great men sometimes rejoice in adversity, no differently than brave soldiers rejoice in wars. §. 2. Regarding how many kinds of prophecy the heathens possessed and from where they were derived, *Cicero* treats this extensively in his books *On Divination* <note>original: "de Divinatione"</note>, and even more extensively *Caspar Peucerus* in his great work *On the Kinds of Divinations* <note>original: "de Divinationum Generibus"</note>, and briefly by *Mr. Bircherod* in his *Exercise on Divination* <note>original: "Exercitat. de Divinatione"</note>. Our intention is solely to investigate those types of prophecies which our ancestors used, as far as we can have knowledge of them. These were primarily: from the <term>casting of lots<gloss>the practice of drawing markers or tokens to determine the divine will</gloss></term>; from the blood and entrails of the sacrificial victim; from the flight and cry of birds; from the gait and neighing of horses; from the combat of two fighters; from fire and water; from the vapors and mists of high mountains; from dreams, sorcery, and magic mirrors, etc. <note>The author cites Adam of Bremen, a medieval chronicler, and Olaus Magnus, a Swedish ecclesiastic and writer.</note>

§. 3. The first type of prophecy, according to the aforementioned order, was from the casting of lots. Our <term>Saxons<gloss>A Germanic people from Northern Germany</gloss></term> had a custom where they would cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree and slice it into various pieces, which were marked with special identifying signs and then thrown together onto a white cloth. In doing so, they looked up toward heaven and called upon the gods, and then picked up or tossed these cut pieces of branches upon the white cloth. From this, they watched and provided an explanation according to the signs they observed. This was done by the priest for public deliberations, but by the <term>father of the household<gloss>the male head of a private family</gloss></term> for private deliberations. <note>Adam of Bremen, Book 1, Chapter 6.</note> The <term>Wends<gloss>A historical name for West Slavic people living near Germanic settlements</gloss></term> had this custom: they took three small pieces of wood which were white on one side and black on the other, and threw them into their lap. Here they paid attention to whether and how many pieces turned up the white or black color; for the white color turned upward was a good sign to them, but the black color was a bad sign. <note>Saxo Grammaticus, Book 14, in the life of King Waldemar I.</note>

§. 4. The second type of soothsaying was from the blood and entrails of the sacrificial victims, both of animals and humans. The <term>Cimbrian<gloss>An ancient Germanic or Celtic tribe who famously fought the Roman Republic</gloss></term> priestesses used to slit the throats of human prisoners with a sword and prophesy from the blood as it flowed into a tub. Other priestesses were appointed to open the body and from the entrails...

§. 5. The third type of prophesying was from the **flight and cry of birds**: <note>original: "Adamus B. & Olaus M. l. 1. d."</note>. It is written of King Friedleff the Second in Denmark: <note>original: "Saxo lib. 6. p. 100."</note> and of King Dag in Sweden: <note>original: "Snoro P. 1. Chron. Among the heathens, there were several unlucky birds: such as ravens, screech-owls, eagle-owls, swallows, vultures, bees, etc. Others, however, were lucky birds: such as doves, storks, falcons, woodpeckers, nightingales, etc. Just as with their flight and cry, the former were meant to signify evil, while the latter signified good. Otherwise, the flight and cry of birds—depending on whether they flew and let their voices be heard toward the morning <note>The East</note> or evening <note>The West</note>, midday <note>The South</note> or midnight <note>The North</note>, to the right or to the left—possessed different meanings. From the untimely crowing of the rooster, one prophesied good things; but from the unusual cackling of the hens, evil was predicted. The flocking together of different kinds of birds, such as eagles, vultures, ravens, etc., was meant to signify war and bloodshed: but the flocking of storks signified peace and unity: <note>Compare "Peucerus l. d. f. 203. seq. Alex. ab Alex. l. 5. c. 13."</note>. The Indians <note>Likely referring to Indigenous peoples of the Americas or East Indies as described by 17th-century travelers.</note> of today hold much by this; they make a distinction, however, among the birds and their flight to the right and to the left: <note>original: "Roger. P. 1. Off. Thür. c. 14."</note>. The objection that the birds do not know future things, and therefore cannot indicate them with their flight and cry, **Ammianus Marcellinus** intends to resolve through consideration of **divine direction**, as if God the **LORD** should direct the flight and voice of the birds according to man’s intention, in order to discover future things. # Cimbrian Customs

...knowledge is gathered, for not even a fool would say such a thing; but God directs the flights of birds so that the sounding beak or a wing flying by in a turbulent or gentle path might foretell things to come: <note>original Latin: "scientiam colliguntur... vel leni futura præmonstret : Marcellilib.xxi." Referring to the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who discussed how the divine might use natural signs like birds to communicate with humans.</note> This is what it means to prove the uncertain through the uncertain and the false through a false premise. Others have believed that birds were the messengers and secret counselors of the gods because they fly up and down toward the heavens. This pagan superstition has not completely died out among us Christians; the common man is still of the opinion that the excessive chattering of magpies <note>original: "Heister"</note> near a house signifies foreign guests; the shrieking of owls at night signifies a corpse; the flight of storks away from a house signifies a conflagration; the fighting of storks among themselves signifies war; the croaking of ravens on a journey signifies misfortune, and so on. This is condemned in Holy Scripture: *Leviticus 19:26, Deuteronomy 18:10.*

§. 6. The fourth type of prophesying was from the gait and cries of **horses** (and other animals) <note>original: "Adamus Bremensis l. d." Referring to the medieval chronicler Adam of Bremen.</note>. Among the **Wends** <note>A group of Slavic people living in Northern Europe.</note>, there was a great white horse consecrated to the idol **Svantovit** <note>original: "Schwantevit," the four-headed Slavic god of war and divination.</note>. When a war was to begin, six spears were stuck into the ground in front of the temple of the idol, with the iron points down, two and two, crossed over each other, so that three pairs of spears were set up in a row, each pair several paces distant from the next. After a preceding prayer, the holy horse was led out by the priest to jump over these crosswise-set spears. If the horse, in jumping over these spears, set its right foot forward before the left, it was held to be a good sign; but if it set its left foot forward before the right, it was held to be an evil sign. Depending on this jump or gait of the horse, the war was either pursued or abandoned: <note>original: "Saxo lib. 14. in vita R. Wald I. p. 321." Referring to Saxo Grammaticus’s history of Denmark.</note> When they rode out, they paid attention to the first animal that encountered them; depending on whether that animal was considered lucky or unlucky—or, as others suspect, whether it was first seen on the right or left side—the journey was either continued or postponed: <note>original: "Saxo l. d."</note>. Among the unlucky animals were counted wolves, hares, pregnant dogs, and foxes, as well as snakes, weasels, etc., which were not thought to be good signs when encountered: <note>original: "Peucerus de divin. tit. de Aruspic. f. 206. seq. Alex. ab Alex. l. 5. c. 13." Caspar Peucer and Alexander ab Alexandro were prominent Renaissance scholars of ancient customs and divination.</note>

§. 7. The fifth type of prophesying was from the combat of two fighters.

# Pagan Religion

<margin>Divination through combat</margin>
When our **Cimbrian Saxons** <note>An ancient Germanic people from the Jutland Peninsula</note> intended to start a war, they would take a prisoner from the enemy's people and have him fight one of their own men. If the prisoner gained the upper hand in this duel, they considered it an evil sign, as if the enemy nation would also gain the upper hand in the coming war. But if their own fighter was victorious, it was taken as a good sign that they would carry away the victory in the war: <note>original Latin: "Adamus Bremenf. lib. 1. cap. 6." referring to the medieval chronicler Adam of Bremen.</note> <note>original Latin: "Aubanus l. 3. de M. G. c. 13." referring to Johannes Boemus's work on the customs of nations.</note> This method of prophesying the outcome of an impending war through the combat of two fighters was observed not only by our Saxons but also by the Germans in general: <note>original Latin: "Tacitus lib. de Germ." Referring to the Roman historian Tacitus and his work *Germania*.</note> Likewise, the Wends, Danes, and Swedes followed this custom: <note>original Latin: "Witf. in Chron. M. p. 2." Referring to the chronicler Widukind of Corvey.</note>

§. 8. The sixth type of fortune-telling was from **fire**: <note>original Latin: "Olaus M. l. 3. c. 12." referring to the Swedish writer Olaus Magnus.</note> called <term>Pyromancy</term> <note>divination by fire</note> among the Greeks. The **Wends** <note>Slavic people of Central Europe</note> called these fire-prophets <term>Swakones</term>: <note>original Latin: "Hartknoch, diss. 9. Rer. Pruß. num. 6." referring to the historian Christoph Hartknoch's work on Prussian history.</note> I do not find it recorded how our ancestors practiced this. The Greeks and Romans took their prophecies from the sacrificial fire; if it began to burn quickly and ignite the offering, if it burned quietly and clearly, directing its flame straight upward and consuming the sacrifice entirely, it was held as a good omen and a sacrifice pleasing to the gods. Otherwise, it was considered a bad sign, and the sacrifice was thought to be displeasing to the idols. They also paid attention to the smoke: how high it rose, how it swirled, and in which direction it drifted, etc.: <note>original Latin: "Peucerus de divinat. tit. de Extispic. f. 192. seq." referring to Caspar Peucer's 16th-century treatise on divination.</note> <note>original Latin: "Rosinus lib. 3. Mag. c. 2. q. 1. f. 1. p. 412. seq." referring to Martin Delrio's *Disquisitions on Magic*.</note>

...gathered from those who know, <note>original Latin: "ſcientium colliguntur"</note> for not even a fool would say such a thing; but God directs the flight of birds, so that the sounding beak, the wing flying past in a turbulent path, or a gentle one, may forewarn of the future: <note>original Latin: "Marcelli- lib. xxi." referring to the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who discussed how the divine spirit communicates through augury.</note> That is to say, proving the uncertain through the uncertain, and the false through a false premise. Others have supposed that the birds were the messengers and secret counselors of the gods because they fly up and down in the heavens.

This pagan superstition has not entirely vanished among us Christians; the common man is still of the opinion that the frequent chattering of <term>magpies</term> <note>German: "Heiſter"</note> near a house means strange guests will arrive; the hooting of owls at night means a corpse; the departure of storks from a house means a fire; their fighting among themselves means war; the croaking of ravens during a journey means misfortune, etc. This is condemned in Holy Scripture: Leviticus 19:26, Deuteronomy 18:10.

§. 6. The fourth way of prophesying was from the gait and cries of horses (and other animals) <note>original Latin: "Adamus Bremenſis l. d." referring to the medieval chronicler Adam of Bremen.</note>. Among the Wends <note>A Slavic people living near Germanic territories</note>, there was a large white horse consecrated to the idol <term>Svantovit</term> <note>A powerful Slavic deity associated with war and prophecy</note>. When a war was to begin, six spears were stuck into the ground with the iron tips downward in front of the idol's temple, two by two crosswise together, so that three pairs of spears were placed in a line, each pair being several steps apart from the next.

After a preceding prayer, the holy horse was led out by the priest to jump over these crosswise-placed spears. If the horse, in jumping over these spears, put its right foot forward before its left, that was supposed to be a good sign; but if it put its left foot forward before its right, it was held to be a bad sign. According to this jump or gait of the horse, the war was either pursued or called off: <note>original Latin: "Saxo lib. 14. in vita R. Wald I. p. 321." referring to Saxo Grammaticus, who chronicled the deeds of the Danes.</note>. When they set out on a journey, they paid attention to the first animal that met them; depending on whether it was considered a lucky or unlucky animal, or, as others suggest, whether it appeared first on the right or left side, the journey was continued or postponed: <note>original Latin: "Saxo l. d."</note>. Among the unlucky animals were counted wolves, hares, pregnant dogs, and foxes, as well as snakes, weasels, etc., which were said to be no good sign when encountered: <note>original Latin: "Peucerus de divin. tit. de Aruſpic. f. 206. ſeq." referring to Caspar Peucer’s work on divination; "Alex. ab Alex. l. 5. c. 13." referring to the scholar Alessandro Alessandri.</note>

When our Cimbrian Saxons <note>An ancient Germanic tribe; the author uses "our" to indicate ancestral connection</note> wished to begin a war, they would have a prisoner from the enemy's people fight against one of their own men. If the prisoner gained the upper hand in this duel, they considered it a bad omen, as if the enemy nation would also gain the upper hand in the coming war. However, if their own fighter was victorious, it was taken as a good sign that they would carry away the victory in the war: Adam of Bremen, Book 1, Chapter 6 <note>original: "Adamus Bremenſ. lib. 1. cap. 6."</note>; Aubanus, Book 3, *Concerning the Customs of the Germans*, Chapter 13 <note>original: "Aubanus l. 3. de M.G. c. 13."</note>. This method of prophesying the outcome of a looming war from the combat of two fighters was observed not only by our Saxons, but by the Germans in general: Tacitus, *Book on the Germans* <note>original: "Tacitus lib. de Germ."</note>. # Cimbrian Customs

...[ho]ly women <note>The text likely begins with "holy" or "wise" women (German: *Heilige* or *Wahrsagerliche*)</note> prophesied from the swirls and sounds of the water, claiming it was not advisable to attack the Emperor <note>Julius Caesar</note> before the new moon: Plutarch in his *Life of Julius Caesar*. This agrees with what Clement of Alexandria writes in Book 1 of the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromat."</note> concerning the divination of German women from water-swirls: Cited by Delrio in *Investigations into Magic*, Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 2, page 397. To this also belongs the Celtic water ordeal for newborn children. Whenever a son was born among the Celtic—that is, the German and Gallic—peoples, and the father wished to know if it was his true, natural child and if his wife had been honorable, he took the infant, naked as it was born into the world, to the Rhine river and threw it into the water. If the child kicked and floated on the surface of the water, the father judged it to be his true son and his wife to be honest. However, if the child sank to the bottom, it was considered a child of adultery <note>original: "Hurenkind"</note> and the wife unfaithful. For this reason, the Rhine is called a "judge of uncertain birth" by Nonnus in his 46th book: Cluverius, *Ancient Germany*, Book 1, Chapter 21.

§. 10. The eighth method of divining was by the distinction of time. The Saxons believed that the new or full moon was the most fortunate time to begin or accomplish anything: Adam of Bremen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, Chapter 6. Out of this imagination, the prophetesses advised the German King Ehrenvest <note>A Germanized version of the name Ariovistus, a leader of the Suebi who fought Caesar</note> that he should not do battle with the Emperor before the new moon: Plutarch in his *Life of Julius Caesar*. There was a widespread superstition among the pagans that some days were lucky and others unlucky. This was believed by the Egyptians, Greeks, Romans, Gauls, and the Northern peoples <note>original: "Mitternächtige Völcker," literally "peoples of the midnight lands"</note>: Worm, *On the Calendar* <note>original: "Fast." referring to the *Fasti Danici*</note>, Book 1, Chapters 22, 23, 24. The modern Indians: Rogerius, *Open Door to Heathendom*, Part 1, Chapter 14. The Chinese: Trigault, *Concerning the Kingdom of China*, Book 1, Chapter 9. The Persians: Olearius, *Persian Journey*, Book 4, Chapter 17, page 123, and Chapter 19, page 483. Consequently, when our Princely Holstein ambassadors, during their Persian journey, wished to travel from the Caspian Sea toward Shamakhi in Media on December 29th, the Khan of the aforementioned city sent word to them, requesting that they remain still on that day because it was an unlucky day, as the well-regarded author reports in the first-mentioned place.
