# Cimbrian <note>Referring to the Cimbri, an ancient people of the North; here used to describe Northern or Germanic traditions.</note>

to seduce/ to make them fall away from God and His Word: Jeremiah 23, verses 27, 28, and 32. Thirdly, there are **natural dreams**, which have their natural causes and arise either from a person’s <term>temperament<note>In early modern medicine, a person's temperament or "complexion" was determined by the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</term> or the business of their profession. For whatever a person is inclined toward, and whatever they have to deal with, and whatever they think upon intensely throughout the day, they commonly dream of at night: Ecclesiastes 5, verse 2.

Therefore, a merchant usually dreams of buying and selling; a sailor of seafaring, of the wind and water; a miser of money and profit; a drunkard of drinking and feasting; and a lewd person of the company of women. Otherwise, these natural dreams generally align with a person’s temperament and <term>complexion</term>. One who is of a **sanguine** and blood-rich complexion dreams of pleasant and merry things. One who is of a **melancholic** temperament dreams of sad and terrifying things. One who is of a **choleric** complexion dreams of fire and the danger of fire. One who has a **phlegmatic** temperament dreams of water and the danger of water: see Calixtus in his commentary on Genesis, chapter 40, page 119; Titelman, book 10 of *Natural Philosophy*, chapter 24; and Velcurio, book 4 of *Physics*, chapter 13.

Such natural dreams have no particular significance, except that doctors of medicine can, to some extent, determine the nature and illness of the patient from them. The heathens misused such natural dreams and wished to prophesy future things from them. The Jews also fell into these heathen superstitions: Jeremiah 27:9, 29:8. And some among us Christians, who hold dreams in high regard—indeed, they even dare to publish entire books of **dream interpretations** to the world, following the instructions of Aristotle and Galen, both of whom wrote on prophesying from dreams.

Such dreamers in this day and age are the fanatics, enthusiasts, Quakers, and "new prophets," and in former times the Manichaeans, to whom the teacher Sirach (chapter 34, verses 1–8) has already given an answer. These dreamers were accustomed to sleeping at night in the houses of idols and wrapping and winding themselves in the skins of animals slaughtered for sacrifice, so that they might dream all the more certainly of future things: Peucerus, *On Divination*, in the section on Dreams, folio 257. In this "midnight world" <note>A poetic reference to the Northern regions or Scandinavia.</note>, some were accustomed to sleeping in pigsties when they wished to have certain dreams and prophesy from them: Snorri [Sturluson], part 2 of the *Chronicle of Norway*.

Just as Satan has been a liar from the beginning (John 8:44), he has also trafficked in lies through his oracles, which the Platonist philosopher **Iamblichus** admits: "Evil demons exist in every way, who both lie and deceive in the oracles." <note>original: "Improbi dæmones sunt omnino, qui & in Oraculis mentiuntur, & fallunt" from Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries*, Chapter 31, p. 105. Iamblichus was a Syrian Neoplatonist who wrote extensively on theurgy and the nature of spirits.</note> By this, he means that it is certainly the evil spirits who both lie and trick people through the oracles. Furthermore, Satan has been unable to predict anything certain regarding future events that are purely accidental (Isaiah 41:22–23), for that belongs to God alone (Isaiah 46:9–10). Therefore, the devilish oracles were either false or so doubtful, confused, and deceptive that one could either not understand them correctly or interpret them in two opposing ways, as shown by <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop whose works often sought to prove the superiority of Christianity over paganism.</note> in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 5, Chapters 8, 9, 10, and Book 4, Chapters 1, 20, and following verse 26.

§. 10. It is remarkable that these oracles of Satan ceased and fell silent at the incarnation of Christ, according to the prophecy of the prophet **Zechariah** (13:2–3). <note>Compare the commentaries on this passage by Lucas Osiander and Johann Tarnov, Lutheran theologians who argued that the coming of the Messiah ended the era of demonic prophecy.</note> This is attested not only by church histories but also by the pagans themselves, who marveled at the downfall of the oracles at that time. **Porphyry**, in his book *On the Philosophy of Oracles*, <note>original: "περὶ ἐκ λογίων Φιλοσοφίας" (Peri ek logion philosophias).</note> cites the following verses:

> Woe, woe is me! Mourn, O tripods; Apollo has perished.
> He has perished, because a burning heavenly light overpowers me.
> <note>original: "Væ væ mihi! tripodes lugete, periit Apollo, Periit, quoniam ardens mihi vim infert cœleste lumen." This quote reflects a late-antique tradition that the Delphic Oracle announced its own end upon the birth of Christ.</note>

The aforementioned **Porphyry** confesses this in his book written against the Christians, where he attributes the cause of the oracles falling silent to the honor and teaching of Christ: "For since Jesus has been honored," he says, "men have no longer experienced any benefit from the gods."

§. 11. The world-wise heathen Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher and priest at Delphi (c. 46–120 AD).</note> wrote a special book under the title *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: "de Defectu Oraculorum"</note>, in which he philosophized marvelously on both the origin and the downfall of the oracles. He believes that the oracles had their origin in the exhalations or vapors of deep caverns in the earth (where the temples of the oracles stood). These exhalations, according to his imagination, possess a prophetic power and are said to affect the minds of the idol-priests. He offers a comparison: just as the soil is not equally good and fertile in all places, nor at all times, so too it is with the prophetic exhalations of the deep caverns, which do not appear everywhere or at all times, but only where and when the goodness of the earth manifests itself most strongly through the influence of the heavens. Depending on whether these exhalations of the caverns were found to be penetrating or mild, subtle or coarse, pure or impure, he says the oracles were accordingly clear or dark, certain or uncertain. Such washing and cleansing may not take place in any flowing water; rather, the water must be specially dug out and stand still. It must also be consecrated by their Brahmins <term>Braminen: members of the highest priestly caste in Hinduism</term> with many superstitious words and ceremonies; otherwise, it has no power to wipe away sin.

By the pagan inhabitants of Hindustan, the water of the main river, the Ganges, is held to be very holy and blessed; so much so, that they firmly believe that all those who wash and bathe in it even once will have all their sins forgiven and pardoned, no matter how heavy they might be. Indeed, they become as pure and clean as if they were born anew. But whoever does not wash in it can never attain salvation. For this reason, a great crowd and frequent pilgrimages occur there from all over the East Indies. Thus far the account of Mr. Erasmus Francisci, Book 3, *Speculum*, page 922. # Cimbrian Beliefs #

It was believed that people did not die by chance, but rather that the end of their lives was determined by the gods in times of both peace and war, as the poet says: *Silius Italicus, Book 3, verse 154:*

->*In peace and in war, the end of life stands fixed for all.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Et pace, & bello cunctis stat terminus ævi." Silius Italicus was a Roman poet whose epic *Punica* was often cited by early modern scholars for its descriptions of ancient customs.</note>

Regarding this "goal of life" for humanity, they established three goddesses, whom our ancestors called the **Norns** <note>original: *Nörner*; in Norse mythology, these are the deities who govern the fates of gods and men</note> and the Romans called the **Parcae**. They were held as the rulers over human life and death, fortune and misfortune: *Edda, Part 1, Fable 15; Olaus Magnus, Book 3, Chapter 6.* The poets imagine that these three Fates unchangeably determine the lifespan of every person, such that one spins the thread of life, the second winds it up, and the third is meant to cut it off—or, as the well-known verse goes: *Clotho holds the distaff, Lachesis spins, and Atropos cuts.* <note>original Latin: "Clotho colum retinet, Lachesis net, & Atropos occat." This is a classic mnemonic for the roles of the three Roman Parcae.</note> *Rosinus, Book 2, Antiquities, Chapter 15.* Our ancestors also believed that the hour of death was so fatal and unchangeably determined by **God** <note>The author here blends the Germanic/Roman concept of Fate with his own 17th-century theological language</note> that the span of life could neither be lengthened nor shortened. Indeed, the entire northern world believed in **Stoic Fatalism** <term>Stoic Fatalism: the belief that all events are predetermined and inevitable, a philosophy often attributed by early modern writers to the ancient Germanic tribes</term> and necessity, against which neither counsel nor deed could prevail. Consequently, the **Cimbri** <note>an ancient Germanic or Celtic people who famously invaded the Roman Republic in the late 2nd century BCE</note> did not fear death, holding the view that whoever is meant to die in battle cannot escape death, and whoever is not meant to die in battle cannot run into the jaws of death: *Brynjólfur Sveinsson in the notes of Stephanus on Saxo, Book 1, page 53.* Not only our ancestors and the Stoics held this belief, but many other philosophers and pagan nations did as well, even subjecting their own gods to this unchangeable divine destiny. For this reason, **Homer** in the 16th book of the *Iliad* introduces **Jupiter** <note>The author uses the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note> lamenting that he could not rescue his son **Sarpedon** from his impending death: *Compare Chemnitz, Part 1, Loci Theologici, Section 4, Chapter 6, page 130.*

<header>Cimbrian Beliefs</header>

It was believed that people did not die by chance, but that their span of life was determined by the gods during times of peace and war, as the poet says: Silius Italicus, Book 3, verse 154:

> In peace and in war, the boundary of life stands fixed for all. <note>original Latin: "Et pace, & bello cunctis stat terminus ævi."</note>

Over this life-span of humans, three goddesses were placed, whom our people called **Norns** <note>Fates in Norse mythology who dwell by the Well of Urd</note> and the Romans called **Parcae** <note>The three personifications of destiny in Roman mythology</note>, and who were held as rulers over human life and death, fortune and misfortune: *Edda*, Part 1, fable 15. Olaus Magnus, Book 3, chapter 6. The poets imagine that the three Parcae unchangeably determine the end of every person's life, so that one shall spin the thread of life, the second wind it up, and the third cut it off, or as the well-known verse goes: **Clotho holds the spindle, Lachesis spins, and Atropos cuts** <note>original Latin: "Clotho colum retinet, Lachesis net, & Atropos occat"</note>: Rosinus, Book 2, *Antiquities*, chapter 15. Our ancestors also believed that the hour of death was so fated and unchangeably determined by God that the span of life could neither be lengthened nor shortened, for the entire northern world <note>original: "mitternächtige Welt," literally "midnight world," a common archaic term for the Nordic and Germanic regions</note> believed in **Stoic fatality** <note>The philosophical belief that all events are predetermined and inevitable, a hallmark of Stoicism</note> and necessity, against which neither counsel nor action could be found. Therefore, the **Cimbri** <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic tribe known for their migrations and conflicts with Rome</note> did not fear death, holding that whoever is meant to die in battle cannot escape death, and whoever is not meant to die in battle can run into the very jaws of death: Brynjólfur according to Stephen in *Notes on Saxo*, Book 1, page 53. Not only our people held this in common with the Stoics, but also many other philosophers and pagan nations believed it, and even subjected their gods to this unchangeable divine fate. Thus, Homer in the 16th book of the *Iliad* introduces Jupiter mourning that he could not save his son **Sarpedon** <note>A son of Zeus (Jupiter) in Greek mythology who was fated to die in the Trojan War despite his father's divinity</note> from impending death: See Chemnitz, part 1, *Loci Theologici*, chapter 6, page 130.

The immortality of the soul was believed by the pagans not only in this land, but also everywhere, in almost the entire world. <note>original Latin: "Consensu omnium Gentium arbitramur, permanere animam post mortem superstitem," which translates as: "By the consensus of all nations, we hold that the soul remains surviving after death."</note> Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 3. §. 4. Furthermore, it is often argued whether the Northern peoples believed that souls pass into other bodies after death. This opinion is attributed to the Goths and the Wends <note>The Wends were a group of Slavic tribes living near Germanic settlements.</note>, and to all Northern peoples: Hartknoch, *Dissertation 13 on Prussian Matters*, §. 8 and following; the anonymous commentator in Roger, Part 2, *Theological Office*, chapter 21, question 445 and following. Regarding the Germans, Diodorus Siculus writes in Book 5, chapter 13, that the Pythagorean opinion has prevailed among them—that the souls of men are immortal and pass from one body into another. <note>The "Pythagorean opinion" refers to metempsychosis, or reincarnation, a doctrine associated with the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</note> Appian, in his works on the Celts, also holds that the ancient Germans were of this opinion. Concerning the Gallic Druids, Julius Caesar relates in Book 6 of the *Gallic War*, page 124, that they also believe that souls do not perish, but after death pass from one body to another. Clüver, in Book 1 of *Ancient Germany*, chapter 32, page 263, wishes to prove both the Emperor [Caesar] and Diodorus wrong in this matter, and seeks to demonstrate from Pomponius Mela that the Celtic peoples did not believe in the Pythagorean transmigration of souls. It is left to the sensible consideration of the kind reader whether the authority of Pomponius Mela can outweigh that of the two aforementioned authors.

Indeed, it could rather be said of the Gothic and Northern peoples that they knew nothing of the Pythagorean teaching regarding the transmigration of souls. I firmly hold that our local Goths and Wends constantly believed that souls were immortal and, immediately after death, did not enter other bodies but instead wandered directly from this world into another, as is clearly evident from the preceding section. It could be, however, that the Gothic and Vandalic peoples adopted the Pythagorean teaching as they moved out of this land and traveled through or occupied many foreign countries. Or, more likely, that we should understand these authors to mean not the Goths but the Getae, and not the Wends but the Slavs <note>The author is highlighting a common historical confusion where Goths were often conflated with the Getae (a Thracian people) and Wends with other Slavic groups.</note>, which are peoples commonly confused with one another.

# Cimbrian [History]

... [to be] lost. The Egyptians / as Herodotus reports / are said to have been the first who taught / that souls are immortal / and after death wander from one body into another / both of animals / and of humans / and when they have wandered through all kinds of creatures on earth / in the sea and in the air / they then return into a human body / and finally after three thousand years travel to heaven: Herodotus, Book 2, number 60, page 142. In this, their master teacher is said to have been the Egyptian Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient secret wisdom.</note> in *Poimandres*, chapter 10. Pythagoras is said to have learned this error from the Egyptians / and propagated it in the East and West. This philosopher is said to have taught / that his soul was first in Euphorbus, thereafter in Hermotimus, then in Pyrrhus / and finally entered into his own / Pythagoras’s body: Diogenes Laertius, Book 8, *On the Lives of the Philosophers*, chapter 6, page 484. Plato is also caught in this error, having followed Pythagoras in this matter: Laertius, Book 3, *On the Lives of the Philosophers*, chapter 31, page 201. Plato calls this <term>transmigration|metempsychosis</term> of souls a "rebirth" in his *Phaedo* / and in Book 10 of *The Republic* <note>The original cites "de L.L.", likely referring to *Legibus* (Laws), but the specific stories of Orpheus and Ajax appear in the Myth of Er at the end of *The Republic*.</note> he relates / how after death Orpheus was changed into a swan / Thamyris into a lark / Ajax into a lion / and Agamemnon into an eagle.

The followers of Pythagoras are said to have philosophized thus: that the souls of men, because of their sins, must enter the bodies of such irrational animals / that they resembled during life. Thus, the souls of the wrathful wander into snakes: the greedy into wolves: the cruel into bears: the filthy into pigs: the deceivers into foxes: and the tyrants into crocodiles: Compare Agostino Steuco, Book 9, *On Perennial Philosophy*, chapter 28. Ovid introduces Pythagoras speaking thus in Book 15 of the *Metamorphoses* in the preface, verse 158:

> Souls do not die; they always leave their previous
> Dwellings to live and inhabit new homes.
> All things change; nothing perishes. The spirit wanders,
> Coming from there to here, and from here to there, occupying
> Whatever limbs it pleases; it passes from beasts into human bodies,
> And our soul passes into beasts, yet it never perishes in any body.
> <note>original Latin: "Morte carent animæ, semperque priore relicta / Sede, novis domibus vivunt, habitantque receptæ. / Omnia mutantur; nihil interit, errat, & illinc. / Huc venit, hinc illuc & quoslibet occupat artus / Spiritus, êque feris humana in corpora transit, / Inque feras noster, nec corpore deperit ullo."</note>

This error has afflicted the wisest pagans in both the East and West / and is attributed to the Chinese philosophers; Trigault, Book 1, *On China*, chapter 9. <note>Refers to Nicolas Trigault, a Jesuit missionary whose writings introduced Chinese culture and philosophy to Europe.</note>

# Chapter XLII
## On the Pagan Burials of our Ancestors.

->Contents:<-

1. This chapter is composed briefly to avoid excessive length, and a separate work on Cimbrian <note>The Cimbri were an ancient tribe; the author uses the term to refer to the inhabitants of the Cimbrian Peninsula, which includes modern-day Jutland and Schleswig-Holstein.</note> pagan burials is promised.
2. The Cimbri first buried their dead and later burned them.
3. The cremation of the dead was ordained by Odin <note>original: "Othin"</note>; how this was conducted is illustrated with the examples of the two Kings of Denmark, Harald and Balder.
4. The funeral ceremonies are described.
5. As well as the tombs of the pagans.
6. The Cimbri held their graves and burials to be holy and religious, though many were destroyed by Christians.
7. Concerning the barbaric burials of the Wends <note>A historical name for Slavic people living near Germanic settlement areas.</note>.

---

Since this chapter grew so much under my hands and, beyond expectation, became so large that I feared the work would become too sprawling, I have deemed it advisable to make a short excerpt from it and only recount the main points in a summary fashion. If the Almighty, according to His gracious will, grants further life and health, and the ecclesiastical ministry <note>original: "Ministerium Ecclesiasticum"; referring to the author’s professional duties as a clergyman.</note> allows for enough remaining hours, I intend to publish a separate work on this under the title: *Cimbrian Pagan Burials*, and to divide it into three parts according to what occurred before, during, and after the burials. However, we wish to remain here with the order we have long maintained in recording the pagan burials of our ancestors in this chapter.

§. 2. Our ancestors had two ways and methods of interring the dead. The first and oldest custom was to bury the dead bodies, which the world after the Great Flood <note>original: "Sündfluth"</note> learned from their father Noah and passed down to their descendants. Thus, the burial of dead bodies was the practice for a considerable time among the Cimbrian and all pagan...

§. 7. We will conclude this chapter with the barbaric burials of our Wends <note>The Wends (Wenden) was a historical term for Slavic people living in proximity to Germanic settlements</note>, who were accustomed to burying their elderly parents, blood-relations, and kin alive—specifically those who were no longer fit for war or labor: Albert Krantz <note>Albert Krantz (c. 1450–1517) was a prominent German historian; his "Wandalia" (1519) describes the history of the Wends and Vandals</note>, Book 7 of *Wandalia*, Chapter 48; Johann Petersen <note>Johann Petersen (d. 1552) was the author of the "Chronica Holstatia" or Holstein Chronicle</note>, Part 1 of the *Holstein Chronicle*, page 17. Yet, they were granted the "mercy" of being stabbed to death upon the woodpile just as the fire broke out: Procopius <note>original: "Procopius lib. 2. Goth. Bell."; refers to the Byzantine historian Procopius of Caesarea’s "History of the Gothic War"</note>, Book 2; Clüver <note>Philipp Clüver (1580–1622) was a founding figure in historical geography</note>, Book 1 of *Ancient Germany* <note>original: "Antiq. Others among our Vandalic peoples were even more cruel; they are said to have slaughtered their aged parents and relatives alive and devoured them like fierce tigers, thus burying them within their own bellies, as Albert Krantz and Johann Petersen report in the aforementioned places. This was common among many pagan peoples in both the Old and New Worlds in times past, and is still practiced today by some. God willing, this and everything else briefly contained in this chapter shall be set forth and expanded upon further.

# Heathen Religion

There is no article of faith over which the heathens <note>The author uses "Heyden" (heathens/pagans) to refer broadly to non-Christians, including ancient Romans, Greeks, and contemporary non-Christian ethnic groups.</note> have stumbled more than this one: the **Resurrection of the Dead**. Pliny, in the seventh chapter of his second book, does not shrink from declaring that God cannot raise the dead. His words are:

->Truly, the principal comforts for the imperfect nature of man are that not even God can do all things; for He cannot bring death upon Himself even if He wished—which He granted to man as the best thing amid such punishments of life—nor can He grant eternity to mortals or recall the deceased. <note>original Latin: "Imperfectæ verò in homine naturæ præcipua solatia, ne Deum quidem posse omnia; Namque nec sibi potest mortem consiscere si velit, quod homini dedit optimum in tantis vitæ pœnis: nec mortales æternitate donare, aut revocare defunctos."</note><-

O, what a pagan comfort! To comfort oneself with the idea that God cannot do everything, and specifically that He cannot raise the dead. And in the fifty-fifth chapter of his seventh book, he calls the resurrection of the dead a vanity and emptiness of **Democritus** <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BC) was a Greek philosopher who proposed an atomic theory of the universe where the soul was material and perished with the body.</note>, adding: *What a terrible madness it is for life to be repeated by death.* <note>original: "Quæ malum est dementia iterari vitam morte."</note> Likewise, the pagan philosopher Caecilius, in the eighth book of Arnobius, mocks the resurrection of the dead, and in Minucius Felix's *Octavius*, he calls it: *an old wives' tale* <note>original: "Fabulam anilem"</note>. The Platonic philosopher **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD) was a philosopher who became a Bishop; he famously struggled to reconcile his Neoplatonic views on the soul with the Christian doctrine of bodily resurrection.</note> is said to have been not disinclined to accept our articles of faith, except for this one regarding the resurrection of the flesh, which he entirely rejected: Evagrius, Book 1, Chapter 15; Nicephorus, Book 14 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 55.

We find similar examples in Holy Scripture: the Athenians laughed at the Apostle [Paul] over his preaching of the resurrection: *Acts 17:18*. When the Roman Governor **Festus** heard the Apostle preaching about the resurrection, he cried out with a loud voice: "Paul, you are out of your mind! Your great learning is driving you mad": *Acts 26:24*. Thus, the doctrine of the resurrection was considered a frenzy among the heathens.

->In no matter is the Christian faith so vehemently, so stubbornly, so forcibly, and so contentiously contradicted as regarding the resurrection of the flesh.<-

That is: *In keinem Ding wird so hefftiglich: so hallstarrig: so mit gantzer Gewalt: so zanckzüchtiglich dem Christl. Glauben wiedersprochen / als in der Aufferstehung des Fleisches*, as **Augustine** writes in *Psalm 88, page 985*. When the late **Olearius** <note>Adam Olearius (1599–1671) was a German scholar and diplomat who wrote a famous account of his travels to Persia and Russia.</note>, during his journey to Persia, spoke of religion with the **Cheremis Tatars** <note>The Cheremis are today known as the Mari people, a Finno-Ugric ethnic group living in the Volga region of Russia.</note> and mentioned the resurrection, a Tatar began to laugh and with his

We wish to conclude this chapter with the barbaric burials of our **Wends** <note>A historical term used by Germanic speakers to describe Slavic peoples living in or near Germanic territories.</note>, who were accustomed to burying their elderly parents, blood-relatives, and kin alive when they were no longer fit for war or labor: see Albert Krantz, Book 7 of *Wandalia*, Chapter 48; and Johannes Petersen, Part 1 of the *Chronicle of Holstein*, page 17. Likewise, among the Vandalic **Heruli** <note>An East Germanic tribe who migrated throughout Europe; the author places them in Mecklenburg or Pomerania.</note>, old and sick people were not permitted to live any longer; instead, as soon as they became old, helpless, or infirm, they were required to lie down alive upon a prepared wood-pile and be burned. However, they were granted the "mercy" of being stabbed to death on the pyre as the fire began to catch: see Procopius, Book 2 of the *Gothic War* <note>original Latin: "Goth. Bell." for De Bello Gothico</note>; and Cluverius, Book 1 of *Ancient Germany* <note>original: "Antiq. Germ."</note>, Chapter 53, pages 396 and 397. Others among our Vandalic peoples were even more cruel; they are said to have slaughtered their elderly parents and relatives alive and devoured them like fierce beasts, thus "burying" them in their own bellies, as Albert Krantz and Johannes Petersen report in the aforementioned places. This practice was common among many heathen peoples in both the Old and New Worlds in former times—and even today among some—which, God willing, shall be elaborated upon more extensively in its proper place, as everything in this chapter has been briefly summarized.

# Heathen Religion #

->U u 2<-

There is no article of faith that the heathens have stumbled over more than this one: the resurrection of the dead. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note>, in the second book, seventh chapter, does not shy away from stating that God cannot awaken the dead. His words are: *Indeed, the primary solace for the imperfect nature of man is that not even God can do all things; for He cannot even bring death upon Himself if He wished—the best gift He gave to man amidst such pains of life—nor can He grant eternity to mortals or recall the deceased.* <note>original Latin: "Imperfectæ verò in homine naturæ præcipua solatia, ne Deum quidem posse omnia; Namque nec sibi potest mortem consiscere si velit, quod homini dedit optimum in tantis vitæ pænis: nec mortales æternitate donare, aut revocare defunctos."</note> Oh, what heathen comfort! To comfort oneself with the idea that God cannot do everything, and specifically that He cannot raise the dead. And in the seventh book, fifty-fifth chapter, he calls the resurrection of the dead a vanity and emptiness of Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who formulated an atomic theory of the universe.</note>, adding: *What a wicked madness it is for life to be repeated by death.* <note>original Latin: "Quæ malum est dementia iterari vitam morte."</note> Likewise, the heathen philosopher Caecilius, in the writings of Arnobius <note>An Early Christian apologist of the 4th century.</note>, Book 8, mocks the resurrection of the dead and calls it, in Minucius Felix's *Octavius*: *An old wives' tale* <note>original Latin: "Fabulam anilem"</note>. The Platonic philosopher Synesius <note>A Greek philosopher and Bishop of Ptolemais who struggled to reconcile his Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine.</note> is said to have been not disinclined to accept our articles of faith, except for this one regarding the resurrection of the flesh, which he entirely rejected: see Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus, a 6th-century Byzantine historian.</note> Book 1, Chapter 15; and Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century church historian.</note> Book 14 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 55. We find similar examples in Holy Scripture: the Athenians laughed at the Apostle over the sermon on the resurrection: Acts 17:18. When the Roman governor Festus heard the Apostle preaching about the resurrection, he cried out with a loud voice: "Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you mad": Acts 26:24. Thus, the doctrine of the resurrection was considered a form of madness among the heathens. *In no matter is the Christian faith so vehemently, so stubbornly, so forcefully, and so contentiously opposed as concerning the resurrection of the flesh.* <note>original Latin: "In nulla re tam vehementer: tam pertinaciter: tam obnixè, & contentiosè contradicitur Fidei Christianæ, sicut de carnis resurrectione."</note> That is: in nothing is the Christian faith so violently, so headstrongly, so with all might, and so quarrelsomely contradicted as in the resurrection of the flesh, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Church Fathers.</note> writes in his commentary on Psalm 88, page 985. When the late Olearius <note>Adam Olearius (1599–1671), a German scholar and traveler who journeyed to Muscovy and Persia.</note>, on his journey to Persia, spoke of religion and mentioned the resurrection to the Cheremissian Tatars <note>The Mari people, a Finno-Ugric ethnic group living near the Volga River in Russia.</note>, one Tatar began to laugh and with his

### Cimbrian ###

...clapping their hands and saying: "The dead will rise like my horses and cows." <note>This anecdote refers to Adam Olearius (1603–1671), a German scholar and ambassador who wrote extensively on his travels to Persia.</note> *Olearius, Book 4, Persian Travels, Chapter 4.* Not only the heathens, but also many among the ancient heretics denied this article of faith; a long register of them is drawn up by *Dr. Gerhard, Volume 8, Theological Commonplaces, Article on the Resurrection, number 37.*

§. 2. Nevertheless, many among the heathens did believe in the resurrection of the dead. Of the ancient Germans, *Appian* <note>An ancient Roman historian of Greek origin.</note> writes in *The Germanic Wars, Chapter 1*, that they held the **hope of coming back to life** <note>original Latin: "spem reviviscendi"</note>; a point also referenced in *Hildebrand’s Disputations, VII, Sacred Institutions, thesis 3.* This hope of resurrection is also attributed to our Wendish peoples <note>The "Wends" refers to Slavic populations living near Germanic territories.</note>. They possessed an idol named **Flins**, upon whose shoulders stood a roaring lion with a wide-open maw, which was meant to awaken the Wends from the dead: *The True Saxon Chronicle, edited by Pomarius, page 245; Schedius, Section 3, On the German Gods, Chapter 7, page 486.* Naturalists report that lion cubs lie as if dead and motionless for three days after birth—or, as others write, they do not move for two months: *Bartholomew the Englishman, Book 18, On the Properties of Things, Chapter 63; Gessner, Volume 2, On Quadrupeds, under the title "On Lions," folio 103 a.*—but they are said to be awakened by the lioness through a powerful roar. This is usually explained as a symbol for our own resurrection, when the Lord shall roar out of Zion, causing heaven and earth to shake <note>Joel 3:16</note>, and the dead shall hear His voice and come forth <note>John 5:28</note>. When a young lion is born, he lies and sleeps for three days; finally, the old lion comes and lets out a terrifying roar, by which the young lion is awakened and, as it were, made alive. We also lie and sleep in the graves, but there the **Lion of the tribe of Judah** <note>Revelation 5:5</note> shall come in the clouds; He will let His voice resound, and all who are in the graves shall hear His voice and come forth: *John 5:28–29. Dr. Meißner in the Augsburg Confession, Article XVII, Sermon 2, page 44.* **The lion awakens his cubs with his roar; shall not the voice of Christ, who is the Lion of the tribe of Judah, awaken the dead?** <note>original Latin: "Leo clamore suo catulos excitat, annon Christi vox, qui est Leo de tribu Juda, mortuos excitaret?"</note> *Gerhard in Sacred Aphorisms, under the title "Resurrection," page 633.* It appears that the Wends pointed toward this through the image of the roaring lion standing upon the idol Flins, considering that they [received] this from the ancient tradition...

Regarding the Wends in Prussia, **Peter von Dusburg** <note>A 14th-century chronicler of the Teutonic Knights.</note> writes in his *Prussian Chronicle* that they believed the dead would rise: **The Prussians believed in the resurrection of the flesh** <note>original Latin: "Prutheni resurrectionem carnis credebant"; Peter von Dusburg, *Chronicon terrae Prussiae*, part 3, chapter 5.</note>. When her father and husband fell into enmity and single combat, and both remained dead on the field, Queen Hilde is said to have raised her father and husband from the dead (through sorcery), so that they fought one another anew after death, just as they had in life: *Saxo Grammaticus, Book 5, in the Life of King Frotho III, pages 89–90.* <note>Saxo Grammaticus was a 12th-century Danish historian; this story refers to the legendary "Everlasting Battle" or Hjaðningavíg.</note> When King **Baldr** died in Denmark, everyone is said to have mourned him so greatly that they hoped to awaken him from the dead through their loud and bitter lamentations: *Prose Edda, Part 1, Fables 44–45.* It was believed that at the end of the world the dead would live again, as told of King Baldr and **Höðr** in the *Prose Edda, Part 1, Fable 49.* <note>Baldr and Höðr are figures in Norse mythology predicted to return after the events of Ragnarök.</note>

# Cimbrian Antiquities #

...there are also said to be peculiar members of a religious order in the Empire of **China** <note>original: "Sina"</note> named **Trimechou**, who make a profession of the doctrine of the resurrection: **The same author, in the aforementioned book, chapter 10, page 686.** Similarly, the **Tartar peoples** are said to hold the resurrection of the flesh to be true. **Ferdinand Pinto** <note>Fernão Mendes Pinto (c. 1509–1583), a Portuguese explorer whose travel memoirs, though sometimes considered exaggerated, were widely read in the 17th century.</note> reports in his wondrous travels how, during his journeying in Tartary, he encountered a large district where 164 long and wide houses stood, filled with human skulls. Between these houses were huge piles of bones stacked high, standing about three fathoms <note>A "Klauffter" or Klafter was a measurement of about six feet; thus, these piles were nearly 18 feet high.</note> above the said houses, so that one could not have imagined otherwise than that these houses had been excavated within such piles of bone, with only their gables visible. He reports that nearby on a hill stood a monstrously large idol of brass, of which he was told that this idol, on the **Last Day** during the awakening of the dead, would restore to every person their own bones. Certain religious sects in **India** believe that at the end of the world the dead will come to life: **Erasmus Francisci, book 3, *Spectaculum*, page 980.** <note>Erasmus Francisci (1627–1694) was a prolific German polymath and writer of encyclopedic works on history and curiosities.</note> The inhabitants of the Indian kingdom of **Tranziane** are also of the opinion that the dead shall rise: **The same author, book 5, *Spectaculum*, page 1502.** The **Saracens** believed the same: **Micraelius, book 1, *Ethnopolitica*, Dialogue 4, chapter 1, page 140.** Likewise the **Greeks**, from the teachings of their philosophers, of which more in the following paragraph. In the **New World**, the **Americans** <note>Referring here to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.</note> recognized the resurrection of the flesh: **Ross, part 3, *Concerning the Religions of the World*, question 18, page 139.** When the **Spaniards** in the New World threw the bones of the dead out of their graves, the inhabitants pleaded that the bones of the dead be spared, so that they might all the more conveniently rise again one day: **Camerarius, Century 1, *Historical Meditations*, chapter 97.**

### Pagan Religions ###

...clearly, that the dead will become living again. **Eusebius** (in book 11 of *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 18) writes that **Plato** learned the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead from Holy Scripture. He is also said to have taught that within 36,000 years (others suggest 48,000) everything will be restored to its previous state as it is now. This is called the <term>Platonic Great Year</term> <note>original: "grosse Platonische Welt-Jahr"; a concept where the sun, moon, and planets return to the same relative positions, signifying a total rebirth of the world's history.</note>, when all humans, along with all creatures, shall be brought forth again and restored to their old condition: **Augustine, book 12, *City of God*, chapter 13; Leonhard Coqueau’s commentary on Augustine; Lauremberg, century 1, *Philological History*, 62.**

**Zeno** and his disciples, the **Stoic philosophers**, taught that at the destruction of the world, the deceased would rise again to this life: **Magdeburg Centuries, century 2, chapter 15, page 237.** **Seneca**, who was raised in the Stoic school, agrees: <note>original Latin: "Mors, quam pertimescimus, intermittit vitam, non eripit. Veniet iterum dies, qui nos in lucem reponat... Observa Orbem rerum in se remeantium..."</note> "Death, which we so greatly fear, interrupts life but does not snatch it away. A day will come again to restore us to the light; he who is destined to return ought to depart with a calm mind. Observe the cycle of things returning upon themselves: Has summer gone? Another year brings it back. Winter falls; its own months will bring it back again. Night overwhelms the sun, but day will immediately drive it away." **Seneca, *Epistle 36*.**

This resurrection of the dead is also said to have been believed by **Chrysippus** (according to Joannes Ludovicus Vives' commentary on **Augustine**, *City of God*, book 22, chapter 28), **Democritus** (according to **Pliny**, book 7, chapter 55), as well as the poets, such as **Silius Italicus** in book 13:

> By this path souls seek heaven again, and after a thousand cycles <note>original: "lustris"; a Roman period of five years, here used to mean many ages.</note> 
> have passed, forgetting the underworld <note>original: "Ditem," referring to Dis Pater, the god of the underworld.</note>, they return into bodies.

Regarding this opinion, **Lactantius** (book 6, *Divine Institutes*, chapter 22) cites **Virgil** (from book 6 of the *Aeneid*, verse 819 and following):

> O father! Is it then to be thought that any souls go hence 
> aloft to heaven, and return again to sluggish bodies? 
> What so dire a longing for the light possesses these poor souls?

->And later in verse 847 and following:<-

> All these, when they have turned the wheel for a thousand years, 
> God summons in a great column to the **River Lethe** <note>The mythical river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>, 
> so that, truly forgetful, they may see the vaulted sky above once more, 
> and begin to wish to return again into bodies.

### Cimbrian History ###

Servius, commenting on an earlier passage in this place, states: <note>original: "Servius ad prior. h. l. Credendum est, animas ab inferis reverti posse, ad corpora."</note> "It must be believed that souls can return from the underworld to their bodies."

The **Eastern Philosophies** are also said to have held the opinion that the dead shall rise again. **Camerarius** writes this concerning **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Iranian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism.</note> in *Century 1, Historical Hours, chapter 97.* **Marsilio Ficino** writes the same of **Hermes Trismegistus** in the preface to his works, and **Laertius** mentions it regarding the **Persian Magi** in his *Preface on the Lives of the Philosophers, page 5.*

§. 5. From these examples, some have wished to conclude whether the pagans recognized this article of faith—the resurrection of the flesh—through the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>The concept that certain truths can be discovered through human reason and observation of the world without the aid of divine revelation.</note>. Indeed, **Julius Pacius** published a special treatise on this subject, in which he endeavors to prove the resurrection of the dead through various arguments drawn from the light of nature. However, although the light of nature might provide a probable glimpse of the resurrection of the dead, it cannot serve as a solid guide or teacher in the darkness following the Fall of Man. **Dr. Calovius** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a prominent Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> discusses this in *Part 3, Polemical Theology, folio 6, article 3, chapter 1, thesis 1, page 509.* The "natural man" <note>A theological term for a person relying solely on human reason without spiritual grace.</note> struggles mightily against this idea, as was noted at the beginning of this chapter. Whatever these pagans knew of the matter, they learned from ancient tradition and their historical interactions with **God’s** people <note>The Israelites.</note>, as well as from the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament which had been translated into the Greek language: **Gerhard, Volume 8, *Loci Theologici* on the Resurrection, Numbers 40, 41;** **Brochman, Volume 2, *Loci Theologici*, article 27, chapter 2, question 2.**

§. 6. Furthermore, our ancestors believed in the resurrection not only of humans but also of irrational animals. Regarding the **Prussians**, **Peter von Dusburg** writes that they believed in the resurrection of the flesh, though not in the proper manner. They believed that if someone were noble or common, rich or poor, powerful or weak in this life, they would remain so after the resurrection in the next life. Consequently, it happened that when a nobleman died, his weapons, horses, servants, maids, clothes, hunting dogs, birds of prey, and other items pertaining to warfare were burned with him. For commoners, the tools of their trade were burned. They believed that these burned items would rise again with them and be useful in the next world. His own words are: <note>original: "Prutheni resurrectionem carnis credebant; nõ tamen ut debebant."</note> **"The Prussians believed in the resurrection of the flesh; yet not as they ought."**

§. 8. The question arises: from where did the pagans obtain this knowledge of the world’s destruction? Considered as a simple fact, they might have been able to deduce the destruction of the world to some extent through the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" refers to human reason and observation without the aid of divine revelation.</note>; however, that this destruction of the world should occur specifically through fire is hidden from the light of nature. Our ancestors undoubtedly obtained this knowledge from the Christian doctrine preached in this land in ancient times by the Apostles or apostolic men, of which some elements were retained from old tradition within paganism. The ancient philosophers, on the other hand, most of whom lived before the birth of Christ, may have received word of this: (1) From the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, which were translated into the Greek language <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> long before Christ's birth and were known to the worldly-wise pagans; *Philosophers, in their accounts of the divine predictions of the Prophets, have imitated the shadow of a corrupted Truth* <note>original Latin: "Philosophi de divinis prædictionibus Prophetarum umbram interpolatæ Veritatis imitati sunt"</note>, as **Minucius Felix** <note>An early Christian apologist, likely 2nd or 3rd century AD.</note> writes in *Octavius*. (3) From the prophecies of the **Sibylls** <note>Ancient prophetesses of the Greek and Roman world whose "books" were often cited by early Christians as foretelling Christ.</note>, who are said to have announced the destruction of the world by fire, as may be read in **Augustine**, *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 23; **Eusebius**, *The Life of Constantine the Great*, Book 5, Chapter 18; and **Lactantius**, *On the Wrath of God*, Chapter 23. **Lactantius** relates in his *Divine Institutes*, Book 4, *On True Wisdom*, Chapter 15, that the pagans, when refuted by the Sibylline prophecies, answered that these had been forged by the Christians. This opinion is also held by **Casaubon** <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar who proved several "ancient" texts to be later forgeries.</note> in his *Exercises on the Annals of Baronius*, Number 10, page 66 and following; as well as **Grynæus** in **Schmidt’s** *Third Oration on the Sibylls*. **Hornius** also aims at this point in his *History of the Church*, Part 1, pages 13 and 14. To this, **Lactantius** responds in the aforementioned place, saying: that the Sibylline prophecies were not forged by Christians, but were cited and read before the birth of Christ by **Varro** and **Cicero**, as well as by **Virgil** in his *Fourth Eclogue*. This objection of the pagans—whether the Sibylline prophecies regarding Christ were forged by Christians—is also mentioned by **Augustine** in *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 46. This matter is discussed by **Ludovicus Vives** and **Leonhardus Coquæus** in their commentaries on Augustine; by **Franz** in *Interpretation of Oracles*, Part 2, page 203 and following; by **Dorsch** in *Admirable Dissertations*, Number 3, page 226; by **Erasmus Schmidt** in his *Second and Third Orations on the Sibylls*; and by **Micrelius** in *The Gentile-Thinker*, Book 3, Dialogue Chapter 7. be established: Augustine, book 12, *The City of God*, chapter 13.

§. 3. Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for his complex and sometimes controversial theories on the soul and the cosmos.</note> agrees with the pagans on this point, holding that there was another world before this one, and that after the destruction of this world, another new world will follow: Origen, book 2, *On First Principles*, chapter 3 and chapter 5, where he strives to maintain this from Holy Scripture: Ecclesiastes 1:8, 9, 10 and Isaiah 65:17. Origen's words—as Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar famous for the Vulgate Latin Bible translation.</note> quotes and translates them in Letter 59 to Avitus—read as follows: *“It is our view that there was another world before this one, and after this one another shall be. Do you wish to learn that after the corruption of this world another shall follow? Listen to Isaiah (chapter 65:17) speaking: There shall be a new heaven and a new earth. Do you wish to know that before the construction of this world other worlds existed in the past? Listen to Ecclesiastes (chapter 1:8, 9, 10): What is it that has not been? etc.”* <note>original: "Nobis placet, ante hunc alium fuisse mundum, & post hunc alium futurum. Vis discere, quod post corruptionem hujus mundi alius sit futurus? audi Esaiam (c. LXV. v. 17) loquentem: Erit coelum novum, & terra nova. Vis nosce, quod ante fabricam hujus mundi alii mundi in praeterito fuerint? ausculta Ecclesiasten: (cap. I. v. 8,9,10,) Quid est quod non fuit &c."</note> The Jewish Rabbis are also of this opinion: Scherzer in *Brev[iarium] Eustach[ii] Phys[icum]*, question 69, page 187.

§. 4. Those among the ancient church and school teachers, as well as the Catholics <note>The original uses 'Päbstlern' (Papists), a common early modern term for Roman Catholics.</note> and Reformed <note>Followers of the Calvinist tradition of the Reformation.</note>, who defend the downfall of the world according to its mere qualities <note>Theologians debated whether the world would be destroyed in its essence (substance) or merely transformed in its appearance and properties (qualities).</note> must also establish a new physical world and the renewal of all creatures, as Dr. Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran theologian of the 17th century.</note> shows. For if this world is only to be renewed by fire at its downfall, then certainly a renewal of the other creatures must follow, seeing as no significant reasons can be given as to why some, and not all, creatures should be renewed. For if the elements are to be renewed, a renewal of the bodies mixed from those elements must also occur. For what kind of elements would they be if they were deprived of all the creatures living and moving within them? Then the earth would be empty and void, waste and desolate without plants and animals; the water without fish; and the air without birds and meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred broadly to any atmospheric phenomenon—such as rain, snow, or wind—not just falling stars.</note>: Gerhard, volume 9, *Loci Theologici: On the Consummation of the World*, number 45.

# Chapter XLVI
## What our ancestors believed regarding eternal salvation and damnation after death.

->Contents:<-

1. Our ancestors, along with the Pagans in general, believed in another life after this one.
2. What they believed regarding eternal salvation.
3. And regarding eternal damnation.
4. As well as the various locations in Hell.
<column-break/>
5. Wherein the Papists <note>A term used by the author, likely a Protestant scholar, to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> agree with the Pagans.
6. And of the Hellish Valhalla or Elysian Fields <note>The "Elysian Fields" are the paradise of Greek mythology; the author is comparing them to the Norse Valhalla.</note>.
7. And redemption from Hell.
8. Wherein the Papists also concur with the Pagans.

---

In this, our forefathers agreed with the Pagans in general: they believed in another life after this one, where immortal souls are brought immediately after death and are rewarded or punished according to their works. On this basis, people were exhorted toward virtue and honor and warned against shame and vice; the reward of the pious and the punishment of the wicked were set before them as things prepared for them in the world to come. The Pagans recognized through the light of nature <note>A theological concept referring to knowledge of God or morality accessible through human reason and conscience without the aid of divine revelation.</note> that God, by virtue of His unchangeable justice, rewards the good and punishes the evil. However, because the Lord God does not always execute this justice in this life—since it often goes poorly for the pious but well and fortunately for the wicked—they reached the firm conclusion that another life must be at hand after this one, where God would execute His justice through the rewarding of the good and the punishing of the evil in deed and truth. Compare Virgil, Book 6 of the *Aeneid*; *Scipio’s Dream* in Cicero, Book 6 of *On the Commonwealth*; Macrobius, Book 1 on *Scipio’s Dream*, chapters 4, 9, and following, and Book 2, chapters 13, 15; Micraelius, Book 1 of *Ethnophronius*, Dialogue 1, chapter 3.

§. 2. The state of eternal salvation in the other world is described in the *Edda* <note>The "Edda" refers to the primary collections of Old Norse literature and mythology.</note>, Part 1, Fable 15, with these words: "In the southern part of heaven, there is a..."

And Fable 49 states: What will follow after the incineration of the world, and the death of the gods and heroes? For there are many good and many evil dwellings; but after this miracle (the world’s destruction), it is best to remain in heaven, and there to receive all kinds of good drinks in a hall or palace named **Brimer** <note>original: "Brimer," or Brimir, a hall where the souls of the virtuous are said to drink</note>, situated on **Ockolm** <note>original: "Ockolm," or Ókólnir, a place in the heavens that never grows cold</note>. The *Völuspá* <note>A central poem of the Poetic Edda containing the prophecy of the world's creation and end</note> (Number 58) agrees with the *Edda*, speaking thus of the place of eternal bliss: A hall stands clearer than the sun, covered with pure gold, where the pious dwell for eternity.

§. 3. Regarding the state of Hell, the *Edda* (Part 1, Fable 49) imagines: In **Nastrand** <note>original: "Nastrand," meaning "Corpse Shore"</note> is a large but evil fortress; its doors are directed toward the north, and it is entirely covered with snakes which have their heads turned inward and spit out pure poison, so that streams of poison flow through it, which the perjurers and murderers must wade through. Likewise, the *Völuspá* (Numbers 36 & 37) describes Hell, adding that besides the perjurers and murderers, the adulterers must also wade through the poisonous hell-stream, and they are tormented there by the hellish **Nidhöggur** <note>A dragon or serpent that gnaws at the roots of the world tree and the bodies of the dead; the author identifies him here with Satan</note>. **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian</note> in the first book of his *Danish History* recounts how King **Hadding** in Denmark traveled beneath the earth to Hell, and there first found a dark, misty region where several noble lords were dressed in long purple robes. As he went further into a bright-shining green field, and further still over a hellish stream, he saw two heaps of souls like two contending armies. It is also told in poems as if **Hermod** <note>In Norse myth, the messenger of the gods who traveled to Hel to plead for the return of the god Baldur</note> traveled through deep, shadowy valleys to Hell, and over the hellish stream **Gial** <note>original: "Gial," or Gjöll, the river that separates the living from the dead</note> (otherwise called **Styx** by the pagan poets) with a golden, shi-

§. 4. Thus our ancestors situated the place of eternal bliss in heaven, but placed hell within the earth. Just as they distinguished various dwellings within heaven, they also divided hell into different lodgings: *Edda* Part 1, Fable 49. According to heathen superstition, these can be distinguished into the outskirts of hell <note>original: "Vorbürge," similar to the concept of Limbo</note> and the place of hellish torment. Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a medieval Danish historian</note> describes four distinct places of the underworld during the hellish journey of King Hadding, as was mentioned in the preceding section. Regarding this, one may read Virgil in the sixth book of the stories of Aeneas; there he first describes various dwellings for souls in the outskirts of hell, specifically a separate place for small children at the very first entrance, lines 525 and following:

> And the souls of infants weeping at the very threshold.

In the middle of the underworld, he describes the place of torture for the damned, called Tartarus, surrounded by a triple wall and the hellish, fire-spewing stream Phlegethon, line 648 and following:

> He sees wide walls surrounded by a triple wall,
> Which the swift river of the underworld, the Tartarean Phlegethon,
> Encircles with scorching flames.
> <note>original Latin: "Mœnia lata videt triplici circumdata muro, / Quæ rapidus Flammis ambit torrentibus amnis / Tartareus Phlegethon."</note>

Furthermore, he situates the seat of the pious in another place, within green fields and pleasant forests, line 737 and following:

> They came to the joyful places, and the pleasant greenery

> They pay the penalties; some are stretched out to the empty [winds]...
> <note>original Latin: "Non tamen omne malum miseris nec funditur omnes / Corporeæ exedunt pestes, penitusque nec esse est. / Multa diu concreta modis inolescere miris. / Ergo exercentur pœnis, veterumque malorum / Supplicia expendunt, aliæ panduntur inanes"</note>

§. 5. It is no wonder that the heathens gave credence to such fables, considering that the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Päbstler," a common 17th-century Protestant term for Catholics</note> have accepted these heathen fables as true history and have even made an article of faith out of them. They have likewise situated Hell in the center of the earth and divided it into four places. In the lowest place, they have arranged the location of the damned, where they are eternally tormented. In the second place, they have enclosed the small children who died prematurely without receiving the Holy Sacrament; there they are to be eternally separated from the blessed vision of God, but otherwise are said to feel no torment of Hell. In the third place, they have lit the Purgatory <note>original: "Feg Feuer," literally "cleansing fire"</note>, where souls burdened with venial sins <term>venial sins: in Catholic theology, lesser sins that do not result in complete separation from God</term> must be cleansed and tormented for a time according to their desert. ...souls after death agree with the Papal view. So that no proof should be lacking in this matter, those in the Papacy refer to the testimonies of monks, especially Fursey and Drithelm, as well as Sergius, Thymus, and Theophilus. These men are said to have undertaken pilgrimages to Hell, where they observed and described everything firsthand. §. 6. Regarding Hell, the *Edda* <note>The *Prose Edda*, a primary source of Norse mythology compiled in the 13th century.</note> (part 1, fable 35) assigns a special place for war-heroes, which is called **Valhalla** <note>original: "Walhal"</note>. It is said to be provided with five hundred and forty monstrously large doors or gates. There, after death, the brave heroes are said to practice daily with weapons, arrange themselves in battle formation, and clash with one another just as they were accustomed to doing in this life. After the battle is finished, they ride back together to Odin’s <note>original: "Othins"</note> palace and hold a feast. For this reason, horses and other belongings were buried alongside soldiers, in the hope that they would have need of them in the next world, as was mentioned previously. Similarly, Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian.</note> (book 1, p. 16) reports of King Hadding that during his journey to the underworld, he supposedly found two armies there in conflict. The *Edda* recounts in the aforementioned place that in the hellish Valhalla, the war-heroes are heartily entertained with wine or mead <term>mead: an alcoholic drink made by fermenting honey with water</term>, and also with meat from wolves and wild boars, as is poetically described in fables 33 and 34. The Turks <note>A common 17th-century term for Muslims.</note> also believe that in the next life, the pious shall be delighted with delicious food and drink and other fleshly pleasures, as noted by Schweiger (book 2, *Travels to Constantinople and Jerusalem*, chapter 55, p. 189) and Lonicerus (Vol. 1, *Turkish Chronicle*, book 2, chapter 22, p. 121), as do the Jews (Brochmand, Vol. 2, *System of Theology*, art. 2, q.). Thus Virgil, in his sixth book (line 739), describes the **Elysian Fields** <note>original: "Elyserfeld," the paradise of the Greek and Roman underworld.</note>, saying that the war-heroes present themselves there with their weapons, horses, and chariots; others play and dance; others sing and play instruments; and still others are said to eat and drink.

> Here, a more expansive ether clothes the fields in purple light, and they recognize their own sun and their own stars. Some exercise their limbs on grassy wrestling grounds, compete in sport, and wrestle on the golden sand.
<note>original Latin: "Largior hic campos æther, & lumine vestit, / Purpureo solemque suum sua sidera norunt. / Pars in gramineis exercent membra palæstris, / Contendunt ludô, & fulva luctantur arena." From Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, 640–643.</note>

->Some dance with their feet, and sing songs and poems; likewise the Thracian priest <note>A reference to Orpheus, the legendary musician of Greek myth.</note> in his long robe plays the seven distinct notes of the scale to the rhythms, now striking them with his fingers, now with his ivory pick. The poet [Virgil] intends to show with these words—*The same delight in chariots and armor that they had while alive, etc.*—that souls in the next world occupy themselves with the same things they were concerned with in their living bodies in this world; as Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, a 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil.</note> explains regarding this passage: *This, then, was the interest of the dead, which was that of the living.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc igitur mortuis studium fuit, quod vivis."</note>

§. 7. The pagans believed that the souls of the pious would finally be delivered from the hellish fore-courts <note>The outer regions of the underworld, similar to the concept of Limbo.</note> and be transferred into Heaven. Our own ancestors <note>Referring to the ancient Germanic or Norse peoples, whom the author calls "Cimbrians."</note> believed that this would happen at the end of the world during its destruction <note>A reference to Ragnarok, the "Twilight of the Gods."</note>, when the pious would dwell eternally in heaven and delight themselves there with precious drinks, as was cited in the previous second section from the *Edda* <note>The *Prose Edda*, a 13th-century collection of Norse myths.</note> tables 15 and 49. This is the point of the question Aeneas asks his father Anchises: whether some excellent souls, locked within the hellish fore-courts, would finally travel into heaven? In Virgil, *Aeneid* Book 6, verse 819:

->O Father! must we believe that any sublime souls go from here to the Heaven above?<-
<note>original Latin: "O Pater! anne aliquas ad Coelum hinc ire putandum est / Sublimeis animas?"</note>

§. 8. From this has arisen the "poem" <note>The author uses the word "poem" or "fable" sarcastically to suggest that Catholic doctrine is a work of fiction.</note> of the Papists <note>A common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics.</note>, claiming that the souls of the deceased are delivered from the hellish "Dungeon of the Fathers" <note>The *Limbus Patrum*, where the righteous who died before Christ were said to wait.</note> and **Purgatory** <note>original German: "Fegfeur," literally "sweeping-fire."</note>, and are then transferred into Heaven. Specifically, they claim the deliverance from the Dungeon of the Fathers has already occurred through **Christ's** descent into Hell; however, deliverance from Purgatory is said to still be achievable through Masses for the souls, almsgiving, intercession, fasting, and pilgrimages. *Roman Catechism; Bellarmine; Becanus, Manual of Controversies, book 1, chapter 8, pages 201, 228.* <note>References to major 16th and 17th-century Catholic theological works by Robert Bellarmine and Martinus Becanus.</note>

Idolatry has its origin in the right religion and from the (false) imitation of the true worship of God: Luther’s *Table Talk* <note>A collection of Martin Luther's informal conversations and sayings.</note>, Article 5, on Idolatry, page 86.

Regarding **Chapter 4, Section 10, page 36 following**: Concerning the saints appointed in the Papacy over all creatures and professions, one can read Naogeorgus <note>Thomas Naogeorgus, a Neo-Latin playwright and Protestant reformer.</note> in Book 3 of *The Papal Kingdom*, under the title *Helpers*, page 114 following.

Regarding **Chapter 5, Section 9, page 45**: Concerning the Queen of Heaven <note>original: "Melechet," from the Hebrew *Melekhet ha-Shamayim*.</note>: Jeremiah 7:18; see also 44:17. This is discussed by the Illustrious Ursinus <note>Likely Johann Henrich Ursinus, a 17th-century German scholar.</note> in Volume 2 of *Sacred Selections*, Book 2, Chapter 21, page 79 following.

Regarding **Chapter 8, Section 8, page 66**: Concerning the Epidaurian serpent <note>A reference to the sacred snake of Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine, brought from Epidaurus to Rome.</note>; it is without doubt ruled by the hellish serpent [Satan].

Regarding **Chapter 9, Section 2, page 82**: Concerning the goddess of Hell, "Hel"; she is otherwise regarded as a male idol.

Regarding **Chapter 10, Section 1, page 86**: Concerning the three crowned Nordic idols—Thor, Odin, and Freya—who had their temples, sacrifices, and sanctuaries at Uppsala in Sweden; from this, the Royal Swedish Coat of Arms of the three crowns is said to have its first origin: The Illustrious Schefferus <note>Johannes Schefferus, a 17th-century scholar at Uppsala University.</note> in the book *On the Ancient and True Insignia of the Kingdom of Sweden*, Chapter 12.

Regarding **Chapter 10, Section 6, page 102**: Concerning the idol Fro: Snorri Sturluson <note>An Icelandic historian and poet, author of the Prose Edda and the Heimskringla.</note> calls this idol "Froer" in the preface of his *Norwegian Chronicle*, and recounts that he was a king in Sweden and was buried there in a mountain near Uppsala. This is undoubtedly Frey, the third Swedish king after Odin, who is said to have built the great pagan temple at Uppsala and received divine honors there. He lies buried in a mountain, into whose burial site the Swedes deposited all their taxes for three years: Snorri, in the cited work, Part 1, Number 3, page 9.

Regarding **Chapter 11, Section 2, page 107**: Concerning the deified King of the Germans, Tuisco: Johannes Aventinus <note>A 16th-century Bavarian historian.</note> describes him in Book 1 of the *Annals of the Bavarians*, page 38. His words are: "Tuisco consecrated groves and forests in which divine matters were properly carried out. He believed that the celestial divinity, because of his greatness, should not be confined by walls." <note>original Latin: "Tuisco Lucos, & nemora in quibus res divina rité perpetraretur, consecravit. Arbitrabatur, cæleste numen pro magnitudine sua ne parietibus, Cohiberi."</note>

# Notes

...neither should [the divine] be modeled into any likeness of a human face or appearance, nor any fleeting thing, since that mystery <note>original: "secretum, illud"</note>, being pure from all contamination of earthly dregs, should be beheld with reverence alone. To seek its image and form is a mark of human weakness. He taught the discipline of **auspices** <note>The ancient practice of interpreting omens from the flight of birds.</note> and the casting of lots, from whose observation the priest, after publicly praying to God and looking up at the sky, would interpret future events. He ordered buildings to be made more for necessity, to avoid the harm of the weather, rather than for ambition. He commanded them to build small towns, yet in places naturally fortified. He appointed those who would dispense justice among their own people, establishing princes of regions and districts, and he commanded them to minimize controversies. He permitted no one to have a fixed amount of land or private boundaries. Instead, the magistrates and princes would gather every year with the tribes and families, assigning them as much land as they saw fit in whatever location, and a year later they would force them to move elsewhere. This was to prevent them from seeking to acquire wide borders, or the powerful from driving the humble from their possessions, or from building too carefully to avoid cold and heat, or from letting a greed for money arise, from which factions and dissensions are born. Thus, they maintained the common people with a sense of equity, as each saw his own wealth made equal to that of the most powerful. He ordered that food and clothing be easily procured, consisting of milk, cheese, meat, hides, and small coverings made of reindeer skins <note>original: "rhenonum"</note>. He restrained adultery with immediate punishment; there was no pardon for public unchastity. From early childhood, he commanded the offspring to apply themselves to hardship and labor, so that those who remained celibate <note>original: "impuberes"</note> the longest would receive the greatest praise among their own. He believed that this nourished their stature and strengthened their powers and sinews. He ordered that having knowledge of a woman before the twentieth year be considered among the most disgraceful things. And on page 40: when he had wisely and well completed one hundred and seventy-six years in his reign (for he completed more than two hundred years of life), he departed from this life in the three hundred and seventh year after the world was freed from the waters <note>A reference to the Biblical Great Flood.</note>. And because he was dear to those he ruled due to the merits of his virtues and services, his death left them with a great longing for him. Therefore, the ancients—by the common vote of all and because of the miracle of his wisdom and goodness—consecrated him as a native deity <note>original: "indigetem"</note>, an interpreter and messenger of God (for that is what **Tuisco** means in our language), and they began to hold him as a god. They also enrolled his mother **Hertha** <note>The Germanic goddess of the Earth.</note> (that is, the Earth, from which they believed he was brought forth) among the deities. See Johannes Aventinus <note>A 16th-century Bavarian historian and philologist known for his works on Germanic antiquity.</note>.

Regarding **Chapter 13, Section 1, page 117**: concerning the wicked idol of the Indians called **Drumo**: Sebastian Münster <note>A famous 16th-century German cartographer and scholar.</note> depicts him somewhat differently at the head and hands in Book 5 of his *Cosmography*, page 758.

Regarding **Chapter 17, Section 17, page 147**: Regarding the word ***Nenia*** <note>A Latin term for a funeral dirge or a magical incantation; here used for trifling songs.</note>, which otherwise signifies all sorts of ragged [trifling] songs: Horace <note>The Roman poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus.</note> in Book 1, Epistle 1: "Tell me, please, is the law better, or the children’s **song** <note>original: "NENIA"</note>, which offers the kingdom to those who act rightly?"

# Note.

...which Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher.</note> in Book 2 of *On the Nature of Things*, pages 221 and following, describes in the following manner:

> Therefore, she has been called the Great Mother of the gods, and the mother of wild beasts, and the lone progenitor of our own bodies. Of her the ancient, learned poets of the Greeks sang: that high in her chariot she drives two-yoked lions, teaching that the great Earth hangs in the space of the air, and that the earth cannot rest upon the earth. To her they joined wild beasts, because however wild the offspring, it ought to be softened and tamed by the duties of the parents. They encircled the top of her head with a mural crown <note>original: "murali... corona"; a crown shaped like city walls or battlements, symbolizing her protection of cities.</note>, because, fortified in distinguished places, she sustains the cities; endowed with this emblem, the image of the divine mother is now carried through great lands in a horrific <note>In this context, "horrific" implies "awe-inspiring" or "striking dread."</note> manner. Various nations, according to the ancient custom of sacred rites, call her the Idaean mother. They give her Phrygian bands as companions, because they say that from those borders, crops first began to be created across the orb of the earth. They assign her the Galli <note>original: "Gallos"; eunuch priests of Cybele.</note>, because they wish to signify that those who have violated the divinity of the Mother, and have been found ungrateful to their parents, should be thought unworthy to bring living offspring into the regions of light. Taut drums thunder under their palms, and hollow cymbals clash around; the horns threaten with a hoarse-sounding song, and the hollow pipe stimulates the mind with Phrygian rhythm. They carry weapons before them, signs of violent fury, which might terrify the ungrateful souls and impious hearts of the common folk with the fear of the goddess’s power. Therefore, as soon as she is carried through great cities, silently blessing mortals with a wordless greeting, they strew the entire path of the roads with copper and silver, enriching her with a lavish gift of coins; and they snow down flowers of roses, overshadowing the Mother and her bands of companions. Here an armed group—whom the Greeks call the Phrygian Curetes <note>original: "Curetas"; mythological armed dancers who protected the infant Jupiter.</note>—sometimes play with chains among themselves and leap in rhythm, joyful with blood, shaking the terrifying crests upon their heads with their movement. They represent the Dictaean Curetes, who are said to have once hidden that wailing of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note> in Crete, when the boys, in a swift dance around the boy—armed, they stood in rhythm—with a swift dance...

Thus far Lucretius, from whom Ovid took his own material.

**Regarding Chapter 27, Section 1, page 189.** Concerning the cited testimony of Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> from Book 1 of the *Divine Institutes*, which is "Of False Religion," chapter 21, page 57. The passage is transposed; the last three lines, "Innocent souls," etc., should come first.

**Regarding Chapter 29, Section 11, page 224.** Concerning the feasts of the early Christians which were held in the houses of God after the Holy Supper: whether these have their first origin in paganism—as cited in the text from Polidorus <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555), an Italian humanist priest who wrote on the "inventors" of things.</note> Book 5, Chapter 1, and Book 6, Chapters 4 and 7—or rather from Judaism, where after the completion of the sacrifice a holy meal was held in the Temple or Tabernacle: Leviticus 7:6, 15, 16; Deuteronomy 14:24, 26; 1 Samuel 9:13. I do not wish to argue with anyone: regarding this, one may read Philipp Johann Tilemann’s dissertation *On the Love Feasts of the Ancients* <note>original: "de Agapis Veterum." The "Agape" or love feast was a communal meal shared by early Christians.</note>, who holds another opinion on their origin, though without historical evidence.

**Regarding Chapter 30, Section 10, page 237.** Concerning the ancient groves of the Germans, established by their first kings and tribal ancestors; Johannes Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian humanist and pioneering historian.</note> describes these in his *Bavarian Chronicle* in the following words:

> Theodo dedicated a grove and a mountain near Regensburg <note>original: "Reginoburgium"</note>, overlooking the Danube, according to the custom of his ancestors, to the victorious Germanic Hercules <note>Roman writers often used the name "Hercules" to describe the Germanic god Thor or Donar.</note>, the protector of wars, and ordered it to be called by his name. There he commanded that sacrifices be performed according to the ancestral rite. That forest was later dedicated to the monks of Saint Emmeram <note>original: "D. Haimerani"</note>, following the old custom. There stood on the bank of the Danube, in the land of Germany, two very ancient oaks of prodigious size, twenty miles apart; one was named the Upper, the other the Lower. These also Bojus <note>The mythical ancestor of the Boii, or Bavarians.</note> consecrated with a pagan ceremony: there the people gathered in crowds and immolated victims. When the Bavarians <note>original: "Boji"</note> received the Christian religion, they converted these into temples, and thence into monasteries. Each place preserves its old name and is usually called Altaich, which in the Bavarian tongue signifies an "old oak." For our ancestors held nothing more sacred than the oak; they performed no sacred rites without the foliage of this tree, and after the sacrifices and feasts were duly carried out under this tree, they prayed to the gods. Thus far Johannes Aventinus, Book 3 of the *Annals of the Bavarians*, page 257.

**Regarding Chapter 30, Section 10, page 237.** Concerning the consecration and dedication of the ancient groves; regarding this, the words of Schedius <note>Elias Schedius (1615–1641), a scholar of Germanic antiquity.</note>, Book 2 of *On the German Gods*, chapter 24, page 346, read as follows: "The Druids, by their own consensus and that of all the people, would choose the most beautiful tree of the whole grove, and joined its outstretched branches from both sides again to the firm and main trunk higher up, so that those two arms were united to the stem at the top. Where the union of these occurred, they inscribed upon the bark the word *Tau* <note>original: "Thau"; the Greek letter T, which Schedius believed the Druids used as a symbol for God or a cross-like emblem.</note>, as well as on—"
