### Note.

...and lower down, where the arms extended, they similarly inscribed on the right branch the word Hesus <note>original: "Hefus" (Hesus), a powerful Gaulish god often associated with Mars or Mercury.</note>, on the center trunk Taranis <note>original: "To Tharamis," referring to the Celtic god of thunder.</note>, and on the left branch Belenus <note>A Celtic sun god.</note>. By this arrangement, they suggested that there was indeed one God, but in three persons; who nevertheless were only one God.

**Regarding Chapter 31, Section 9, page 252.** On the houses of idols on Heligoland <note>original: "Heyligland." **Regarding Chapter 32, Section 3, page 260.** The prophetesses advised King Ariovistus <note>A leader of the Suebi and other Germanic tribes who fought against Julius Caesar.</note> that he should not do battle with the Romans—add: before the new moon. Holy women, looking into the whirlpools of rivers and foretelling the future from the noise and surging of the waters, forbade them from fighting before the new moon. Plutarch, in *The Life of Julius Caesar*, Chapter 8, page 525. <note>original Latin: "Mulieres sacræ in vortices fluminum inspicientes..." This describes a form of hydromancy or divination by water practiced by Germanic tribes.</note>

**Regarding Chapter 36, Section 5, page 298 and following.** Because of the heart-stirring maxims on life and teaching by Seneca cited here and elsewhere, some have fallen into the erroneous thought that this philosopher might have been a Christian and exchanged letters with the Apostle Paul. This error is refuted by the Magnificent Doctor Christian Kortholt <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian (1633–1694).</note> in his *Historical Dissertation on the Christianity of Philip the Arab, Alexander Severus’s mother Julia Mamaea, Pliny the Younger, and Annaeus Seneca*. <note>The supposed correspondence between Paul and Seneca was a popular medieval legend, but was recognized as a forgery by Renaissance and Enlightenment scholars.</note>

**Regarding Chapter 44, the final section.** On the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses believed by many early Christians to have predicted the coming of Christ.</note> and their prophecies: The *Sibylline Oracles*, translated by Sebastian Castellio <note>A French theologian and humanist (1515–1563).</note>, were published by Xystus Betuleius with annotations in octavo, and by Johannes Opsopoeus of Brittany with notes in quarto. On the ten Sibyls, Onuphrius Panvinius <note>An Italian Augustinian friar and historian (1530–1568).</note> published a specialized book in octavo, in which he displays the images of them all, along with the testimonies of many philosophers and Church Fathers.

### Ben-hinnom
A beautiful, pleasant valley near the city of Jerusalem, where the Jews sacrificed their children to Moloch, 195. It is called Tophet, which means a drum or kettle-drum, because drums were beaten during the sacrifice of the children so that the parents might not hear the children's cries, ibid. It is also called Gehenna, that is, the Valley of Hinnom, by which the fires of hell are signified, because there the children were burned through the fire with woe and lamentation, ibid. It is called the Valley of Slaughter <note>original: "Würgethal"</note> because the Jews were slaughtered there by the Assyrians, ibid. It was laid waste by King Josiah because of the idolatry, ibid.

## To the Christian Reader!

The following are the larger printing errors: there are also many minor ones present, which were indeed noted, but have not been printed here. I have not been able to include the <term>Errata</term> <note>Latin: "errors."</note> in the <term>Citations of Authors and Places</term> <note>original: "Citatione Autorum & Locorum"</note> because the manuscript was not at hand, and various authors' books had been borrowed and returned to the aforementioned libraries. Furthermore, my physical weakness would not permit me to compare the printed text with the cited authors. In the preface to the Christian reader, I promised to append an index of the authors cited in this work to the back—authors I have had in my hands, numbering some three hundred and fifty books. However, due to bodily infirmity, I have not been able to fulfill this promise. Although the index of the authors' names is completed to that extent, I have nonetheless been unable to reach my study to record the authors in detail.

Where the Most High, according to His gracious will, grants further life and health, and if my ministry permits enough remaining hours, I intend, through His grace, to continue the begun <term>Cimbrian Church History</term> <note>The "Cimbri" were an ancient Germanic people; here, the term refers to the regional history of the North German or Danish territories.</note> and to publish it in several more parts.
